paper_profiles.title: Clinical Laboratory Diagnostics and Medical Biotechnology: Principles and Applications
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This publication is a broad textbook-style treatment of clinical laboratory diagnostics and medical biotechnology, covering foundational concepts, techniques, and applications across laboratory medicine, biochemical testing, immunological testing, molecular diagnostics, and automation. It discusses how laboratory technologies support diagnosis, monitoring, and decision-making in healthcare, with extensive attention to laboratory workflows, sample handling, quality control, and emerging technologies.

The book does not investigate an educational intervention or a K-12 instructional technology. It is aimed at healthcare/laboratory audiences and functions as a reference overview rather than an empirical study. No K-12 mathematics instruction, generative AI tutoring, or classroom implementation features are reported in the provided text; the content is entirely about clinical diagnostics and biotechnology in adult healthcare contexts.

Because the text is a general scholarly/technical volume rather than an empirical research study, there are no measurable effects, sample sizes, or outcome data to extract for K-12 education outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Chemistry Unveiled: Understanding the Science of Substances
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length work presents an introductory, concept-focused treatment of chemistry for learners, emphasizing how chemical ideas are interconnected rather than isolated. Across chapters on fundamental concepts, atoms and elements, the periodic table, chemical reactions, and other topics, it argues for a more integrated approach to teaching chemistry and repeatedly uses explanatory prose, examples, and suggested laboratory-style activities to make the subject more coherent and accessible.

The text does not report a formal empirical study, intervention trial, or measured outcomes. Instead, it is an educationally oriented publication that reviews core chemistry content and advocates for instructional strategies such as using historical context, structured questions, and laboratory exercises to support understanding. Because the content is presented as narrative exposition rather than research with participants, the paper is best characterized as qualitative/educational descriptive material rather than an empirical study.

The publication is not focused on K-12 mathematics instruction or generative AI tutoring. Its substantive focus is chemistry education, primarily at a general or undergraduate level, with attention to conceptual understanding and instructional organization. No outcome data, effect sizes, or learner-level results are reported.

paper_profiles.title: Clinical Engineering and Medical Physics: A Synergistic Approach to Patient Safety and Technology Management
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length chapter collection examines the roles of clinical engineering and medical physics in improving patient safety, technology management, and risk reduction in healthcare settings. Rather than studying an educational intervention or AI system, it offers a conceptual and practice-oriented discussion of how technical expertise, human factors engineering, and interdisciplinary collaboration can improve the acquisition, monitoring, maintenance, and governance of medical technologies.

The text emphasizes that patient safety problems are often not solved by piecemeal initiatives, but instead require systems thinking, better reporting and monitoring, stronger regulatory frameworks, and closer collaboration among engineers, physicists, clinicians, and administrators. It also discusses educational and training needs within medical physics and clinical engineering, along with case-study examples of collaborative technology evaluation and implementation. No generative AI tutoring or K-12 mathematics instruction is described in the provided text; the work is focused on healthcare technology management and safety in adult clinical contexts.

paper_profiles.title: Molecular Mechanisms in Physiology: Insights from Medicinal Chemistry
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length essay surveys molecular mechanisms in physiology through the lens of medicinal chemistry. It is organized as a conceptual review of how proteins, nucleic acids, lipids, receptors, enzymes, transporters, and other molecular targets support physiological function and how these concepts inform drug discovery, drug design, and structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis.

The work is framed as an interdisciplinary educational resource rather than an empirical study. It emphasizes molecular modeling, biochemical reasoning, and the translation of molecular interactions into therapeutic development, with chapters covering physiology, medicinal chemistry fundamentals, drug targets, SAR, and future directions. The text does not describe an intervention, participants, data collection, or outcome evaluation in K-12 education or in generative AI tutoring; instead, it presents a narrative overview of biomedical concepts and research trends.

Because the document is a conceptual/pedagogical book chapter collection with no reported empirical study design, sample, or measured outcomes, it does not provide evidence about educational effectiveness. Its main contribution is descriptive: synthesizing scientific concepts and arguing for interdisciplinary understanding across physiology, chemistry, and biology.

paper_profiles.title: Biomedical Engineering: Principles, Applications, and Future Trends
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This volume is a broad introductory textbook-style treatment of biomedical engineering rather than an empirical study of AI in education or K-12 mathematics instruction. It surveys foundational concepts and major subfields of biomedical engineering, including biomaterials, biomechanics, bioinstrumentation, biomedical signal processing, medical imaging, rehabilitation engineering, and drug delivery systems.

The text’s purpose is educational and descriptive: it explains core principles, common applications in healthcare, and emerging trends in the field. It does not present a research question, intervention, sample, or evaluation of outcomes; instead, it provides narrative background for students and practitioners interested in biomedical engineering education and career pathways.

Because the provided text contains no study methods, participant data, or empirical results related to generative AI tutoring, K-12 instruction, or mathematics learning, there are no extractable outcome findings aligned to the requested education research framework. The document appears to be a publisher-issued book chapter compilation with a general instructional orientation, not an empirical education study.

paper_profiles.title: Health Statistics: Principles and Applications in Public Health
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-length volume is a general educational text on health statistics and epidemiological methods in public health. It is organized into chapters covering descriptive statistics, epidemiological measures, statistical inference, data visualization, health disparities, surveillance systems, research methods, data integrity, health informatics, policy, and emerging trends. The text explains foundational statistical concepts, definitions, and formulas, and repeatedly frames them as tools for planning, implementing, and evaluating public health programs.

The volume does not evaluate an AI tutoring intervention, generative AI integration, or K-12 mathematics instruction. Instead, it presents conceptual instruction for public health students and practitioners, with examples drawn from epidemiology and health data analysis. The only pedagogical implementation features mentioned are broad references to using computer software such as SAS and incorporating examples and exercises; no empirical study design, sample, outcomes, or comparisons are reported.

Because the source is a textbook/publisher book rather than an empirical research study, it does not provide data on learning gains or implementation effects. Its contribution is instructional and reference-oriented, focused on statistical literacy for adult learners in public health contexts rather than K-12 education or mathematics tutoring.

paper_profiles.title: Future and Innovations in Medical Physics
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This volume is an edited book chapter collection on contemporary and future directions in medical physics, including imaging, radiation therapy, telemedicine, workforce development, and artificial intelligence. The material is primarily descriptive and review-oriented, summarizing technical advances and their anticipated implications for clinical practice, professional training, and remote education in medical physics.

The portions most relevant to education discuss teleteaching and remote instruction in medical physics departments. The text argues that live, interactive audio-video teaching systems can support training for students, residents, and other professionals when on-site instruction is limited, and it outlines practical considerations for implementing transcontinental teleteaching systems. However, the book does not report a controlled study, sample, or quantitative evaluation of outcomes; it is largely a conceptual and narrative overview rather than empirical research.

Although the opening abstract mentions education and skill development, the overall work is not focused on K-12 schooling, mathematics instruction, or generative AI tutoring. Its references to artificial intelligence are in the context of medical imaging and radiology, not educational tutoring systems. As a result, the paper has no substantive empirical findings for K-12 learning outcomes and should be treated as a low-evidence, descriptive source.

paper_profiles.title: Essential Health Statistics: From Theory to Practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book-style volume presents a broad, conceptual overview of health statistics, covering foundational definitions, historical development, measurement concepts, data sources, and statistical methods used in public health. The text is organized into chapters on topics such as prevalence and incidence, mortality rates, morbidity indicators, surveys and questionnaires, administrative data, registries, and statistical software, with extensive expository discussion and illustrative formulas/examples rather than a formal empirical study.

The work does not examine an AI or generative-AI tutoring intervention, nor does it address K-12 mathematics instruction. Instead, it serves as a descriptive reference on how health statistics are collected, interpreted, and applied in public health practice. The only context and population implied are adult readers in health statistics/public health, likely including educators or practitioners. No experimental design, comparison group, or outcome evaluation is reported, and the text appears to be a chaptered instructional/edited book rather than a research article.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (broad educational contexts; includes elementary, middle/high school, university, and teacher audiences)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT/GPT-3-style systems, for education. Rather than testing an intervention experimentally, the authors synthesize early applications and propose a framework for where LLMs may support learning and teaching, including content generation, personalized practice, tutoring, feedback, assessment support, and task automation.

The paper discusses use cases across educational levels, with examples relevant to elementary, secondary, tertiary, and professional learning. It highlights potential benefits such as improved engagement, tailored explanations, quiz generation, and support for writing, problem solving, and teacher workload reduction. It also emphasizes limitations and risks, including hallucinations, bias, copyright and plagiarism concerns, privacy and security issues, overreliance by learners and teachers, inequitable access, and the need for human oversight and curricular integration.

Overall, the paper argues that LLMs are promising but immature educational technologies. The authors conclude that responsible adoption requires pedagogical guidance, critical thinking and fact-checking practices, transparency, governance, and further empirical research on effectiveness and best practices before broad educational deployment.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or accelerating tasks such as quiz generation, feedback, grading support, lesson planning, and assessment. No original empirical effect estimate is reported; the paper relies on cited examples and conceptual claims rather than a controlled study.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, and time required to create instructional materials

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames LLMs as tools that can support problem-solving, critical thinking, and fact-checking through explanations, step-by-step solutions, and prompts for deeper questioning. It also warns that overreliance on model-generated answers may weaken learners’ independent reasoning and problem-solving, so the net effect is presented as mixed and contingent on how the tools are used.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking-related learning processes

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs may improve student engagement, participation, and curiosity, particularly through conversational support and curiosity-prompting pedagogical agents. These claims are illustrative and based on early cited work, not on new quantitative findings in this paper.
finding.measure: Engagement, participation, and curiosity expression

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support reading and writing development by offering summaries, explanations, grammar and style corrections, and assistance with research and writing tasks. The evidence presented is conceptual and literature-based, without original outcome data or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, writing quality, grammar/style improvement

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLMs may support middle and high school mathematics learning by generating practice problems, providing explanations, step-by-step solutions, and related questions, and by helping students understand reasoning behind solutions. No empirical mathematics achievement results are reported in the paper itself.
finding.measure: Mathematics practice, understanding of solutions, and problem solving

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education, asking how the field has developed, how AI is conceptualized, what ethical challenges and risks are discussed, and what kinds of AI applications are being studied. The authors screened 2,656 records from three databases and included 146 peer-reviewed journal articles published between 2007 and November 2018.

The review organizes the literature into four main application areas: profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems/personalisation. Across the corpus, most studies were quantitative, focused on undergraduate settings, and authored primarily by researchers in Computer Science or STEM rather than Education. The review finds that AI applications are often presented as technically promising for prediction, feedback, tutoring, and personalization, but most studies are short-term pilots with limited longitudinal evidence.

A major conclusion is that the field shows very little critical reflection on ethical implications, challenges, and risks: only a small number of papers explicitly define AI, and only two papers critically discuss ethics or privacy concerns. The authors argue that AI in higher education is being developed faster than educators’ pedagogical and ethical frameworks, and call for more theoretically grounded, educationally informed, and ethically reflective research.

finding.finding_summary: The review finds that AI applications, especially profiling/prediction, automated grading, and tutoring systems, are frequently framed as tools to reduce administrative or instructional workload. For example, the authors note that machine learning models predicted admission, dropout, and performance with high accuracy, and that automated grading systems achieved computer-human agreement of 94.6% to 98.2%, suggesting potential efficiency gains rather than direct learning impact.
finding.measure: Prediction accuracy, computer-human agreement in grading, and reported workload-reduction potential
finding.study_size: n=146 studies in review; individual studies varied

finding.finding_summary: The strongest direct academic-learning evidence in the review concerns intelligent tutoring systems and adaptive systems that teach subject content, provide feedback, and personalize materials across disciplines such as computer science, mathematics, statistics, medicine, and writing. The review reports mostly positive or satisfactory preliminary results in short-term pilots, with one cited meta-analysis of 39 ITS studies finding a moderate effect on student learning and that ITS outperformed traditional instruction, though still lagging behind human tutoring.
finding.measure: Student learning performance, course-level outcomes, and learning gains in ITS/adaptive system studies
finding.study_size: n=29 ITS studies; broader review n=146
finding.effect_size: moderate effect (meta-analysis cited); exact value not reported

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies focused on student engagement, motivation, self-regulation, and related behavioral indicators. The review summarizes that machine learning was used to evaluate student engagement and that adaptive/ITS interventions often reported positive preliminary results for supporting students, identifying low-engagement learners, and encouraging revision or persistence, although the evidence base was mostly short-term and not longitudinal.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, and self-regulation indicators; VLE clicks and behavioral data in some studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper includes studies on collaboration, problem-solving dialogue, and adaptive support for group work, indicating that some AI tools were intended to support durable skills such as collaboration and problem solving. Reported findings were generally positive or promising, but the review emphasizes that these studies were few and mostly pilot-scale, limiting confidence in their educational impact.
finding.measure: Collaborative learning processes, dialogue/problem-solving interactions, and group-work support

paper_profiles.title: Design an Intelligent System to automatically Tutor the Method for Solving Problems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the design of an intelligent tutoring chatbot intended to guide users through problem solving by combining a knowledge base, hint questions, sample problems, and tutoring scripts. The system is framed as an Intelligent Problem Solver (IPS) and is meant to simulate an instructor by asking step-by-step questions, providing hints, and eventually showing full solutions when needed.

The authors apply the architecture to two contexts: (1) high-school mathematics, especially the Vietnamese high-school topic of surveying a function, and (2) public administration consulting for online printing-license procedures in Vietnam. The mathematics component is positioned as a tutor assistant for 12th-grade students, while the public-administration component helps citizens identify the right documents and procedure steps. The paper is primarily a system-design and prototype-evaluation study rather than a controlled educational experiment.

For the mathematics use case, the chatbot is tested on exercises collected from Vietnamese exams and textbooks, and the paper reports that it can solve several standard exercise types and tutor learners step-by-step. The authors report that the system works best for routine problems and is less flexible for harder cases requiring additional knowledge domains or complex reasoning. Overall, the paper concludes that the tutoring architecture is promising for interactive problem solving, but it needs further improvement for more difficult and less structured tasks.

finding.finding_summary: The chatbot was tested on five types of high-school mathematics exercises about surveying a function. Across the reported test set, it solved 20/20 exercises for kind 1 (100%), 21/25 for kind 2 (84%), 20/24 for kind 3 (83%), 7/9 for kind 4 (78%), and 25/28 for kind 5 (89%), indicating that it could handle many routine problems and guide students step-by-step.
finding.measure: Number and proportion of solved high-school mathematics exercises about surveying a function
finding.study_size: n=106 exercises total across five kinds

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (commentary/opinion article; discusses students broadly, including undergraduate, vocational, and high school examples)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion article examines the promise and risks of artificial intelligence in education, framing AI as a potential cognitive enhancer as well as a source of cognitive erosion. The authors organize the discussion around Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory to argue that AI can improve personalization, efficiency, and access while also encouraging cognitive offloading, reduced retention, weaker critical thinking, and lower intrinsic motivation if used excessively.

Rather than reporting new empirical data, the paper synthesizes prior studies and illustrative examples on AI-assisted learning, including conversational AI, adaptive learning systems, and AI tutoring. It highlights evidence that AI may improve procedural performance and standardized test scores, but can also depress conceptual understanding, memory retention, and higher-order thinking when students rely too heavily on AI-generated support.

The article’s main conclusion is that AI should complement, not replace, human instruction. The authors recommend careful implementation: align AI use with learning goals, preserve teacher guidance, prompt reflection and AI-free problem solving, and address fairness, transparency, and bias. The paper is best read as a conceptual and normative framework for responsible AI integration rather than as an empirical evaluation of a specific intervention.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI-based tutoring can improve standardized test performance and procedural practice, but may also weaken conceptual understanding. It cites a Stanford-related example of a 15% increase in scores with AI platforms versus traditional instruction, and a University of Pennsylvania example in which students using ChatGPT answered 48% more problems correctly but scored 17% lower on a concept-understanding test.
finding.measure: Standardized test scores; concept understanding test; problem-solving practice accuracy
finding.effect_size: 15% score increase; 48% more problems correct; 17% lower concept-understanding score

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims that over-reliance on AI may reduce motivation, engagement, and intrinsic drive to learn independently. It also notes that AI can erode autonomy and relatedness if it replaces human interaction and self-directed effort, though these claims are presented as risks drawn from prior literature rather than results from a new study.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, autonomy, relatedness

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that AI can support lower-order cognitive tasks but may undermine durable skills such as critical thinking, problem solving, and metacognition when students depend on AI outputs without scrutiny. The article cites prior work suggesting reduced active recall and cognitive engagement, along with examples where AI-assisted learners performed better on immediate tasks but may have weaker deep understanding.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem solving, higher-order thinking, memory retention

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses institutional risks and design considerations for AI adoption, especially algorithmic bias, fairness, transparency, and the need for monitoring and feedback systems. These are framed as implementation concerns and governance implications rather than measured institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Fairness/bias, transparency, implementation monitoring

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing healthcare: the role of artificial intelligence in clinical practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical practice, focusing on how machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and large language models are being applied across healthcare settings. The paper asks how AI can improve diagnosis, treatment selection, laboratory testing, population health management, patient education, and decision support, while also noting ethical, legal, privacy, and bias-related concerns.

Methodologically, the authors conducted a broad literature review of indexed studies from PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and EMBASE with no time restrictions and English-language limits. The review is not a primary intervention study; instead, it synthesizes examples of AI applications such as diagnostic imaging, predictive analytics, virtual assistants, personalized medicine, and therapeutic drug monitoring. Across these areas, the paper concludes that AI can improve accuracy, efficiency, and cost-effectiveness, but that responsible adoption requires high-quality data, human oversight, transparency, and safeguards against bias, hallucination, privacy breaches, and cybersecurity risks.

Although the review briefly mentions intelligent tutoring systems and notes that AI has improved learning outcomes in math and science, those claims are peripheral and not the paper’s substantive focus. The article is primarily about healthcare rather than K-12 education, so it does not provide comparative evidence on generative AI tutoring or mathematics achievement in school settings.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI has broad potential to improve healthcare delivery, but implementation requires governance, data quality, human oversight, and regulatory safeguards. It emphasizes benefits such as improved accuracy, efficiency, and decision support, alongside risks including bias, privacy breaches, hallucination, and cybersecurity threats; no pooled effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Narrative synthesis of AI implementation, governance, privacy, bias, and cybersecurity considerations in healthcare systems

paper_profiles.title: Editorial: Generative AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial introduces a Frontiers Research Topic on generative AI in education and summarizes the 11 included papers. The piece frames generative AI as a set of tools that may personalize content, feedback, assessment, and tutoring, while also raising concerns about accuracy, interpretability, ethics, privacy, and the emotional tone of AI responses.

Rather than reporting a single empirical study, the article synthesizes the themes and findings of the included papers. It highlights examples spanning AI-generated feedback, adolescent schoolwork use, critical thinking, mathematical proof support, whole-learner modeling, personalized assessment, AI mentoring, integrity, interactive listening tasks, and deception detection in educational robots. The editorial's main conclusion is that generative AI shows promise for learning support and assessment, but that further research is needed to establish effectiveness, fairness, and responsible implementation.

Because the paper is an editorial, it does not present original data on K-12 mathematics achievement or tutoring outcomes. It mentions one included paper on pre-service teachers' mathematical reasoning and proof construction with ChatGPT, but this is not a K-12 student achievement study and no comparative effect estimates are reported in the editorial itself.

finding.finding_summary: The editorial does not report any original empirical findings on K-12 mathematics achievement or generative AI tutoring. It only references a separate paper on pre-service teachers using ChatGPT to construct mathematical proofs, without effect sizes or comparative outcome data in this editorial.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: How Does ChatGPT Perform on the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE)? The Implications of Large Language Models for Medical Education and Knowledge Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates whether ChatGPT can answer multiple-choice medical knowledge questions drawn from the USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 context, and whether its responses are interpretable enough to function as a tutoring tool. The authors tested ChatGPT on four question sets: AMBOSS Step 1 and Step 2 questions, and NBME free Step 1 and Step 2 questions. They also compared ChatGPT’s performance with GPT-3 and InstructGPT, and qualitatively assessed the presence of logical reasoning, internal question information, and external information in ChatGPT’s explanations.

ChatGPT achieved 44% and 42% accuracy on the AMBOSS Step 1 and Step 2 sets, respectively, and 64.4% and 57.8% accuracy on the NBME free Step 1 and Step 2 sets, outperforming GPT-3 and InstructGPT across all datasets. Performance declined as question difficulty increased in AMBOSS Step 1 without the Attending Tip (P=.01), and the Attending Tip generally improved performance. The model’s responses were almost always logically articulated, usually included internal question information, and correct answers were more likely than incorrect answers to incorporate external information. The authors conclude that ChatGPT shows promise as an interactive medical education tool, but they also note limitations related to training-data cutoff, model closedness, and version drift.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered USMLE-style medical knowledge questions above chance and at or near a passing threshold on the NBME free Step 1 set. Accuracy was 64.4% (56/87) on NBME-Free-Step1, 57.8% (59/102) on NBME-Free-Step2, 44% (44/100) on AMBOSS-Step1, and 42% (42/100) on AMBOSS-Step2, indicating stronger performance on the more exam-like NBME items and weaker performance on harder AMBOSS items.
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice medical knowledge questions (USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 style items)

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s secondary qualitative analysis suggests ChatGPT can support explanation, reasoning, and follow-up discussion in a tutoring-like format. All ChatGPT responses contained logical reasoning, 96.8% (183/189) contained internal information, and correct responses were more likely than incorrect responses to include external information (NBME-Free-Step1: 92.9% vs 48.4%, P<.001; NBME-Free-Step2: 89.8% vs 62.8%, P=.001).
finding.measure: Narrative coherence / explanation quality indicators (logical reasoning, internal information, external information)
finding.study_size: n=189 NBME free questions for qualitative analysis

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that ChatGPT may improve study efficiency by serving as an on-demand interactive tutor, but they did not directly measure productivity or time savings. The strongest empirical support is indirect: the model produced coherent explanations on every response and could be queried in a dialogic format, which the authors frame as potentially useful for self-directed learning and small-group-style review.
finding.measure: Qualitative assessment of dialogic output and interpretability
finding.study_size: n=189 NBME free questions for qualitative analysis

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) has been used in higher education from 2016 through 2022, addressing a field-level question rather than testing a single intervention. The authors used PRISMA methods to identify 138 peer-reviewed journal articles and coded them for geography, author affiliation, academic level, subject domain, intended user, and functional use of AI.

The review found that AI in higher education research expanded sharply in 2021–2022, with most studies conducted in Asia and the United States/China shift noted in publication leadership. Undergraduate students were the most commonly studied population, and the most frequent subject domains were language learning, computer science, and engineering. The most common uses of AI were assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The paper concludes that the field is growing quickly but remains concentrated in high-income countries and undergraduate contexts, with relatively little work on graduate learners, low-income settings, or managerial uses of AI.

Because this is a broad systematic review of higher education AI research, it does not report effect sizes for a specific generative AI tutoring intervention or K-12 mathematics outcomes. Its main contribution is mapping research trends, use cases, and gaps, including a call for more work on emerging tools such as ChatGPT and more attention to pedagogical and ethical implications.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI was frequently used to increase efficiency in assessment, feedback, predictive analytics, and learning management in higher education. Examples included automatic grading, automatic question generation, learning analytics dashboards, and instructional design support; however, the paper reports counts of studies rather than effect sizes for these efficiencies. The synthesis suggests AI can reduce instructor workload and support data-driven decision-making, but no pooled quantitative impact estimate is provided.
finding.measure: Review coding of AI use cases related to assessment/evaluation, automatic grading, question generation, learning analytics, instructional design, and student-data management

finding.finding_summary: The review identified studies in which AI supported student motivation, persistence, emotion support, and self-regulated learning. For example, AI assistants and intelligent tutoring systems provided diagnostic questions, goal support, personalized feedback, and adaptive guidance, and some assessment systems were used to analyze affect as well as achievement. The paper summarizes these uses qualitatively and does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Review coding of AI uses involving emotion, persistence, self-regulation, and engagement support

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that AI was used in ways that can support metacognition, higher-order thinking, and personalized problem solving, especially through intelligent tutoring systems, feedback systems, and learning analytics. It cites studies evaluating online reflections, achievement goals, community identification, and higher-order thinking, but these are descriptive findings from a review rather than a meta-analytic estimate. No effect size or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Review coding of AI uses related to higher-order thinking, reflection, and adaptive problem solving support

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics appears in the paper mainly as one of several subject domains and through examples such as an online mathematics course and AI support for performance regulation, but mathematics is not a central empirical focus of the review. The review does not synthesize mathematics-specific achievement outcomes or provide effect sizes; instead, it notes that AI was used across subject areas including engineering, language learning, and some mathematics-related contexts. Because of this limited and indirect treatment, the evidence for this outcome is weak within the paper.
finding.measure: Review coding of subject-domain and use-case mentions, including an online mathematics course example

paper_profiles.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory study asks whether a generative AI tutor can safely and effectively support secondary school students in mathematics classrooms. The authors focus on LearnLM, a pedagogy-fine-tuned generative model integrated into the Eedi math platform, and compare it against static, pre-written hints and against human tutor-led chat support.

The study was conducted across five UK secondary schools with 165 Year 9–10 students (ages 13–15). Students were randomly assigned to receive either static hints or interactive tutoring, and tutoring sessions were further randomized to human tutors alone or human-supervised LearnLM. Expert tutors reviewed every AI draft message before it was sent to students, allowing the authors to assess safety, pedagogical quality, immediate mistake correction, misconception resolution, and transfer to the next topic.

The findings suggest that supervised LearnLM was safe, with tutors approving most messages and identifying no harmful content in the audited corpus. For near-term learning outcomes, LearnLM performed about as well as human tutors: students corrected mistakes on the second attempt at similarly high rates and resolved misconceptions at comparable rates. On the transfer outcome, LearnLM outperformed human tutoring alone, with a 5.5 percentage point higher probability of solving a novel problem on the next topic (66.2% vs. 60.7%; 95% credible interval for the difference: -1.4 to +12.4 points), indicating a possible advantage for deeper knowledge transfer.

The study also includes qualitative evidence from tutor interviews and surveys. Tutors generally viewed LearnLM as producing strong Socratic dialogue and helping them work more efficiently, but noted that human supervision remained important for pacing, student affect, and social-emotional nuance. The authors emphasize that this was an exploratory, session-level RCT focused on short-term classroom outcomes in mathematics, so longer-term effects and generalization beyond math remain untested.

finding.finding_summary: Across three math learning outcomes, supervised LearnLM was at least as effective as human tutors for immediate remediation and misconception resolution, and better for transfer to the next topic. Students with LearnLM answered the repeated question correctly on the second attempt 93.0% of the time versus 91.2% for human tutoring and 65.4% for static hints; for misconception resolution the rates were 95.4% versus 94.9% and 86.8%, respectively. For knowledge transfer to the next unit, LearnLM achieved 66.2% correct versus 60.7% for human tutoring, a difference of 5.5 percentage points [95% credible interval: -1.4, +12.4].
finding.measure: Mistake remediation, misconception resolution, and knowledge transfer on Eedi mathematics study units
finding.effect_size: 5.5 percentage point difference for transfer; other outcomes not_reported
finding.confidence_interval: [-1.4%, +12.4%] for transfer difference; not_reported for other outcomes

finding.finding_summary: Student survey responses suggested generally favorable perceptions of the tutoring experience, with interactive tutoring rated slightly more helpful than static hints. Students who received interactive tutoring rated helpfulness at 3.9 [3.1, 4.7] out of 5, compared with 3.6 [2.9, 4.2] for static hints, indicating a modest positive experience effect rather than a large behavioral outcome.
finding.measure: Post-trial student helpfulness ratings of tutoring support

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s strongest durable-skill-relevant outcome is knowledge transfer, interpreted by the authors as students' ability to apply learning to a new topic. Relative to human tutors alone, LearnLM increased the probability of solving the first question in the next unit by 5.5 percentage points, with a 66.2% success rate versus 60.7% for human tutoring; the authors report 93.6% credibility for LearnLM’s advantage over human tutors.
finding.measure: Knowledge transfer to a new mathematics topic in the next study unit

finding.finding_summary: Supervising tutors reported that LearnLM made tutoring more fluid and efficient, especially by supporting multiple students at the same time. In post-trial surveys, 82.4% of tutors selected “supporting multiple students at the same time” as LearnLM’s most useful feature, and tutor comfort with AI rose from 3.4 [2.9, 4.0] to 3.9 [3.3, 4.4] out of 5 (posterior probability of increase: 90.0%).
finding.measure: Tutor surveys and interviews on workflow, AI comfort, and simultaneous student support
finding.study_size: n=17 tutors; n=5 interviewees; n=17 survey respondents

paper_profiles.title: Combining Large Language Models with Tutoring System Intelligence: A Case Study in Caregiver Homework Support
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2025 (The 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how large language models (LLMs) can be combined with intelligent tutoring system (ITS) data and instructional principles to generate better conversational support for caregivers helping children with math homework. The authors build the Caregiver Conversational Support Tool (CCST), which uses real-time tutoring-system context such as correctness, hint use, and next solution steps to prompt Llama 3 to generate caregiver chat recommendations. They evaluate prompt designs qualitatively and then conduct prototyping interviews with ten middle school caregivers.

The intervention is not a student-facing tutoring treatment, but a caregiver-facing conversational support layer embedded in a middle-school equation-solving ITS (Lynnette). The study combines prompt engineering experiments with a design/prototyping study in which caregivers interacted with the tool during simulated homework support sessions, both in-person and over Zoom. Caregivers were asked about message tone, length, usefulness, and the value of content-level versus motivational support.

The main conclusion is that integrating tutoring-system context and tutoring-practice examples into LLM prompts substantially improves the relevance and pedagogical quality of generated caregiver messages. Caregivers preferred messages that gave concrete content help and prompted student self-explanation/metacognition over purely motivational messages. The paper also identifies practical limitations, especially message latency and the need for more personalized, concise, and context-sensitive outputs. It argues that LLMs can be more instructionally reliable when grounded in ITS data, but the evidence here is design-based and qualitative rather than an achievement-impact evaluation.

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on middle-school equation solving support in an ITS, but it does not measure student math achievement directly. Instead, it shows that prompt designs using tutoring-system context produced more contextually relevant and pedagogically appropriate math-help recommendations, and caregivers judged these to be the most desirable. No effect size or achievement outcome is reported.
finding.measure: Quality of LLM-generated math tutoring recommendations for caregiver support in equation solving; caregiver perceptions of usefulness
finding.study_size: n=10 caregivers for prototype evaluation; prompt engineering examples about 50-80 generated responses per round

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers strongly preferred recommendations that prompted student self-explanation and other metacognitive behaviors, indicating support for metacognitive skill development. Five caregivers explicitly valued prompts that asked students to explain their thinking, because these helped caregivers better understand student reasoning and identify knowledge gaps. No quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Caregiver preference for metacognitive/self-explanation prompt types

finding.finding_summary: The tool’s conversational recommendations were generally viewed as feasible, but latency was a limitation. Six of nine caregivers found messages too long, and two of six caregivers felt generation was somewhat slow; average latency was about 25 seconds, which sometimes reduced usefulness during live tutoring. No quantitative productivity or workload effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Perceived message length, generation latency, and usability/feasibility of caregiver support during live tutoring

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging LLMs to Assess Tutor Moves in Real-Life Dialogues: A Feasibility Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This feasibility study asks whether large language models can reliably identify and evaluate specific tutoring moves in authentic, real-world math tutoring dialogues. The broader motivation is to support scalable analysis of tutoring quality, since manually coding tutoring transcripts is time-intensive and limits research on what tutor behaviors are most associated with learning.

The authors analyzed 50 randomly selected audio transcripts from remote, college-student tutors working with middle school students in mathematics. They focused on two tutor skills: providing effective praise and responding appropriately to student math errors. Multiple LLMs were tested, including GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and LearnLM, using iterative prompt engineering approaches such as few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought, rationale forcing, and self-consistency.

Results show that the models performed well on both detection and evaluation tasks. They identified praise with 94–98% accuracy and math errors with 82–88% accuracy, and they assessed tutor quality with 83–89% accuracy for praise and 73–77% for error responses. The authors conclude that LLMs can be useful for scalable assessment of tutor moves in authentic settings, although error-response evaluation is harder than detection and the study is limited by the absence of video, screenshots, chat logs, and sometimes unclear speaker attribution in transcripts.

finding.finding_summary: The study is about using LLMs to assess tutor moves in middle school mathematics dialogues, not student learning outcomes. Across 50 transcripts, the models identified tutor praise with 94–98% accuracy and student math errors with 82–88% accuracy, and graded tutor responses with 83–89% accuracy for praise and 73–77% for error responses. These results indicate strong feasibility for evaluating tutoring practices in math contexts, but they do not estimate an instructional effect on mathematics achievement or conceptual understanding.
finding.measure: LLM accuracy for detecting and evaluating tutor moves in math tutoring transcripts
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap percentile CIs reported for model accuracies (e.g., praise detection 94–100%; error detection 70–96%; praise evaluation 75–95%; error evaluation 62–87%, model-specific)

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Generation of Question Hints for Mathematics Problems using Large Language Models in Educational Technology
paper_profiles.venue: FM-EduAssess at NeurIPS 2024 Workshop (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can be used to generate pedagogically useful hints for mathematics problems in an intelligent tutoring-system setting. The authors focus on a core challenge in generative-AI tutoring: producing hints that help students self-correct without giving away the answer, while still aligning with the intended cognitive approach and the specific error made by the learner.

The study uses secondary-level math exercises from the MIA Seconde educational software, designed for French high-school students. Because the goal is to test hint-generation behavior before deployment with real learners, the authors simulate both students and teachers with LLMs: GPT-3.5-turbo, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 act as students, while GPT-4o and Llama-3-8B-Instruct act as teachers. The pipeline first generates and classifies student errors across multiple temperatures, then tests several hint prompts—specialized prompts tied to error types and baseline prompts that do not use the student's original response.

Main findings are that higher temperature increases error diversity and error frequency, especially for student-model problem solving, and that the best hint prompts are the calculation-based specialized prompt and the BaselineTwo generic prompt. Hints from both GPT-4o and Llama-3-8B-Instruct improved student-model revision accuracy, with GPT-3.5-turbo showing the largest self-correction gains after receiving hints. Unexpectedly, Llama-3-8B-Instruct often outperformed GPT-4o as teacher, but the authors caution that hint quality and pedagogical relevance still require qualitative human evaluation. The paper concludes that LLM-based hint generation is promising for math tutoring, but current results are limited by the small number of exercises, reliance on simulated students, and lack of qualitative assessment of hint quality.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that hint generation by LLM teachers improved math problem-solving revision accuracy for simulated student models across four high-school math exercises. Using the best prompts, especially the calculation-error specialized prompt and BaselineTwo, student models often corrected previously incorrect answers; the largest gains were observed for GPT-3.5-turbo, while Llama-3-8B-Instruct teacher prompts frequently produced the strongest overall accuracy.
finding.measure: Accuracy on solving math exercises and accuracy after hint-guided revision of incorrect answers
finding.study_size: n=4 exercises; 40 simulations per exercise for error generation and 10 repetitions per incorrect response during hint evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies whether LLM-generated hints support self-correction and response revision, which is closely related to problem solving and metacognitive adjustment. The authors find that student models could revise answers more successfully after receiving hints, with temperature and prompt design moderating the extent of self-correction.
finding.measure: Revision success / self-correction after receiving hints
finding.study_size: n=4 exercises; repeated across 10 prompt repetitions per incorrect response

paper_profiles.title: Hierarchical Pedagogical Oversight: A Multi-Agent Adversarial Framework for Reliable AI Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of unreliable LLM-based tutoring, especially in mathematics, where models may validate incorrect student reasoning (sycophancy) or give overly direct answers that reduce learning value. The authors argue that existing multi-agent tutoring systems can drift toward superficial agreement, and propose Hierarchical Pedagogical Oversight (HPO) as an adversarial multi-agent framework to improve pedagogical judgment.

HPO uses a three-phase pipeline: (1) intelligence distillation by specialist agents that extract the mathematical concept, student error type, engagement cues, and understanding trajectory; (2) a structured five-act adversarial debate between permissive and strict critics, moderated by a Devil’s Advocate; and (3) synthesis by a judge, stress analyst, and lead evaluator. The framework is implemented with AutoGen and a Llama-3-8B-Instruct backbone, with QLoRA fine-tuning applied to the lead evaluator. The evaluation is conducted on MRBench, a dataset of 1,214 middle-school mathematics dialogues, with classification tasks for mistake identification and guidance quality.

The main result is that the full HPO-FT system achieves Macro F1 = 0.845, outperforming GPT-4o (0.812) and several alternative multi-agent baselines. Ablation results suggest that the adversarial structure matters more than model scale or fine-tuning alone: removing Phase 1 distillation, the Devil’s Advocate, or the multi-turn protocol all reduce performance. The paper concludes that structured adversarial reasoning can improve reliability in automated math tutoring, but also notes limitations including focus on middle-school mathematics only, added latency (~4.2s per evaluation), and the need for cross-domain validation and deployment testing.

finding.finding_summary: On MRBench, the full HPO-FT system improved classification performance for middle-school mathematics tutoring judgments, reaching Macro F1 = 0.845 versus 0.812 for GPT-4o and 0.785 for the cooperative baseline. The paper reports that the adversarial architecture improves identification of student mistakes and the quality-of-guidance labels in mathematics dialogue, with statistically significant gains over GPT-4o (bootstrap resampling, n=10,000).
finding.measure: MRBench tutoring dialogue classification performance for Mistake Identification and Guidance Quality in middle-school mathematics dialogues

finding.finding_summary: The HPO framework improves automated evaluation quality but at a substantial computational cost. Inference latency is reported as 4.2 seconds per evaluation, about 10× slower than a single Llama-3-8B call (0.4s), though the authors argue this is acceptable for asynchronous grading and batch quality assurance.
finding.measure: Inference latency / computational cost per evaluation

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; no study population)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing an intervention empirically, the authors synthesize emerging applications and discuss how LLMs may support learning and teaching across contexts such as elementary, secondary, tertiary, remote, and professional education.

The paper argues that LLMs can be used to generate educational content, provide explanations and feedback, support tutoring, assist lesson planning, and reduce teacher workload. It highlights potential educational uses in reading, writing, mathematics, science, and problem solving, while also emphasizing that the models are brittle, can hallucinate, and may amplify bias or plagiarism risks.

A major contribution of the paper is its structured discussion of implementation risks and mitigation strategies, including privacy, copyright, fairness, overreliance, verification, sustainability, and the difficulty of distinguishing machine-generated from human-generated work. The authors conclude that LLMs may be valuable in education if deployed with human oversight, critical thinking, transparent policies, and further research on best practices.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models could meaningfully reshape educational systems through new policies, governance, curriculum design, privacy protections, and institutional workflows, but only if careful safeguards are in place. It does not report empirical effect sizes; instead, it presents a conceptual synthesis of opportunities and risks such as bias, copyright, verification, data privacy, and sustainability.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, ethical and institutional considerations for LLM adoption in education

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly states that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by assisting with lesson planning, quiz generation, feedback, grading, and content creation. These claims are illustrative rather than empirical, and no quantitative estimates are reported, but the paper positions operational efficiency as one of the main anticipated benefits of LLM use in education.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, content generation, and feedback efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs may support critical thinking and problem-solving when used for explanations, step-by-step solutions, and prompts, but it also warns that overreliance could undermine these same skills. No empirical effect sizes are provided; the finding is a theoretical balance of possible benefits and risks for durable skills.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, and related 21st-century skills

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics is discussed as a relevant application area, especially for generating practice problems, quizzes, and math word problems, and for supporting step-by-step solutions and contextualization of equations. However, the paper provides no direct empirical evidence on math achievement or conceptual understanding, so the conclusion is prospective and speculative rather than measured.
finding.measure: Mathematics practice problems, quizzes, word problems, and problem-solving support

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support reading and writing development by suggesting grammatical corrections, generating summaries, explaining complex texts, and assisting with writing tasks. These claims are not backed by direct outcome data in the paper, so the finding reflects a conceptual expectation of benefit rather than an empirical estimate.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension, writing support, grammar/style correction, and summarization

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests LLMs may increase student engagement, curiosity, and participation, particularly through conversational support, personalized guidance, and interactive tutoring. At the same time, it cautions that easy access to generated answers may reduce learner effort and motivation if not carefully designed.
finding.measure: Student engagement, curiosity, participation, and motivation

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the quality of generative AI responses for conceptual middle-school math question answering. The authors focus on a practical tutoring problem: LLMs can answer math questions in ways that are fluent but incorrect, insufficiently grounded in curricular materials, or mismatched to the student’s educational context. They propose using an OpenStax prealgebra textbook as a retrieval corpus and compare prompts with different levels of guidance.

The study evaluates a RAG-based math QA system on 51 real student questions from Math Nation and investigates two main properties: groundedness in the retrieved textbook and human preference for the generated responses. In Study 1, automated groundedness metrics increased with stronger prompt guidance, but the most grounded responses were not necessarily the most useful. In Study 2, nine educators and education-technology designers ranked responses from no guidance, low guidance, and high guidance conditions; low-guidance responses were preferred overall, while high- and no-guidance responses were statistically indistinguishable. Low guidance appears to strike a balance between conversational usefulness and textbook anchoring.

Study 3 tested whether document relevance explains the preference results by having authors rate retrieved textbook-document relevance. Relevant documents were associated with more grounded responses, but relevance did not significantly predict human preference. The authors conclude that RAG can improve response quality for conceptual math QA, but excessive grounding can reduce preference, and future systems should optimize for faithfulness rather than groundedness alone. The paper is preliminary, uses expert raters rather than students, and does not measure learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure math achievement or learning gains directly; instead it evaluates response quality for middle-school math question answering. Across 51 student queries, low-guidance RAG responses were preferred over no-guidance and high-guidance responses, while higher guidance produced more grounded responses in the textbook. This suggests potential usefulness for math tutoring, but no student learning outcome was assessed.
finding.measure: Human preference rankings of generated math QA responses; groundedness/faithfulness ratings against a textbook
finding.study_size: queries=51; annotators=9 educators/designers for preference study

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the potential of LLM to enhance teaching plans through teaching simulation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can improve teachers’ lesson planning by simulating classroom interaction and generating reflective feedback before instruction. The authors argue that prior work focused mainly on LLMs as student tutors, while teacher-facing uses—especially for pre-class planning and revision—have been underexplored.

Using high school mathematics as the context, the study constructed four baseline teaching-plan datasets and four enhanced datasets. The enhancement pipeline prompted GPT-4 (and in one condition Claude 3.5 Sonnet) to first simulate teacher-student dialogue across varying student ability levels, then generate teaching reflections from that simulation, and finally revise the original teaching plan using both the simulation and reflection text. The evaluation covered 480 lesson plans across four knowledge modules (Algebra, Functions, Geometry, Statistics) and used teacher ratings on 19 dimensions including problem chains, instructional activities, knowledge content, teaching methods, assessment, interdisciplinarity, practical value, and lesson scope.

The main finding is that simulation-plus-reflection prompting substantially improved the quality of LLM-generated teaching plans. Enhanced plans generally scored higher than baseline LLM outputs and, in several conditions, matched or exceeded plans written by experienced human teachers. The strongest performance was observed in the Statistics module, while Geometry remained comparatively weaker, likely because purely text-based generation struggles with diagram-dependent content. The authors conclude that LLMs can serve as practical, low-code tools for teacher preparation, with the clearest benefit being operational efficiency and instructional design support rather than direct student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that an LLM-based simulation-and-reflection workflow significantly improved the quality and practicality of teaching plans, suggesting reduced preparation burden and more effective lesson-plan refinement for teachers. Across 480 lesson plans (N=480), enhanced plans generally outperformed baseline LLM plans and often matched or exceeded experienced teachers’ plans on manual ratings; however, no standardized effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-rated teaching-plan quality, practicality, and instructional-design dimensions (8-point Likert ratings across 19 indicators)

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively focuses on high school mathematics lesson planning, showing that LLM-enhanced plans improved mathematics-specific instructional quality across Algebra, Functions, Geometry, and Statistics. On the 8-point teacher rating scale, enhanced plans typically reached around 6.5-7.6 across many dimensions, with the strongest gains in Statistics and more limited gains in Geometry, but the study did not measure student math achievement or conceptual understanding directly.
finding.measure: Human evaluation of high school mathematics teaching plans across math content modules and problem-chain dimensions
finding.study_size: n=240 baseline plans + n=240 enhanced plans (N=480 total)

paper_profiles.title: Systematic review of research on artificial intelligence applications in higher education – where are the educators?
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This systematic review examines how artificial intelligence has been studied in higher education, with a particular concern for what educators can actually learn from the literature about pedagogical uses, ethical implications, and risks. The authors searched three databases and screened peer-reviewed English- and Spanish-language journal articles published from 2007 through November 2018, ultimately including 146 articles for synthesis.

The review maps AI applications into four main areas: profiling and prediction, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation, and intelligent tutoring systems. Most studies were quantitative, most first authors came from Computer Science or STEM departments, and only a small minority explicitly defined AI or critically discussed ethical issues such as privacy and cost.

Across the included studies, AI systems were generally reported as accurate and promising for tasks such as predicting dropout, automating grading, and providing adaptive tutoring or feedback, but the evidence base was dominated by short-term, small-scale, or descriptive/pilot studies. The authors conclude that higher education research on AI has paid insufficient attention to educators’ perspectives, theoretical grounding, and the risks and governance challenges of AI adoption, and they call for more pedagogically informed and ethically reflective research.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI applications frequently aimed to automate or streamline assessment, prediction, feedback, and administrative tasks in higher education, with many studies reporting high accuracy and efficiency. For example, automated essay scoring reached 94.6%–98.2% agreement with human raters in one study, and machine-learning prediction models often outperformed logistic regression for classification tasks such as dropout or admission prediction, suggesting workload-reducing potential for staff.
finding.measure: Accuracy/agreement of AI systems for prediction, grading, feedback, and administrative classification tasks
finding.study_size: n=146 studies in review; individual studies varied

finding.finding_summary: A substantial portion of the reviewed literature used AI for institutional and administrative functions such as admissions, course scheduling, retention monitoring, and alignment of curricula with industry needs. The review reports that 48 studies focused on administrative/institutional services and that AI systems were often described as useful for decision support and early warning, but the evidence was mostly short-term and did not include robust longitudinal institutional evaluations.
finding.measure: Institutional decision-support applications (admissions, retention, scheduling, competency alignment)
finding.study_size: n=146 studies in review; 48 institutional/administrative studies

finding.finding_summary: The review includes a large body of work on academic support in higher education across domains such as computer science, mathematics, medicine, business statistics, accounting, and writing. The overall pattern was favorable: adaptive systems and intelligent tutoring systems were usually reported to support learning content delivery, feedback, and personalized support, though most studies were pilot or short-term implementations rather than definitive efficacy tests.
finding.measure: Learning-support applications across subject domains and instructional settings

finding.finding_summary: Several studies addressed engagement, motivation, self-regulation, and at-risk identification, including machine-learning models that predicted student engagement and academic motivation from learning-system behavior. The review characterizes these findings as generally promising for identifying low-engaged students and enabling timely intervention, but notes that most evidence came from quantitative prediction studies rather than direct measures of skill growth.
finding.measure: Student engagement, motivation, and related behavioral indicators

finding.finding_summary: The review reports AI applications related to collaboration, problem solving, and self-regulatory support, including tutoring systems for collaborative writing, peer-dialogue agents, and tools that support learning strategies. However, effects were uneven: most studies suggested positive or satisfactory preliminary results, one study reported negative results for more advanced learners, and the review cautions that novelty effects and limited designs make the evidence tentative.
finding.measure: Collaborative learning, problem-solving performance, self-regulation support, and related learner processes

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics appears as one of the subject areas addressed by intelligent tutoring systems, but the review does not synthesize a dedicated math-outcome effect. It notes at least one mathematics ITS study and the broader pattern that ITS were usually reported as improving learning outcomes relative to baseline conditions, with a prior meta-analysis of ITS cited as finding a moderate effect on learning overall; however, the review itself does not provide a math-specific pooled estimate.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning within intelligent tutoring system studies

finding.finding_summary: The review includes automated essay scoring, writing feedback, reading comprehension, and second-language learning applications. The synthesis suggests these tools often produced high agreement with human scoring and were intended to improve writing revision and feedback efficiency, although it also notes concerns about feedback quality and suitability for some learners or genres.
finding.measure: Writing, reading comprehension, and automated essay scoring outcomes

finding.finding_summary: A smaller subset of studies addressed second-language learning and dialogue-based systems, including intelligent tutors for language learning and teaching. The review does not report a pooled effect for speaking or listening outcomes, but the studies it summarizes generally describe supportive feedback and interaction features rather than negative effects.
finding.measure: Second-language learning and dialogue-based language instruction

paper_profiles.title: Editorial: Generative AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial introduces a Frontiers Research Topic on generative AI in education and summarizes the 11 papers included in the volume. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it frames the broader educational questions motivating the topic: how generative AI can support personalized learning, feedback, assessment, tutoring, student emotions, and AI-mediated interactions, while also raising concerns about accuracy, ethics, privacy, bias, and responsible implementation.

The editorial briefly synthesizes each contribution, including work on chatbot feedback, adolescents’ use of generative AI for schoolwork, critical thinking, mathematical proof construction with ChatGPT, whole-learner modeling, personalized assessment, AI mentors for STEM career exploration, academic integrity, interactive listening assessment generation, deception detection with AI robots, and a mini-review of students’ cognitive and emotional needs. It emphasizes that the field is still early and that most claims are preliminary or conceptual.

For K-12 relevance, the editorial highlights some student-facing findings, such as no significant association between generative AI use and academic achievement in an adolescent sample, and mixed evidence around motivation, learning effectiveness, and trust when students interact with AI systems. Overall, it concludes that generative AI has promise for enhancing engagement, personalization, and support, but that more rigorous research is needed on effectiveness, emotional effects, fairness, and implementation risks.

finding.finding_summary: The editorial summarizes one included study on adolescents’ use and perceived usefulness of generative AI for schoolwork, reporting no significant link between generative AI use and academic achievement. No mathematics-specific achievement effect size is reported in the editorial, and the mathematics-related content in the volume is limited to an exploratory proof-construction study rather than K-12 numeracy outcomes.
finding.measure: academic achievement

finding.finding_summary: Across the volume, the editorial reports that generative AI may foster engagement, motivation, and encouragement, but evidence is mixed and context-dependent. For example, the adolescents study found students with more executive functioning challenges perceived generative AI as more useful for assignments, while another included study found no significant differences in motivation and encouragement when students interacted with generative AI robots.
finding.measure: perceived usefulness, motivation, encouragement

finding.finding_summary: The editorial highlights generative AI’s potential to support critical thinking and human interaction, but also notes limitations in the evidence. It cites one opinion piece arguing for critical thinking uses of AI and a mini-review noting that current tools may be insufficiently personalized and may not reliably foster critical thinking in practice.
finding.measure: critical thinking / human interaction

paper_profiles.title: How Does ChatGPT Perform on the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE)? The Implications of Large Language Models for Medical Education and Knowledge Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can answer medical knowledge questions at a level comparable to human examinees and prior large language models. The authors evaluate ChatGPT on four multiple-choice question sets spanning USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 content: AMBOSS questions with and without an attending tip, and NBME free questions for Step 1 and Step 2.

The study does not test an educational intervention with learners; instead, it measures model performance as a proxy for potential educational utility. ChatGPT is compared with GPT-3 and InstructGPT, and its responses are qualitatively coded for logical reasoning, use of information from the question, and use of external information. The population/context is adult medical education, specifically medical licensing exam preparation and knowledge assessment.

Results show ChatGPT outperformed GPT-3 and InstructGPT on all datasets, reaching 64.4% on NBME-Free-Step1 and 57.8% on NBME-Free-Step2, with lower accuracy on AMBOSS sets (44% Step 1; 42% Step 2). Performance declined as question difficulty increased on AMBOSS Step 1 without the tip (P=.01), and the attending tip improved performance. Qualitatively, ChatGPT provided a logical explanation for every response, used internal information in nearly all outputs, and used external information more often in correct than incorrect answers. The authors conclude that ChatGPT shows promise as an interactive medical education tool, while emphasizing limitations related to model versioning, closed access, and inability to assess fine-tuning or stochasticity.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT answered medical licensing exam questions at moderate accuracy, outperforming GPT-3 and InstructGPT across all four datasets. Accuracy was 64.4% (56/87) on NBME-Free-Step1, 57.8% (59/102) on NBME-Free-Step2, 44% (44/100) on AMBOSS-Step1, and 42% (42/100) on AMBOSS-Step2; performance decreased with question difficulty on AMBOSS-Step1 without the attending tip (P=.01).
finding.measure: Multiple-choice medical knowledge question accuracy on USMLE Step 1/Step 2–aligned item sets

finding.finding_summary: The paper found strong evidence that ChatGPT produces coherent reasoning-style responses, which is relevant to explanation quality and analytical dialogue rather than learner outcomes. Every response contained logical reasoning (100% across NBME datasets), and correct answers were more likely than incorrect ones to include external information (NBME-Free-Step1: 92.9% vs 48.4%, P<.001; NBME-Free-Step2: 89.8% vs 62.8%, P=.001).
finding.measure: Presence of logical reasoning, internal information, and external information in model responses

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests ChatGPT may support medical education workflows by serving as a dialogic tutoring aid, but this was not directly measured as productivity or workload. The paper infers potential utility from the model’s ability to generate coherent explanations and answer questions at a level approaching passing performance on some exam sets.
finding.measure: Potential tutoring utility inferred from response quality and accuracy

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing healthcare: the role of artificial intelligence in clinical practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical practice, with a broad focus on how AI can improve diagnosis, treatment selection, population health management, patient education, and decision support. The authors synthesize indexed literature from PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and EMBASE and describe applications of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and large language models across healthcare settings.

The review is not an empirical study of patients or learners; rather, it surveys prior studies to outline potential benefits, implementation challenges, and ethical risks. It highlights examples where AI has improved diagnostic performance, assisted with dose optimization, supported virtual health assistants, and enhanced patient education, while also emphasizing limitations such as data privacy, bias, hallucination, cybersecurity risk, and the continuing need for human oversight. Because it is centered on healthcare rather than K-12 education, it does not directly address the sub-question on generative AI tutoring in mathematics; however, it includes a brief mention that intelligent tutoring systems in academia have improved learning outcomes in subjects such as math and science.

finding.finding_summary: The review briefly notes that, in academia, AI has been used to develop intelligent tutoring systems that adapt to individual students and have improved learning outcomes in subjects including math and science. No primary educational study is reported in this paper, and no effect sizes, sample sizes, or achievement measures are provided for the education example.
