finding.measure: general learning outcomes in intelligent tutoring systems (math and science mentioned)

paper_profiles.title: Novice Learner and Expert Tutor: Evaluating Math Reasoning Abilities of Large Language Models with Misconceptions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates large language models (LLMs) on a different kind of math reasoning task than standard accuracy benchmarks: can they intentionally produce an incorrect answer that corresponds to a specific student misconception, and can they identify the misconception behind an incorrect answer? The authors frame these two tasks as simulating a novice learner and an expert tutor, respectively, drawing on ideas from educational learning sciences and intelligent tutoring systems.

The study uses a dataset of grade-school multiple-choice math questions from Eedi. After preprocessing, the dataset contains 213 questions, 482 answer choices, and 319 expert-curated misconceptions. The authors test GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 with several prompting strategies, including zero-shot and few-shot settings, sometimes with explanations. They compare conventional correct-answer accuracy to the ability to generate a specific wrong answer linked to a misconception, and to the ability to infer the correct misconception from a wrong answer and a candidate set of misconceptions.

Results show that both models answer the math questions correctly at high rates, with GPT-4 reaching 94.8% accuracy when prompted with explanations. However, performance is much lower when the task is to mimic a novice learner: GPT-4 reaches 61.7% in the best zero-shot-with-explanation setting and 67.9% with few-shot examples from the same misconception type. On the expert-tutor task, GPT-4 performs well when given only a small set of candidate misconceptions (91.9% with 4 candidates) but degrades sharply as the candidate set grows, falling to 39.8% when 100 misconceptions are provided. The authors conclude that LLMs are strong at answering grade-school math correctly, but substantially weaker at controlled error generation and robust misconception diagnosis, which limits their current suitability for nuanced educational tutoring applications.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports very high correct-answer performance on grade-school math questions, but substantially weaker performance when models must operate under misconception constraints. GPT-4 reached 94.8% accuracy on standard question answering with explanations, yet only 61.7% accuracy when asked to produce the specific incorrect answer matching a given misconception in the best novice-learner zero-shot setting, and 67.9% with few-shot examples from the same misconception type. On the expert-tutor task, GPT-4 achieved 91.9% accuracy with 4 candidate misconceptions, but accuracy dropped to 39.8% when 100 misconceptions were included.
finding.measure: Accuracy on multiple-choice grade-school math questions; accuracy on generating misconception-linked incorrect answers; accuracy on identifying the correct misconception behind an incorrect answer
finding.confidence_interval: GPT-3.5/GPT-4 accuracy reported as mean ± SD across 4 trials: e.g., GPT-4 0.948 ± 0.009; 0.617 ± 0.005; 0.679 ± 0.020; 0.919 and 0.398 reported in figure text

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly examines misconception diagnosis and controlled error simulation, both of which are tied to reasoning about others’ knowledge and to model interpretability in educational settings. GPT-4’s performance was strong only under constrained candidate sets for misconception identification (91.9% with 4 candidate misconceptions) and declined as the task became more cognitively demanding, suggesting limited robustness in deeper diagnostic reasoning. The study argues this reveals gaps in robust student simulation and expert tutoring behavior rather than conventional math skill alone.
finding.measure: Accuracy in identifying misconceptions from an incorrect answer; accuracy in selecting a specified incorrect answer based on a misconception

paper_profiles.title: Beyond Final Answers: Evaluating Large Language Models for Math Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models (LLMs) are suitable for mathematics tutoring, focusing on both final-answer correctness and the quality of step-by-step instructional support. The authors argue that benchmark-style evaluations that score only final answers miss important tutoring-specific failures, especially when students need scaffolding, feedback, and accurate intermediate reasoning.

To study this, the paper introduces two evaluation methods using college algebra problems from the Apprentice Tutors intelligent tutoring system. First, the authors compare several ChatGPT-family models (GPT-3.5 Turbo, GPT-4, GPT-4o, o1-mini, and o1-preview) on tutor-generated algebra problems and score whether the final answers match the tutor’s solution. Second, human evaluators interact with the same models as if they were students seeking help, and reviewers rate each dialogue for pedagogical quality and correctness using a rubric covering clarity, feedback, scaffolding, strategy modeling, and encouragement.

The study finds that LLMs can often produce correct final answers, but their tutoring dialogues are substantially less reliable. In the tutor-based test set of 110 problems, average final-answer accuracy was 85.5%, with GPT-4o performing best at 97.3%. In interactive tutoring with 150 dialogues, average final-answer accuracy was 88.6%, but only 56.6% of dialogues were fully correct overall. Reviewers judged many interactions as high quality pedagogically, yet still found frequent errors in intermediate steps, inconsistencies in equivalence checking, and occasional refusals to accept correct answers.

The authors conclude that current LLMs are not yet suitable as standalone math tutors without human oversight or additional correctness mechanisms. They highlight potential benefits such as flexible answer formats, hint generation, and positive reinforcement, but emphasize that errors in stepwise tutoring can undermine trust and possibly create misconceptions. The paper therefore recommends using LLMs as components that support existing intelligent tutoring systems rather than as direct replacements for them.

finding.finding_summary: The models showed reasonably strong final-answer performance on college algebra, but not reliable tutoring performance overall. In the tutor-based benchmark of 110 problem-answer pairs, average final-answer accuracy was 85.5% (GPT-4o 97.3%); in interactive tutoring across 150 dialogues, average final-answer accuracy was 88.6%, but only 56.6% of dialogues were fully correct end-to-end.
finding.measure: Final-answer correctness on college algebra problems; full correctness of interactive tutoring dialogues

paper_profiles.title: A Benchmark for Math Misconceptions: Bridging Gaps in Middle School Algebra with AI-Supported Instruction
paper_profiles.population: Middle School (Grades 4-8; especially Grades 6-10 educators and students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of identifying and responding to common algebra misconceptions and common errors in middle school mathematics, especially for students in underserved populations. The authors argue that accurate diagnosis of misconceptions is important for personalized support, equitable math instruction, and improving conceptual understanding, but that both teachers and AI systems often struggle to recognize these patterns reliably.

To support AI-based educational tools, the paper introduces a benchmark dataset of 55 algebra misconceptions/common errors with 220 diagnostic examples drawn from 145 peer-reviewed sources. The benchmark is organized by algebra topic and designed for use with large language models (LLMs). The authors evaluate GPT-4-turbo with in-context learning in two experiments: one using randomly selected examples from the full dataset and another constrained by topic. They also collect feedback from five middle school math educators and conduct follow-up structured interviews with four of them to assess clarity, classroom relevance, and possible classroom uses.

The empirical results show that GPT-4-turbo performed substantially better when evaluation was topic-constrained and when educator feedback was incorporated. On exact benchmark matching, performance rose from precision/recall of 0.526/0.529 in the unrestricted experiment to 0.753/0.748 in the topic-constrained experiment; with expert re-labeling of ambiguous cases, accuracy reached 83.91% in the topic-constrained setting. Performance was weakest for ratios and proportional thinking, indicating that proportional reasoning remains difficult for the model and for students. Educators largely agreed that the misconceptions were real and classroom-relevant (80% or more indicating they encounter them), and four of five expressed interest in using the dataset with AI for diagnosis or teacher training. The paper concludes that AI can be a useful support for misconception diagnosis, but that topic-specific design, educator expertise, and multimodal/visual inputs are important limitations and future directions.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is centrally about diagnosing middle school algebra misconceptions as a way to support mathematical understanding, but it does not test student achievement gains from an intervention. The main empirical results show GPT-4-turbo achieved precision/recall of 0.526/0.529 in unrestricted testing and 0.753/0.748 with topic-constrained testing; with expert relabeling in the topic-constrained setup, accuracy reached 83.91%.
finding.measure: LLM precision and recall for identifying algebra misconceptions/common errors; expert-reviewed classification accuracy
finding.study_size: n=5500 iterations in Experiment 1; n=1100 iterations in Experiment 2; benchmark of 55 misconceptions and 220 examples

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark is intended to help educators diagnose student misconceptions more efficiently, and surveyed teachers reported interest in using it for diagnosis and teacher training. Four of five educators said they would want to use AI with the dataset for diagnosing misconceptions, suggesting potential workflow support, but the paper does not measure time savings or workload directly.
finding.measure: Educator survey/interview responses about potential use for diagnosis and teacher support

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that a shared benchmark could bridge research and classroom practice and support more equitable math instruction, especially for low-income and minoritized learners. Educator feedback suggested the benchmark is relevant to classroom practice, but the paper offers no direct policy or institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Educator ratings of relevance/clarity and stated interest in classroom use; benchmark relevance to underserved populations

paper_profiles.title: Leveraging LLMs to Assess Tutor Moves in Real-Life Dialogues: A Feasibility Study
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This feasibility study asks whether large language models can reliably identify and evaluate specific tutor moves in authentic tutoring transcripts. The authors focus on two tutoring practices that are known to matter for learning: giving effective praise and responding appropriately to student math errors. Rather than testing a tutoring intervention, the paper benchmarks whether LLMs can score these behaviors in real-world dialogue at scale.

The dataset consists of 50 randomly selected audio transcripts from remote math tutoring sessions in which college-student tutors worked with middle school students. The authors compare several LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-4o, GPT-4-turbo, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and LearnLM) against human annotations using two-stage prompts: a filter stage to detect whether a relevant tutoring situation occurred, and an evaluation stage to judge whether the tutor response met best-practice criteria. They report high agreement with human coders for detecting praise and math errors, and somewhat lower but still strong agreement for evaluating the quality of tutor responses.

The main conclusion is that LLMs can be used as a scalable and cost-effective method for assessing tutor moves in lightly processed transcripts from authentic tutoring settings. Performance was generally high across models, with no single model clearly outperforming the others. The paper also shows that prompt design matters: few-shot prompting, self-consistency, and task-specific rationale prompting can improve performance, but the best prompting strategy differs by task. Key limitations include missing video/screenshot/chat context and difficulty identifying speakers in transcripts, which may constrain accuracy in more complex tutoring interactions.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not evaluate student mathematics achievement or learning outcomes directly. Instead, it benchmarks how accurately LLMs can detect and rate math-tutoring behaviors in 50 transcripts of middle school tutoring sessions, including tutor praise and responses to student math errors. No effect size or student outcome is reported because the study is a feasibility assessment of coding performance, not an intervention study.
finding.measure: LLM accuracy for identifying tutor praise and student math-error episodes, and for rating tutor response quality in math tutoring transcripts
finding.confidence_interval: 95% bootstrap CIs reported for model accuracy: praise filter 94-98%, error filter 82-88%, praise evaluation 83-89%, error evaluation 73-77% depending on model

paper_profiles.title: AI tutoring can safely and effectively support students: An exploratory RCT in UK classrooms
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI tutor can safely and effectively support K-12 students in real classroom mathematics settings. The motivation is the long-standing challenge that one-to-one tutoring is highly effective but too expensive and difficult to scale, so the authors test whether a pedagogically fine-tuned model (LearnLM) can help extend tutoring access without sacrificing quality or safety.

The study was an exploratory randomized controlled trial across five UK secondary schools with N=165 Year 9 and 10 students (ages 13–15). Students were assigned either to static, pre-written hints or to interactive tutoring; within the tutoring condition, each session was randomized to a human tutor alone or to LearnLM supervised by a human tutor who could approve, edit, or rewrite every message before it reached the student. The intervention was implemented through the Eedi mathematics platform and used students' normal study-unit activity as the outcome source.

The main quantitative findings show that supervised LearnLM tutoring was at least as effective as human tutoring for immediate learning outcomes and was somewhat better for transfer to a new topic. Students using LearnLM were more likely than those with human tutors to solve the next-unit problem correctly (66.2% vs. 60.7%), a 5.5 percentage-point advantage with a reported difference interval of [–1.4%, +12.4%]. Both tutoring conditions substantially outperformed static hints on mistake remediation and misconception resolution, and the audit found no harmful content and only five factual errors in 3,617 drafted messages. The paper concludes that supervised generative AI tutoring can be safe, pedagogically sound, and potentially scalable, while noting limitations around longer-term learning, generalization beyond mathematics, and the need for human judgment on pacing and social-emotional nuance.

finding.finding_summary: The trial directly evaluated mathematics learning outcomes in UK secondary classrooms. Supervised LearnLM tutoring was at least as effective as human tutoring for immediate remediation and misconception resolution, and it produced better transfer to a new mathematics topic: 66.2% of students answered the next-unit question correctly versus 60.7% with human tutoring, a +5.5 percentage-point difference [–1.4%, +12.4%].
finding.measure: Accuracy on Eedi mathematics study-unit questions, including second-attempt correctness, misconception resolution within a unit, and correctness on the first question of the next unit (knowledge transfer)
finding.confidence_interval: [–1.4%, +12.4%] for the LearnLM vs human-tutor transfer difference

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports qualitative and survey evidence that supervised LearnLM made tutoring feel more fluid and efficient for the human tutors. In post-trial surveys, 82.4% of tutors selected 'supporting multiple students at the same time' as LearnLM's most useful feature, but the authors state that the RCT design did not allow a rigorous measurement of throughput or efficiency.
finding.measure: Tutor surveys and interviews on perceived workload, fluency, and ability to support multiple students simultaneously
finding.study_size: n=17 tutors; interviews with n=5 tutors

finding.finding_summary: The strongest learning advantage for LearnLM was on knowledge transfer, which is a durable skill closely related to applying learning to novel problems. Students tutored by LearnLM were 5.5 percentage points more likely than students with human tutors to answer the first question of the next study unit correctly (66.2% vs. 60.7%), suggesting better transfer to new mathematical situations.
finding.measure: Knowledge transfer to a new topic, operationalized as correctness on the first question in the next study unit

finding.finding_summary: The study includes student survey feedback and tutor interviews indicating generally positive learner experience, but also notes that LearnLM's Socratic style sometimes frustrated students and required human moderation of pacing and tone. Students in interactive tutoring rated helpfulness slightly higher than static hints (3.9 vs. 3.6 out of 5), though the paper frames these as supportive perceptions rather than a formally estimated causal effect.
finding.measure: Student post-trial helpfulness ratings and qualitative interview feedback about frustration, engagement, and rapport
finding.study_size: n=27 student survey responses; n=5 tutor interviews

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that supervised generative AI tutoring could help expand access to one-to-one tutoring at scale, potentially improving delivery efficiency in schools. However, this conclusion is based on feasibility, safety, and tutor-reported scalability signals rather than direct institutional outcome measurement.
finding.measure: Tutor-reported scalability/feasibility observations and informal post-trial simulation of additional sessions

paper_profiles.title: Combining Large Language Models with Tutoring System Intelligence: A Case Study in Caregiver Homework Support
paper_profiles.venue: LAK 2025 (Proceedings of the 15th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates how large language models (LLMs) can be combined with an intelligent tutoring system’s instructional model to generate real-time conversational support for caregivers helping children with math homework. The core problem is that caregivers often want to help with homework but lack the curricular and instructional knowledge to provide effective guidance, especially in modern, technology-mediated math practice.

The authors developed the Caregiver Conversational Support Tool (CCST), embedded in a middle-school equation-solving tutor (Lynnette). CCST uses tutoring-system context such as problem accuracy, hint use, chat history, and next-step solution paths to prompt an open-source Llama 3 model to generate message recommendations for caregivers. The work reports prompt-engineering experiments and then a prototype evaluation with ten middle-school caregivers (in-person workshop and remote Zoom interviews). Caregivers generally preferred content-level, context-specific guidance over purely motivational messages, especially prompts that encouraged students to explain their thinking and revealed metacognitive processes.

The study does not measure student achievement or learning outcomes directly; instead, it is a design/prototyping and qualitative user-study paper focused on caregiver perceptions, feasibility, and implementation issues. Main conclusions are that tutoring-system intelligence can meaningfully improve the instructional quality and contextual relevance of LLM-generated messages, but practical limitations remain, especially latency, message length, and the need for more personalized tone and customizable support.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is about middle-school equation-solving practice in a math tutoring system, but it does not report any student math achievement, conceptual understanding, or problem-solving gains attributable to the LLM-supported caregiver tool. The study evaluates prompt quality and caregiver perceptions of message recommendations rather than learning outcomes, so no empirical effect on mathematics performance is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers preferred recommendations that prompted students to self-explain and articulate their reasoning, indicating that the system supports metacognitive prompting. Five caregivers specifically valued these prompts because they provided insight into the child’s thought process and helped identify knowledge gaps, but this was a qualitative preference finding rather than a measured effect on student metacognition.
finding.measure: Caregiver interview feedback on self-explanation / metacognitive prompting

finding.finding_summary: Caregivers valued content-level support and some motivational language, but many said motivational messages were less useful than direct instructional help. The tool’s recommendations were viewed as encouraging and helpful for reducing caregiver uncertainty, yet these are perceptions of message usefulness rather than measured changes in student motivation or engagement.
finding.measure: Caregiver perceptions of message usefulness, tone, and support during homework help

finding.finding_summary: The system was feasible for generating three caregiver message recommendations in real time, but latency was a notable limitation. Average generation time was about 25 seconds, and six caregivers said messages were too long; two of six found the system somewhat slow while four found it reasonably quick. These findings suggest mixed operational performance for live use.
finding.measure: Observed generation latency and caregiver feedback on message length / responsiveness

paper_profiles.title: Stepwise Verification and Remediation of Student Reasoning Errors with Large Language Model Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a core challenge in LLM-based dialog tutoring for math: tutors often misdiagnose student errors and generate responses that are correct in tone but factually wrong, generic, or poorly targeted. The authors argue that effective tutoring should first verify the student’s reasoning, identify the first erroneous step, and then generate feedback grounded in that verification, rather than producing a response in a single pass.

To study this, they build a dataset of 1,002 teacher-annotated incorrect student solutions drawn from MathDial/GSM8K-style multi-step math word problems. They evaluate several verification methods: overall correctness classification, stepwise error localization, free-form error descriptions, and step alignment against reference solutions. They then condition tutor response generation on these verification outputs and compare prompted and finetuned models (including GPT-3.5, Llama2/Llama3, and Flan-T5) using automatic metrics, LLM-based judging, and human evaluation by teachers.

The main conclusion is that separating verification from generation improves tutoring quality. In particular, detailed verification signals—especially free-form error descriptions—make tutor responses more targeted, more correct, and more actionable, while reducing hallucinations. The results also show that verification itself is difficult: even strong LLMs struggle to localize errors, performance improves when a reference solution is available, and gains are larger when verification is correct. The paper’s scope is limited to multi-step math problem solving, and it evaluates tutor output quality rather than direct student learning outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that verify-then-generate tutoring improves the quality of math tutoring responses for multi-step word problems, but it does not measure student achievement directly. On the human-evaluated response-generation task, adding verification increased targetedness, correctness, and actionability; for example, few-shot GPT-3.5 improved from 30.0/37.5/30.0 on target/correct/actionable in the baseline to 57.5/62.5/45.0 with Error Description, and Flan-T5-3B improved from 7.5/20.0/25.0 to 20.0/35.0/35.0. Verification quality itself was also substantial but imperfect, with Llama3-70B achieving 82.4% correct Error Description judgments on the evaluated subset.
finding.measure: Teacher- and LLM-judged quality of generated tutoring responses for K-12 multi-step math word problems; verification accuracy on stepwise error detection/localization
finding.study_size: n=1002 for verification dataset; n=40 conversations for human evaluation of responses; n=30 alignments for alignment ablation

paper_profiles.title: MATHDIAL: A Dialogue Tutoring Dataset with Rich Pedagogical Properties Grounded in Math Reasoning Problems
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL 2023)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a data bottleneck in building effective dialogue tutors for mathematics: existing tutoring corpora are small, low-quality, or lack rich pedagogical annotations. The authors propose MATHDIAL, a semi-synthetic dataset collection framework that pairs expert human teachers with LLM-simulated students to create one-to-one tutoring dialogues grounded in grade-school math word problems.

Using this framework, they collect 2,861 tutoring conversations based on GSM8K problems and annotate them with student confusions, teacher move types, and whether the confusion was resolved. The paper does not test learning gains in real students; instead, it evaluates the dataset and models trained on it using automatic metrics, human judgments, and an interactive simulation with a student model. Results show that fine-tuned smaller open-source models can outperform much larger prompted LLMs on tutor response generation, and that the fine-tuned model achieves similar student-solving success to ChatGPT while telling the answer less often.

The study is situated in K-12 math tutoring and is most directly relevant to educator-facing AI tools rather than student-facing deployment. The authors conclude that high-quality, pedagogy-rich data can improve generative AI tutors, but also highlight important limitations, including reliance on simulated students, possible mismatch with real classroom interactions, and limited coverage of the full range of tutor goals. They also note that the models still struggle to generalize to unseen problems and that immediate problem-solving success is only a partial proxy for long-term learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper is about math tutoring dialogues grounded in grade-school math word problems, but it does not measure student math achievement directly. Instead, it shows that fine-tuned models on MATHDIAL improve tutor-response quality on generation metrics and in simulated tutoring, with Flan-T5780M reaching 30% Success@5 and 39% Success@10 versus ChatGPT's 29% and 53%, while keeping Telling@5 below 1% and Telling@10 at 4%.
finding.measure: Tutor response generation quality; interactive student-solving success (Success@k) and telling rate (Telling@k) in simulated math tutoring
finding.study_size: n=2,861 dialogues; interactive evaluation on a subset of problems (exact n not_reported)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the collected dialogues and the fine-tuned tutor better support equitable tutoring, defined as giving students room to explore rather than immediately revealing answers. In human evaluation, Flan-T5780M scored 2.19 on equitable tutoring compared with ChatGPT's 1.43 and close to ground truth's 2.42, suggesting better pedagogical support for engagement in the problem-solving process.
finding.measure: Human ratings of equitable tutoring and dialogue coherence/correctness
finding.study_size: n=50 responses per model rated by 3 expert annotators

finding.finding_summary: The dataset is explicitly designed around scaffolding, probing, and prompting students to reason through solutions, which aligns with problem solving and metacognitive support. The paper reports that teachers resolve confusion in almost 89% of conversations, largely through scaffolding questions (about 75% of conversations), indicating the approach is effective for supporting structured reasoning rather than just answer delivery.
finding.measure: Resolution of student confusion; distribution of teacher moves (Focus, Probing, Telling, Generic)

finding.finding_summary: The paper's main practical contribution is a scalable semi-synthetic data collection pipeline for tutoring-dialogue creation, intended to reduce reliance on privacy-sensitive recordings and costly crowdsourcing. The authors argue that this approach yields a much larger tutoring corpus than prior public datasets and can be used to train better tutors more efficiently, but they do not provide direct cost or workload measurements.
finding.measure: Dataset scale and feasibility of semi-synthetic data collection for tutoring corpora

paper_profiles.title: SAFETUTORS: Benchmarking Pedagogical Safety in AI Tutoring Systems
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a gap in evaluating AI tutors: most LLM benchmarks focus on answer accuracy or generic safety, but do not assess whether a model is pedagogically safe over the course of tutoring. The authors argue that tutoring-specific risks include over-disclosing answers, reinforcing misconceptions, reducing learner agency, and collapsing scaffolding, all of which can quietly undermine learning even when responses look helpful or harmless.

To study this, the paper introduces SAFETUTORS, a benchmark of 3,135 single-turn and 2,820 multi-turn synthetic tutoring interactions spanning mathematics, physics, and chemistry. The benchmark is built from a learning-science-grounded taxonomy with 11 harm dimensions and 48 sub-risks, and it evaluates 11 LLMs (10 open-weight and 1 closed-weight) using automated judges plus human validation. The study does not test a real classroom intervention; instead, it measures how models behave under risky tutoring scenarios and how behavior changes in extended dialogue.

The main conclusion is that pedagogical harm is widespread across models and subjects. Larger models are not reliably safer, and multi-turn interaction substantially worsens tutoring behavior: average harm increases across subjects, and pedagogical harm rises sharply from 17.7% in single-turn settings to 77.8% in multi-turn settings. The results suggest that single-turn, accuracy-only, or generic safety evaluations can badly overestimate how suitable an LLM is for tutoring, especially in STEM contexts where sustained scaffolding and misconception repair matter.

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark finds substantial pedagogical failure in mathematics tutoring scenarios, especially over multi-turn interaction. In mathematics, mean harm increases from single-turn to multi-turn by 11.13 percentage points, and pedagogical harm rises from 14.29%–25.00% in single-turn models to 62.16%–94.59% in multi-turn models depending on the model, indicating that tutoring behavior degrades rather than supports mathematical learning.
finding.measure: Pedagogical harm rate and model behavior on mathematics tutoring dialogues
finding.study_size: n=1,237 single-turn mathematics questions; n=1,054 multi-turn mathematics conversations

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates AI tutor behavior in physics and chemistry, both of which require scientific reasoning and multi-step explanation. Harm is widespread in both domains, with multi-turn interaction increasing average harm by 6.16 percentage points in physics and 6.26 percentage points in chemistry; pedagogical harm also remains very high in multi-turn settings (physics: 50.00%–95.65%; chemistry: 64.52%–91.94% across models).
finding.measure: Pedagogical harm rate, misconception repair, and learning-support behavior in physics and chemistry tutoring dialogues
finding.study_size: n=797 multi-turn physics conversations; n=969 multi-turn chemistry conversations

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark directly measures motivational and engagement-related failures, including shortcut temptation, reduced curiosity, emotional disengagement, and motivation improvement in multi-turn tutoring. Across subjects, motivation improvement scores remain modest, and the paper reports that multi-turn dialogue worsens motivational/affective behavior in many cases; for example, pedagogical harm associated with motivation-related risks rises sharply in extended interactions and student-facing support often fails to promote persistence or autonomy.
finding.measure: Motivational/affective risk rates; trajectory-level motivation improvement judgments

finding.finding_summary: This paper centrally studies durable skills such as metacognition, critical thinking, reflective judgment, and self-regulation, because these are explicit dimensions in the tutoring-safety taxonomy. Metacognitive harm is consistently high, exceeding 60% in single-turn for all models and surpassing 90% in multi-turn across subjects; in mathematics multi-turn, the highest metacognitive harm reaches 97.44% for Qwen2.5-32B. The authors also report that challenge scores are near zero and that models rarely prompt students to reason independently.
finding.measure: Metacognitive harm rate, reflective harm, challenge score, and learning-trajectory judgments about misconception reduction and learning gains
finding.study_size: n=3,135 single-turn instances; n=2,820 multi-turn conversations

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests that automated benchmarking can efficiently surface tutoring risks across many models, subjects, and dialogue formats, replacing slower manual inspection of every interaction. However, this is an evaluation-paper use of efficiency rather than a measured classroom productivity outcome, and no teacher-workload or task-time effect is reported.
finding.measure: Benchmarking coverage across models, subjects, and interaction formats

paper_profiles.title: Retrieval-augmented Generation to Improve Math Question-Answering: Trade-offs Between Groundedness and Human Preference
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2023 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED) / arXiv
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can improve the quality of generative AI responses for middle-school math question-answering, with a focus on conceptual explanations rather than procedural steps. The authors argue that educational math chatbots need responses that are both accurate/grounded in curricular materials and also useful and preferred by students, and that these goals may conflict.

To study this, the authors built a RAG system using OpenStax Prealgebra content as the retrieval corpus and GPT-3.5 as the generation model. They tested three prompting conditions (none, low guidance, high guidance) plus an information-retrieval baseline on 51 real student questions from Math Nation posts in pre-algebra, Algebra 1, and geometry. Study 1 evaluated automated groundedness metrics, Study 2 surveyed 9 educators and education-technology designers to rank response preferences and judge groundedness, and Study 3 had authors rate retrieved document relevance to query.

The main finding is that RAG and prompt guidance can increase groundedness, but more grounded responses are not always preferred. The low-guidance condition produced the most preferred responses, while high-guidance responses were judged most grounded; no-guidance and high-guidance were statistically indistinguishable in preference. Retrieval relevance was associated with greater groundedness, but not with human preference. The paper concludes that math QA systems need to balance faithfulness to curricular sources with conversational usefulness, and that students’ actual learning outcomes remain an open question.

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies middle-school math question-answering quality for conceptual algebra and geometry questions, but it does not measure student achievement or learning gains. Across 51 queries, low-guidance RAG responses were preferred by humans, while high-guidance responses were judged more grounded; the study frames this as a trade-off in math tutoring quality rather than an instructional efficacy result.
finding.measure: Human preference rankings and groundedness judgments for generated math QA responses

paper_profiles.title: Automated Feedback in Math Education: A Comparative Analysis of LLMs for Open-Ended Responses
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether large language models can improve automated scoring and feedback for K-12 mathematics open-ended responses. The authors compare three approaches: a fine-tuned Llama/Mistral-based model called GOAT, the prior state-of-the-art SBERT-Canberra similarity method, and GPT-4 used zero-shot with an illustrative math rubric. The motivation is to support online learning platforms and reduce teacher workload while providing timely feedback on student work.

The study uses a dataset from an online learning platform containing 50 middle-school math problems, each with 100 student responses, teacher scores, and teacher-written feedback. Models are trained and tested on an 80/20 split, and scoring performance is evaluated with AUC, RMSE, and Cohen’s kappa. Feedback quality is judged by two experienced teachers on accuracy, relevance, motivation, and preference. GOAT performs best on automated scoring, outperforming SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on all scoring metrics, but GPT-4 produces the highest-rated feedback overall according to human evaluators.

The paper concludes that fine-tuned open-source LLMs can improve automated math scoring relative to prior non-generative methods, but high-quality feedback generation remains challenging. GPT-4’s feedback is judged more accurate, relevant, and preferred, while GOAT appears to capture teacher scoring patterns better than SBERT-Canberra. The authors emphasize limitations in the quality and consistency of the teacher feedback used for training, differences in teacher grading norms, and the need for better datasets and more refined feedback training in future work.

finding.finding_summary: GOAT, the fine-tuned Llama/Mistral-based model, outperformed SBERT-Canberra and GPT-4 on automated scoring of middle-school open-ended math responses. On the 1,000-item test set, GOAT achieved AUC=0.697, RMSE=1.119, and Cohen’s kappa=0.422, compared with SBERT’s AUC=0.662, RMSE=1.364, kappa=0.362, and GPT-4’s AUC=0.639, RMSE=1.160, kappa=0.266.
finding.measure: Automated scoring of teacher-rated open-ended math responses (AUC, RMSE, Cohen’s kappa against teacher scores)

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on automated scoring and feedback generation as a way to reduce teacher workload in math platforms. Although no direct workload outcome was measured, the authors argue that the models—especially GOAT for scoring and GPT-4 for feedback—can serve as helpful starting points for teachers and reduce the time needed to produce scores and comments.
finding.measure: Human-rated usefulness of generated feedback and discussion of automation for scoring/feedback workflows
finding.study_size: n=100 sampled feedback cases for teacher review; n=1000 test scoring cases

finding.finding_summary: Feedback was evaluated for motivational quality as well as demotivating language. GPT-4 had the highest motivation rate (52% consensus) and the lowest demotivating rate (1%), while GOAT was close behind on motivation (48%) but had more demotivating feedback (5%); SBERT was lowest on motivation (46%) and highest on demotivating feedback (11%).
finding.measure: Human ratings of feedback motivation and demotivation

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether generated feedback supports accurate and relevant mathematical reasoning guidance, which indirectly reflects the quality of conceptual guidance students receive. GPT-4 produced the most accurate and relevant feedback (86% consensus accuracy; 91% consensus relevance), while GOAT was moderately strong (68% accuracy; 88% relevance) and SBERT lagged behind (52% accuracy; 76% relevance).
finding.measure: Human ratings of feedback accuracy and relevance

paper_profiles.title: Hierarchical Pedagogical Oversight: A Multi-Agent Adversarial Framework for Reliable AI Tutoring
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a reliability problem in AI tutoring: large language models often validate incorrect student reasoning or give overly direct answers that may hinder learning. The authors argue that the core issue is not model scale alone, but the lack of a structured separation between generation and evaluation in pedagogical judging.

To address this, they introduce Hierarchical Pedagogical Oversight (HPO), a multi-agent framework built around three phases: intelligence distillation, structured adversarial debate, and synthesis. In Phase 1, specialist agents extract the mathematical concept, engagement signals, and learning trajectory from a dialogue. In Phase 2, opposing pedagogical critics debate the quality of a tutor response, with a Devil’s Advocate agent challenging unsupported assumptions. In Phase 3, a judge, stress analyst, and lead evaluator synthesize the final decision. The system is implemented with AutoGen and a Llama-3-8B-Instruct backbone, with QLoRA fine-tuning applied to the lead evaluator.

The empirical evaluation is on MRBench, a benchmark of 1,214 middle-school mathematics dialogues. HPO-FT achieves the best Macro F1 (0.845), outperforming GPT-4o (0.812) and several single-agent, cooperative, and unstructured-adversarial baselines. Ablations indicate that removing the first distillation phase causes the largest performance drop, and removing the Devil’s Advocate also reduces performance substantially, suggesting that the structured adversarial protocol is central to the gains.

The paper’s main conclusion is that adversarial multi-agent structure improves reliable automated oversight of math tutoring responses more than simply increasing model size or using cooperative agents. It also emphasizes practical tradeoffs: the full system is slower than single-model inference, but may be useful for asynchronous grading or batch quality assurance. The authors note that validation is limited to middle-school mathematics and that cross-domain testing and deployment studies are needed.

finding.finding_summary: On MRBench, which consists of 1,214 middle-school mathematics dialogues, the proposed HPO-FT system achieved Macro F1 = 0.845, outperforming GPT-4o (0.812) by 3.3 percentage points. The task measures correct identification of math-related student mistakes and guidance quality in tutoring dialogues, not student learning gains.
finding.measure: Macro F1 on mistake identification and guidance quality classification for middle-school mathematics tutoring dialogues
finding.confidence_interval: 95% CI ±0.015 vs. GPT-4o for the reported significance test

finding.finding_summary: The full HPO-FT pipeline is substantially slower than a single Llama-3-8B call, with reported inference latency of 4.2 seconds total versus 0.4 seconds for a single-agent call and 1.2 seconds for a GPT-4o API call on average. The paper frames this as acceptable for batch evaluation but not ideal for real-time tutoring.
finding.measure: Inference latency / runtime per evaluation

paper_profiles.title: MathRobust-LV: Evaluation of Large Language Models’ Robustness to Linguistic Variations in Mathematical Reasoning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models used in educational math tools remain reliable when mathematically equivalent problems are reworded. The authors argue that real tutoring and assessment settings often involve instructors or students paraphrasing the same underlying problem, so a robust model should preserve accuracy under benign linguistic variation.

To test this, they introduce MathRobust-LV, a benchmark built from 130 high-school-level math problems drawn from MATH and scraped AoPS competition items, with 520 manually checked variants. The variants preserve numerical structure, solution logic, and final answers while changing surface wording, contexts, and/or variables across four controlled perturbation types, with the main experiments focusing on full rewriting plus variable substitution. They evaluate 34 open- and closed-source models in zero-shot pass@1 and compare baseline accuracy to variant accuracy.

The main finding is that many models, especially smaller ones, lose accuracy under linguistic variation: most open-source models drop by about 2-6 percentage points, with some 1.5B models dropping about 9-12 points. Larger models are more stable, and frontier models such as Gemini-2.5-pro and GPT-5 are comparatively robust, but even strong models show measurable degradation in some settings. The paper also shows that AoPS problems are substantially harder than MATH for many models, suggesting that linguistic/structural diversity stresses generalization beyond standard benchmark performance. The authors conclude that benchmark scores alone do not establish robust mathematical reasoning and note limitations including the small seed set, reliance on pass@1, and difficulty disentangling surface-form sensitivity from broader generalization.

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates whether LLMs can solve high-school math problems consistently under meaning-preserving linguistic variation. Across 34 models, most open-source systems showed lower pass@1 on the variant set than on the baseline, with typical drops of about 2-6 percentage points and larger drops for smaller models (e.g., OpenMath-Nemotron-1.5B: 75.36% to 63.84%, drop -11.52%; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: 58.44% to 48.85%, drop -9.59%). Frontier models were more stable, with Gemini-2.5-pro slightly improving (96.13% to 96.35%, +0.21) and GPT-5 dropping only 0.77 points.
finding.measure: Pass@1 accuracy on high-school-level math problem solving under baseline vs. linguistically varied equivalent problems
finding.study_size: n=34 models; n=130 seed problems; n=520 variants

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics educators (elementary, middle, and high school teachers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This exploratory comparative study asks how K-12 mathematics educators evaluate lesson plans created by human curriculum designers versus two generative AI systems: a customized GPT-4 model and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model. The paper focuses on educator preferences rather than student learning outcomes, examining which lesson plan source is preferred for warm-up, main tasks, cool-down, and overall quality across elementary, middle, and high school contexts.

The authors built a controlled web-based pairwise evaluation study in which experienced math educators (more than 10 years of teaching experience) reviewed anonymized lesson-plan pairs generated from 400 math curriculum queries aligned to Common Core State Standards. Twenty educators participated initially, and after attrition the final quantitative dataset included 529 complete lesson-plan pairs evaluated by 16 educators, with 2,116 binary preference judgments and 2,979 optional comments. The analysis combined descriptive pairwise comparisons, bootstrapped summaries, and qualitative thematic analysis of educator comments.

Overall, human-created lesson plans were preferred for warm-up activities, main instructional tasks, and overall quality, especially in elementary school, while GenAI plans were comparatively stronger in cool-down/concluding activities. Custom GPT-4 generally outperformed fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b among the AI systems, and the fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b became more competitive at higher grade levels, sometimes outperforming human plans in high school comparisons. Educator comments suggested that human plans were valued for differentiation, discourse, scaffolding, and student support, whereas AI plans were praised for structure and consistency but seen as weaker in pedagogical nuance and inclusive instruction. The paper concludes that GenAI is best positioned as a collaborative planning assistant rather than a replacement for teacher expertise.

finding.finding_summary: The study suggests GenAI lesson-plan generation could reduce educator planning burden by providing structured, adaptable lesson plans. Although no direct workload reduction was experimentally measured, educators and the authors describe GenAI as an assistive tool that may streamline lesson planning, and the discussion explicitly frames it as a collaborative planning aid rather than a replacement for teacher expertise.
finding.measure: Educator perceptions of lesson-plan usefulness and discussion of planning efficiency/workload
finding.study_size: n=16 educators (529 complete lesson-plan pairs; 2,116 binary evaluations; 2,979 comments)

finding.finding_summary: Educators evaluated whether lesson plans supported higher-order instructional features such as student discourse, collaboration, scaffolding, and lesson coherence. Human-authored plans were preferred for meaningful student discourse, group work, and differentiation, while GenAI plans were often seen as strong in structure but weaker in pedagogical nuance and interaction prompts.
finding.measure: Pairwise preferences for instructional quality dimensions and thematic analysis of comments about discourse, group work, and cognitive demand

finding.finding_summary: The paper examines educator preferences related to student engagement, usefulness of warm-up activities, and supportive instructional design. Human-created plans were generally preferred for warm-ups and for younger students because they were judged more engaging and developmentally appropriate, while GenAI was strongest in structured cool-downs; however, no direct student engagement outcomes were measured.
finding.measure: Educator preference judgments for warm-up relevance/quality/usefulness and qualitative comments about engagement

paper_profiles.title: Findings of MEGA: Maths Explanation with LLMs using the Socratic Method for Active Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper evaluates MEGA (Mathematics Explanations through Games by AI LLMs), an LLM-based tutoring approach that combines the Socratic method, chain-of-thought reasoning, simplified gamification with two answer choices, and formative feedback. The authors ask whether MEGA provides a better learning experience than a traditional step-by-step chain-of-thought (CoT) explanation for mathematics problems.

The study was conducted with university master’s students at Luleå University of Technology, Sweden, who acted as human evaluators. Students compared MEGA and CoT explanations for 120 randomly sampled math problems from two benchmark datasets: GSM8K (easier) and MATH (harder). Only three of six tested LLMs could follow the MEGA prompt; GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet were evaluated in depth. Students judged MEGA to be slightly better for GSM8K and substantially better for MATH, suggesting the interactive Socratic format is more helpful for difficult problems than for easy ones.

The paper also reports model-level accuracy analyses and qualitative feedback. MEGA and the embedded Socratic structure improved explanation quality in some cases, but hallucinations and errors still occurred at sub-question steps, showing that the method does not eliminate LLM unreliability. The authors conclude that MEGA is promising for personalized, student-centered math explanation, especially for harder problems, but its effectiveness depends on model capability and the complexity of the math task.

finding.finding_summary: MEGA was judged by student evaluators to provide better math explanations than traditional CoT, especially on the harder MATH set. For GSM8K, MEGA was only slightly preferred over CoT (26.67% vs 24.17%), while for MATH it was substantially preferred (47.5% vs 26.67%; p=0.0201), indicating stronger benefits for more difficult mathematics problems. However, model accuracy and the student-preference results were mixed because hallucinations still occurred at Socratic steps and some difficult items were answered incorrectly.
finding.measure: Student preference judgments of explanation quality; model accuracy on GSM8K and MATH math problems
finding.study_size: n=120 problems (60 GSM8K, 60 MATH) evaluated by student pairs; 34 students assigned, with pairwise annotations for 15 questions per pair

finding.finding_summary: Students generally preferred the interactive MEGA format over non-interactive CoT for engagement and perceived learning, particularly on harder problems. The paper reports that 77.78% of evaluators preferred interactive learning overall, though 22.22% preferred non-interactive learning, and qualitative comments frequently described MEGA as more engaging, fun, and motivating.
finding.measure: Student preference for interactive vs non-interactive learning; qualitative feedback on engagement and ease of understanding
finding.study_size: n=34 students (course participants); qualitative feedback from pairwise evaluations

finding.finding_summary: The intervention is explicitly framed as supporting active learning, critical thinking, and step-by-step problem solving through Socratic questioning and formative feedback. Students reported that the method helped them understand complex solutions by breaking problems into manageable parts, although the paper measures this through subjective comparison rather than direct skill tests.
finding.measure: Student judgments about clarity, understanding, and step-by-step reasoning quality
finding.study_size: n=120 evaluated math problems; 34 student participants

paper_profiles.title: LLM-Driven Rubric-Based Assessment of Algebraic Competence in Multi-Stage Block Coding Tasks with Design and Field Evaluation
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of assessing students’ mathematical competence in online learning environments when answers are multi-step, process-oriented, and not fully captured by correctness alone. The authors propose a rubric-based assessment framework powered by a large language model (LLM) to evaluate algebraic competence in multi-stage block coding tasks, with rubric dimensions covering knowledge and understanding, procedural skills, and values/attitudes.

The intervention was implemented on a Korean web-based learning platform (Algeomath) that recorded intermediate student responses and provided rule-based grading for closed-ended items and LLM-based scoring for open-ended explanations. The field study involved 42 middle school students who had previously learned quadratic equations and the quadratic formula, with varying prior experience in block-based programming. Students worked through a six-stage task sequence centered on solving consecutive-number problems formulated as quadratic equations and implemented with block coding.

The main findings concern the validity and practical usefulness of the assessment system rather than student learning gains from tutoring. LLM-generated rubric scores showed strong agreement with expert ratings (r=0.79, ρ=0.76; MAE=12.4, RMSE=15.8), and the platform revealed meaningful variation across rubric dimensions and learner clusters. Students performed relatively well on conceptual understanding and structured problem-solving, but weaker on block-based programming and proactive use of engineering tools; the authors conclude that the approach is scalable and useful for process-sensitive assessment, while noting limitations including the small dataset and restriction to quadratic equation problems.

finding.finding_summary: The paper primarily evaluates a rubric-based assessment system for algebraic competence in quadratic-equation block-coding tasks rather than testing an instructional intervention. In the field study with 42 middle school students, overall performance averaged 69.81 (SD=17.03), and rubric scores showed stronger performance on conceptual understanding (Rubrics 1 and 2 near 80) than on more complex computational application (Rubric 3 mean around 65) and proactive tool use (Rubric 5 mean around 50).
finding.measure: Overall achievement scores and rubric scores for algebraic competence in quadratic-equation/block-coding tasks

finding.finding_summary: The framework explicitly assessed process-oriented competencies such as metacognition, procedural reasoning, and explanation quality. Stage 6 required students to explain the relationship between block-coding outputs and algebraic solutions, and the rubric included knowledge/understanding plus procedural and attitudinal dimensions; however, the paper did not report a causal effect on these skills, only descriptive performance and alignment of LLM scoring with expert judgment.
finding.measure: Rubric dimensions, self-check survey, and open-ended reflection/explanation quality

finding.finding_summary: The study measured persistence, willingness to tackle real-world problems, and proactive use of computational tools as part of the rubric and self-check survey. Students showed relatively strong performance on the attitude-related Rubric 4 (mean near 80), but weaker performance on Rubric 5 (mean near 50), indicating uneven evidence of persistence and proactive tool use across the sample.
finding.measure: Rubric 4 and Rubric 5 scores; five-item self-check survey (Likert) and reflection
finding.std_deviation: Rubric 4 and 5 variability reported qualitatively; Rubric 5 described as having a comparatively wide SD

finding.finding_summary: The paper found that the LLM-based rubric assessment reduced manual grading burden while providing timely, process-sensitive feedback. In the field implementation, students received immediate grading and feedback after up to four attempts per item, and the authors conclude that LLM synthesis substantially reduced the cognitive and temporal burden of manual grading compared with expert scoring.
finding.measure: Assessment turnaround, automated grading/feedback workflow, expert burden reduction (descriptive)

paper_profiles.title: Automatic Generation of Question Hints for Mathematics Problems using Large Language Models in Educational Technology
paper_profiles.venue: FM-EduAssess at NeurIPS 2024 Workshop / Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can be used to generate pedagogically useful hints for secondary-level mathematics exercises. The authors focus on a specific tutoring task: given an incorrect student response to a math problem, can an LLM acting as a teacher produce a hint that helps another LLM acting as a student self-correct without revealing the answer? To study this, they build a two-stage pipeline: first, student models solve exercises and their errors are categorized; second, teacher models generate hints using either error-specific prompts or baseline prompts, and the student models revise their answers after receiving the hint.

The study uses four French high-school mathematics exercises from EvidenceB’s MIA Seconde software, grounded in cognitive-science-informed pedagogical summaries. The student models are GPT-3.5-turbo, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3; the teacher models are GPT-4o and Llama-3-8B-Instruct. The paper examines how temperature affects error rates, which hint prompts are most effective, and whether hints improve post-feedback accuracy. Results show that higher temperatures generally increase errors, specialized calculation-error prompts and the BaselineTwo prompt are the strongest hint generators, and hints improve revision accuracy—especially for GPT-3.5-turbo. The authors also find that Llama-3-8B-Instruct as a teacher sometimes performs as well as or better than GPT-4o, but they caution that the work is limited by a small exercise set, synthetic student simulation, and the lack of qualitative human evaluation of hint quality.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLM-generated hints can improve performance on high-school mathematics problem solving and answer revision, especially for GPT-3.5-turbo. Using the best prompts, the student models often corrected previously incorrect responses after receiving a hint; the paper reports accuracy increases across four exercises, but does not provide a single overall effect size. One concrete result reported is that the mean revision error rate for some prompt/model combinations reached 0.00 at certain temperatures (e.g., Mistral with baseline prompts at temperature 0.5, and GPT-3.5-turbo with BaselineTwo), indicating all sampled errors were corrected in those settings.
finding.measure: Accuracy on math exercise solving and post-hint revision; mean revision error rate

paper_profiles.title: Personalized Auto-Grading and Feedback System for Constructive Geometry Tasks Using Large Language Models on an Online Math Platform
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how large language models can be used to support automated grading and personalized feedback for open-ended and constructive mathematics tasks, with a focus on geometry. The authors develop and deploy an auto-grading and feedback system on the Korean Algeomath platform for constructive geometry tasks centered on circumcenter and circumcircle reasoning, including both open-ended explanations and dynamic geometry constructions.

The intervention combines rule-based grading for closed-ended and construction-based items with GPT-4-based few-shot grading for open-ended explanations. Feedback is generated from teacher-authored exemplars and adapts to the number of attempts remaining, aiming to scaffold student revisions without immediately revealing solutions. The system was piloted in four middle-school classes in South Korea with 79 students across 18 questions.

Results show strong agreement between automated grading and teacher judgments for closed-ended and construction tasks, and substantial agreement for open-ended explanations overall (agreement 0.866, κ=0.737 across 878 responses), though reliability varied by item. Expert review found feedback generally serviceable but inconsistent, with issues such as answer leakage, imprecise terminology, and tone escalation. Student response data suggested that feedback helped many learners correct errors quickly: 36.7% of initially incorrect responses were fixed on the next attempt, and most learning gains occurred after the first retry. However, carry-over effects to later questions were not statistically significant, and longer-term transfer remained unclear. The study concludes that LLMs can support scalable, teacher-aligned formative assessment in mathematics, but they require tighter control of terminology, scaffolding, and feedback design.

finding.finding_summary: The system supported mathematics learning in constructive geometry tasks, especially through iterative revision. Across all questions, 36.7% (260/708) of initially incorrect responses were corrected on the subsequent attempt after feedback, and the aggregate learning curve rose from about 0.60 correct on the first attempt to about 0.73 on the second attempt, then more slowly to about 0.80 by the fourth attempt.
finding.measure: Post-feedback correctness conversion rate; attempt-level cumulative correctness on geometry tasks
finding.study_size: n=79 students; 708 feedback-supported incorrect attempts; 18 questions

finding.finding_summary: Feedback appeared to support persistence and re-engagement in mathematics problem solving. The study reports that many students revised incorrect answers successfully after retries, with an overall 36.7% conversion rate, and feedback was designed to provide encouragement and sustain motivation across attempts; however, no direct validated motivation scale was reported for this main outcome analysis.
finding.measure: Attempt-level revisions; student survey items on learning experience and open-ended comments

finding.finding_summary: The system aimed to foster conceptual reasoning and iterative refinement rather than rote answer matching. Qualitative analysis showed that some students improved from vague answers to more precise, conceptually grounded explanations (e.g., moving from 'Equal' to correctly describing equal distances from the circumcenter to each vertex), but direct quantitative evidence for durable transfer or generalized critical thinking gains was limited.
finding.measure: Iterative answer refinement quality; qualitative rubric-based analysis of revised explanations

finding.finding_summary: The automated system substantially improved grading scalability and aligned closely with teacher judgments, especially for objective item types. Closed-ended and CGT items achieved 100% agreement with teacher scoring, and open-ended explanatory items achieved 0.866 agreement overall (Cohen’s κ=0.737 across 878 responses), indicating that LLM-assisted grading can reduce teacher workload while remaining reasonably consistent with human evaluation.
finding.measure: Agreement with teacher judgments; Cohen’s κ; automated grading performance

finding.finding_summary: The paper also focused on learners’ ability to represent and explain geometric concepts using digital tools, which goes beyond general numeracy into geometry-specific task performance. Survey ratings on five learning-experience items ranged from about 4.1 to 4.5/5, suggesting students perceived gains in using the tool to represent the circumcenter and explain its properties, though these were self-report outcomes rather than direct achievement tests.
finding.measure: Five-item student Likert survey on geometry understanding and digital representation

paper_profiles.title: Tutor CoPilot: A Human-AI Approach for Scaling Real-Time Expertise
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a generative AI system can improve live tutoring by providing tutors with real-time, expert-like instructional guidance during math sessions. The central problem is that novice tutors often struggle to respond effectively in the moment, especially when students make mistakes or need conceptual support, and traditional training is too costly and slow to scale.

The intervention, Tutor CoPilot, is a human-AI tool embedded in a virtual tutoring platform that generates strategy suggestions for tutors during live K-12 mathematics tutoring. It uses an adaptation method trained on expert reasoning and lets tutors choose among prompts such as asking guiding questions, prompting explanation, giving hints, or providing a worked example. The study randomized tutors, not students, across treatment and control conditions in a tutoring partnership with FEV Tutor and a Southern U.S. school district serving mostly Hispanic and economically disadvantaged students in grades 3-8.

The authors report that students whose tutors had access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets, with larger gains for lower-rated tutors (up to 9 percentage points) and less-experienced tutors (up to 7 percentage points). Treatment tutors also used more high-quality pedagogical strategies and fewer answer-giving strategies. Overall, the paper concludes that real-time AI support can modestly improve tutoring quality and short-term math learning, particularly for less effective tutors and priority student populations.

finding.finding_summary: Students whose tutors were assigned access to Tutor CoPilot were 4 percentage points more likely to pass exit tickets in mathematics (62% in control vs. 66% in treatment; p<0.01). Conditional on attempting the exit ticket, treated students were 3 percentage points more likely to pass it (p<0.01).
finding.measure: Mathematics exit ticket pass rate (unconditional and conditional on attempt)
finding.study_size: n=4136 sessions; 1800 students; 900 tutors in the abstract, 782 tutors at launch

finding.finding_summary: Tutor CoPilot modestly improved student session participation, with treated sessions showing a 0.09 increase in standardized participation points, though this estimate was not statistically significant. Student survey items on perceived tutor caring, understanding, and confidence that they can learn math did not show significant differences between treatment and control.
finding.measure: Participation points and student post-session survey responses
finding.study_size: n=4136 for participation; n=1931-1952 for survey items

finding.finding_summary: Treatment tutors used more strategies that support student reasoning and comprehension, including prompting students to explain and asking questions to guide thinking. The paper reports these strategies were used about 2 standard deviations more frequently on a z-scored log-odds scale in treatment versus control, while answer-giving and passive strategies were less common.
finding.measure: Classified tutor message strategies from 550,000+ chat messages
finding.effect_size: about 2 z-scored log-odds SD for key high-quality strategies

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed and evaluated as a scalable support tool for tutors, and the paper estimates an annual cost of about $20 per tutor based on observed usage. Although workload was not directly measured with a formal workload scale, the study frames Tutor CoPilot as a low-cost alternative to traditional training and reports practical usability improvements during pilot testing.
finding.measure: Estimated annual per-tutor cost and system usage patterns
finding.study_size: n=2000+ Tutor CoPilot uses; n=900 tutors assigned

paper_profiles.title: Awareness, acceptance, and adoption of Gen-AI by K-12 mathematics teachers: an empirical study integrating TAM and TPB
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines what drives K-12 mathematics teachers in China to adopt generative AI (Gen-AI) tools for instruction. The authors integrate the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), and an added construct of AI awareness to explain actual usage behavior rather than just intentions. The central question is whether perceptions such as usefulness and ease of use, along with social and control-related factors, predict teachers’ real-world Gen-AI use in mathematics teaching.

Data came from 230 mathematics teachers participating in a Beijing Normal University–Tencent WeChat Mini Program innovation group. Participants completed a 26-item survey, and the authors analyzed the data with PLS-SEM. The model included AI awareness, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, facilitating conditions, attitude, subjective norm, perceived behavioral control, and usage behavior. The study is not an instructional impact study and does not compare Gen-AI tutoring against standard instruction or other tutoring conditions; instead, it focuses on teachers’ acceptance and adoption behavior.

Results show that AI awareness significantly predicted perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and attitude, and had an indirect positive effect on usage behavior. Among the adoption predictors, attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control significantly predicted actual usage behavior, while perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and facilitating conditions did not. The authors conclude that teacher adoption of Gen-AI in mathematics is shaped more by awareness, attitudes, and social/behavioral control factors than by straightforward perceptions of usefulness or ease of use, and they recommend training and support that build AI awareness and collaborative implementation structures.

finding.finding_summary: The study finds that AI awareness, attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control significantly predict teachers’ Gen-AI usage behavior, suggesting the technology may support instructional efficiency and adoption in practice. In the structural model, usage behavior was explained by R² = 0.763, but this is a behavioral adoption outcome rather than a direct measure of workload reduction; no direct workload effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Self-reported usage behavior of Gen-AI in mathematics teaching

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly studies institutional and organizational determinants of Gen-AI adoption in K-12 mathematics teaching, including facilitating conditions, subjective norms, and perceived behavioral control. Facilitating conditions were not significant (beta=0.090, p=0.177), while subjective norm (beta=0.315, p=0.000) and perceived behavioral control (beta=0.286, p=0.000) were significant predictors of usage behavior.
finding.measure: Structural equation model paths predicting Gen-AI usage behavior from organizational/social factors
finding.confidence_interval: 95% BC CI reported for the model overall, but not for individual paths in text

finding.finding_summary: AI awareness significantly improved teachers’ attitudes toward Gen-AI (beta=0.525, p<0.001), which the authors interpret as reflecting greater openness and confidence in technology adoption. This is an adoption/attitudinal finding rather than a direct test of student durable skills, but it substantively concerns teachers’ technology-related judgment and control beliefs.
finding.measure: Attitude toward Gen-AI; AI awareness as a predictor in the adoption model

finding.finding_summary: The study shows that teachers’ attitudes toward Gen-AI significantly predicted actual usage behavior (beta=0.329, p<0.001), and AI awareness also significantly improved attitudes (beta=0.525, p<0.001). Although this is not a student affect study, it directly measures motivational and acceptance-related responses to Gen-AI among teachers.
finding.measure: Attitude toward Gen-AI and self-reported usage behavior

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not measure student mathematics achievement or numeracy outcomes, but it does study teachers’ adoption of Gen-AI for mathematics instruction. Because the research is about teachers’ use of a mathematics teaching tool rather than learner performance, no direct numeracy effect was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher usage behavior of Gen-AI for mathematics instruction

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review about how artificial intelligence should be integrated into education, with a focus on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper argues that the rapid adoption of ChatGPT and similar large language models creates both opportunities and risks in academic work and classroom practice, including hallucinations, overreliance on AI, ethical misuse, and uncertainty about appropriate institutional responses.

The article draws on the author’s experience at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences, combined with informal discussions with students and lecturers and a narrative review of prior literature. It uses this context to propose institutional guidelines for transparent AI use, a “culture of AI,” and practical recommendations such as workshops, formal AI literacy courses, and training in prompt engineering. The paper emphasizes that AI should be treated as a sparring partner rather than a tutor or ghostwriter, and that critical evaluation of AI outputs is essential.

Although the paper discusses how these ideas may also be useful for younger learners, its concrete case study and implementation recommendations are rooted in higher education. It does not test an intervention or compare student outcomes experimentally; instead, it offers a conceptual framework for responsible AI adoption and pedagogy. The main conclusion is that students and educators need explicit instruction and institutional support to use AI effectively, ethically, and critically.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are mutually reinforcing skills that should be intentionally taught to help students evaluate AI outputs, avoid hallucinations, and use AI responsibly. No empirical effect size is reported because this is a conceptual/narrative paper rather than an intervention study.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of critical thinking, prompt engineering competence, and AI literacy

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes institutional AI guidelines, workshops, dedicated budgets, and paid roles to support responsible AI adoption in higher education. These recommendations are based on the author’s case study at a Swiss university and narrative review, but the paper reports no quantitative institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Institutional policy/guideline discussion and implementation recommendations

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests that AI tools can help with curriculum design, brainstorming, and classroom preparation, potentially improving efficiency for lecturers and students. However, the paper does not measure workload reduction or productivity gains empirically.
finding.measure: Qualitative discussion of teacher planning, curriculum creation, and academic writing support

paper_profiles.title: Design and evaluation of ChatGPT-MWPS: an AI-enhanced learning system for improving primary students’ mathematical word problem solving
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents the design and evaluation of ChatGPT-MWPS, a generative AI-enhanced learning system intended to support primary students’ mathematical word problem solving. The study is motivated by the difficulty many elementary learners face when translating verbal math problems into mathematical representations and by the need for more adaptive, interactive scaffolding in mathematics instruction.

The system integrates ChatGPT via an API to provide step-by-step, individualized hints, adaptive scaffolding, and real-time feedback within a digital test-paper environment. It is designed for both classroom use and self-directed learning, and it includes teacher-facing functions such as batch question import, worksheet generation, and user management. The evaluation involved 52 fifth-grade students from a public primary school in Guangdong, China, along with three mathematics teachers.
