Methodologically, the study used a quasi-experimental-style system evaluation centered on usability testing rather than a comparative learning-outcome trial. Students completed a 40-minute interaction task and then rated the system on a 13-dimension usability scale; teachers also provided interview feedback about performance, content quality, and design priorities. Findings show generally favorable usability and strong student willingness to use the system, especially on reliability, information quality, and cognitive engagement, but also identify weaknesses in information display and design appeal. The authors conclude that generative AI can support personalized mathematics learning, though the interface, content filtering, and sequencing of hints need refinement for classroom effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: The system was evaluated for supporting fifth-grade mathematical word problem solving, and results indicated favorable usability for this math learning task. In student ratings (n=52), the system was viewed positively on information quality, system reliability, and cognitive engagement, suggesting it has potential to support word-problem solving instruction, though the study did not report achievement gains or a learning effect size.
finding.measure: Usability scale ratings related to mathematical word problem solving; teacher interview feedback on AI-generated solution quality

finding.finding_summary: Students reported generally favorable perceptions of the system’s usability and intention to use, with cognitive engagement emerging as one of the strongest correlates of intention to use (r=0.969, p<0.05). Only 11.7% of intention-to-use responses were neutral/disagree/strongly disagree, indicating strong acceptance and engagement with the AI tutoring environment among the 52 fifth graders.
finding.measure: Usability scale dimensions including Cognitive Engagement and Intention to Use

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests the system supports cognitive and metacognitive processes involved in problem solving through step-by-step reasoning hints and adaptive scaffolding. Cognitive engagement correlated strongly with intention to use (r=0.969), and learnability also correlated with intention to use (r=0.720), indicating that students perceived the system as helping them think through problems more effectively, although no direct test of metacognitive gains was reported.
finding.measure: Usability scale dimensions including Cognitive Engagement, Learnability, and Intention to Use

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed to streamline mathematics support through batch question import, automated worksheet generation, and teacher-controlled hint generation, implying potential productivity benefits. However, teacher interviews reported latency during peak usage, some access failures, and a need to expand server capacity from 100 to about 200 concurrent users, so the operational performance was promising but not yet fully efficient in practice.
finding.measure: Teacher interview feedback on system stability, latency, access, and workflow functions; usability ratings for system reliability and general availability

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a narrative review and conceptual overview of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. The paper asks how AI tools may transform teaching and learning, what educational applications they are already being used for, and what ethical and practical challenges come with their adoption.

Rather than testing an intervention, the authors synthesize prior literature on AI-enabled education tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, automated grading, and learning analytics. The discussion is framed around benefits for students (personalized learning, feedback, motivation, engagement, confidence) and for teachers/administrators (assessment support, workload reduction, monitoring, and decision support), alongside concerns about bias, privacy, reliability, academic integrity, and insufficient teacher preparation.

The paper is not an empirical K-12 mathematics study and does not compare ChatGPT or other generative AI tools against instructional baselines such as standard instruction, tutoring, peer support, adaptive software, homework help, or no intervention. Its main conclusion is that AI may have promise in education, but responsible implementation requires attention to ethics, pedagogy, equity, and teacher support, and further research is needed to establish effectiveness.

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a PRISMA-based systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education from 2016 to 2022. It addresses the broad question of how AI has been used in higher education, where the research has been conducted, who the intended users are, and what trends have emerged over time.

The review screened 371 records and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles. The studies were mostly about undergraduate populations and were concentrated in language learning, computer science, and engineering. The authors coded the literature both deductively and inductively, identifying five major uses of AI in higher education: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning.

The paper concludes that AI in higher education has grown rapidly, especially in 2021–2022, with China now leading publication output. It also finds that colleges of education have become the most common first-author affiliation, suggesting increased educator involvement. Overall, the review argues that AI is being used mainly to extend current instructional and administrative practices, while also highlighting gaps such as limited research on graduate students, managers, and more novel uses of AI.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI was frequently used to improve efficiency in assessment, feedback, learning analytics, question generation, and instructional management. Across 138 studies, 26 studies used automatic assessment and 19 focused on managing student learning, indicating that a substantial portion of the literature targets workload reduction and data-driven support rather than direct learning gains.
finding.measure: Frequency and thematic coding of AI uses across included studies

finding.finding_summary: The review shows AI was used across multiple academic content areas, especially language learning, computer science, and engineering. However, because this is a descriptive systematic review rather than an intervention study, it does not estimate student achievement effects; it only reports where AI applications were concentrated and how they were used.
finding.measure: Subject-domain distribution of included studies

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies used AI to support student persistence, self-testing, feedback, and emotion-related processes, and the review identifies these as recurring purposes of AI assistants and assessment tools. For example, the authors note AI being used to examine student emotions and support goal persistence, but the review itself does not aggregate outcome effects.
finding.measure: Thematic coding of intended AI uses related to motivation, persistence, feedback, and emotion

finding.finding_summary: The review includes several studies involving higher-order thinking, reflection, self-regulated learning, and student support tools that relate to durable skills. These are discussed as uses of AI in assessment and AI assistants, but the paper does not provide pooled effect estimates or causal comparisons for these skills.
finding.measure: Thematic coding of included studies mentioning reflection, self-regulation, and higher-order thinking

paper_profiles.title: War of the chatbots: Bard, Bing Chat, ChatGPT, Ernie and beyond. The new AI gold rush and its impact on higher education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article addresses the rapid emergence of large language model chatbots—especially ChatGPT, Bing Chat, Bard, and Baidu’s Ernie—and asks how these tools are affecting higher education. The paper is primarily a broad review and comparison of the tools’ corporate histories, technical capabilities, risks, and likely implications for assessment, teaching, learning, and academic integrity. It is not a K-12 mathematics study and does not test an instructional intervention in school settings.

The authors review English- and Chinese-language literature and then perform a comparative, hands-on assessment of selected chatbots on a range of higher-education-relevant tasks. The article emphasizes practical issues such as hallucinations, bias, source reliability, the ability to answer current-events questions, and the implications for plagiarism detection and assessment redesign. It also discusses how universities and instructors may need to revise assessment practices, teaching approaches, and integrity policies in response to generative AI.

The main conclusion is that, despite dramatic hype, current chatbots are uneven and unreliable: GPT-4 and ChatGPT-3.5 performed best among the systems compared, while Bing Chat and Bard were substantially weaker on the authors’ tests. The paper argues that chatbot development is moving fast but remains insufficiently trustworthy for many academic uses, and it recommends that higher education institutions adapt assessment and pedagogy accordingly.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI is already forcing institutions to reconsider academic integrity policy, assessment design, and classroom practice. It does not report a formal effect size or experimental outcome; instead, it synthesizes literature and the authors’ comparative chatbot testing to conclude that institutions should adapt because current LLMs are powerful but unreliable.
finding.measure: Literature synthesis and comparative benchmark tasks relevant to higher education policy and assessment

finding.finding_summary: The article notes that chatbots may reduce workload and speed up tasks such as drafting, summarizing, and generating teaching materials, but it treats these benefits as prospective rather than experimentally verified. No quantitative effect estimate is reported; the discussion is based on examples and prior literature on productivity support.
finding.measure: Illustrative task performance and discussion of workload reduction for writing, sourcing, and editing

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main comparative test examines performance on higher-education academic tasks such as answering questions, summarizing, and producing written/code outputs across chatbot systems. The authors report that GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 performed best, while Bing Chat and Bard performed poorly on several tasks; however, no standardized academic score or effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Multi-disciplinary test of chatbot responses on academic assignment/exam-like tasks

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT and large language models in academia: opportunities and challenges
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This editorial discusses the emergence of ChatGPT and other large language models (LLMs) and their implications for academic work, including writing, grant preparation, programming, and education. The paper is not an intervention study; instead, it offers a narrative review and opinion-based discussion of where LLMs may be useful and where they pose risks, especially around hallucinations, plagiarism, bias, and misuse.

In the education section, the authors argue that LLMs may support students and educators across K-12, undergraduate, and graduate contexts by providing quick answers, practice questions, feedback, lesson planning support, and assessment tools. They also warn that overreliance may weaken skill development and enable cheating, and they recommend that educators adapt pedagogy and assessment to account for LLM use. No primary data are collected, and no formal comparison groups or outcomes are tested.

Because the article is a perspective editorial, it does not report empirical results about student learning, teacher effectiveness, or institutional impact. Its main conclusion is normative: LLMs should be embraced cautiously, but their outputs must be checked, their biases measured, and their use transparently documented.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs may improve academic and educational workflows but also create concerns about plagiarism, bias, access inequities, and policy compliance. It does not present empirical institutional outcomes; instead, it recommends that journals, universities, and funders establish rules for disclosure, authorship, and acceptable use of generative AI.
finding.measure: Not an empirical measure; narrative discussion of policies, authorship guidance, and institutional practices

finding.finding_summary: The editorial claims that ChatGPT and related LLMs can increase efficiency in academic writing, lesson planning, assessment creation, coding, and other research tasks. These assertions are illustrative rather than empirical, and the paper reports no measured productivity outcomes, sample sizes, or effect sizes.
finding.measure: Not an empirical measure; narrative discussion of productivity and workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses potential benefits of LLMs for writing, editing, summarizing, and grammar support, while also warning about plagiarism and inaccurate text generation. No direct evidence is presented on writing quality, reading comprehension, or literacy outcomes in K-12 students.
finding.measure: Not an empirical measure; narrative discussion of writing/editing support

finding.finding_summary: The editorial suggests that students may use ChatGPT in ways that support prompt engineering, fact checking, editing, and critical evaluation of outputs, but it also warns that overreliance may undermine critical skills such as writing and independent judgment. These claims are conceptual and not backed by direct measurement.
finding.measure: Not an empirical measure; narrative discussion of critical thinking, editing, and prompt engineering

paper_profiles.title: Facilitating Cognitive Load Management and Improved Learning Outcomes and Attitudes in Middle School Technology and Vocational Education Through AI Chatbot
paper_profiles.venue: Journal of Technical Education and Training
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study asks whether an AI-based chatbot can reduce cognitive load and improve learning outcomes for junior secondary school students in a content-heavy Basic Technology course. The authors frame the work in Cognitive Load Theory, arguing that an AI tutor may help students manage the demands of an overloaded middle-school curriculum by providing individualized, paced, and interactive support.

The intervention was a purpose-built chatbot called iLearnTech, built on the Landbot platform and used as the main tutoring tool for Basic Technology. The study used a pre-test/post-test control group quasi-experimental design with 120 JSS2 students (ages 12–14) from four public schools in Ibadan, Nigeria; 60 students used the chatbot and 60 received traditional instruction without the chatbot over eight weeks (24 class sessions).

Outcomes included perceived cognitive load, Basic Technology achievement, attitude toward learning, and retention measured four weeks later. Compared with the control group, the chatbot group showed significantly lower post-test cognitive load, higher achievement, more positive attitudes, and better retention. The paper concludes that AI chatbots can help address cognitive overload in junior secondary education and may improve learning in resource-constrained settings, though the study is limited to one subject area and short-term retention.

finding.finding_summary: Students who used the iLearnTech chatbot outperformed the control group on the Basic Technology Achievement Test after eight weeks. Post-test scores were 7.8 (SD=1.2) for the experimental group versus 6.3 (SD=1.4) for controls, with a significant difference (t=6.32, p=0.000) and a very large effect size (d=1.15).
finding.measure: Basic Technology Achievement Test (BTAT)

finding.finding_summary: The chatbot group reported more positive attitudes toward learning Basic Technology than the control group. Post-test SAS scores were 76.5 (SD=8.3) for the experimental group and 67.2 (SD=9.1) for the control group, a significant difference (t=5.84, p=0.000) with a very large effect size (d=1.07).
finding.measure: Students’ Attitude Survey (SAS)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved short-term retention of Basic Technology concepts. Four weeks after instruction, the experimental group scored 7.2 (SD=1.3) on the retention test compared with 5.6 (SD=1.5) for the control group, a statistically significant difference (t=6.18, p=0.000) with a very large effect size (d=1.13).
finding.measure: Students’ Retention Test (SRT)

finding.finding_summary: Perceived cognitive load was lower in the chatbot group than in the control group at post-test. The experimental group’s mean cognitive load score was 42.3 (SD=11.2) versus 58.7 (SD=12.1) for the control group, with a significant difference (t=-7.62, p=0.000) and a very large effect size (d=1.39).
finding.measure: Cognitive Load Measure (adapted NASA-TLX)

paper_profiles.title: Improving Online Education Through Constant Feedback Using Deep Learning and Integration with Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether combining a deep learning performance-prediction model with GPT-4-generated feedback can improve outcomes in an online education setting. The authors argue that traditional feedback in virtual courses is too infrequent and not personalized enough, and they propose an automated feedback system (AFS) that continuously monitors student activity and sends weekly, individualized recommendations.

The study was conducted in a Digital Art for Film and Video Games course with two groups of adult learners. A control group (n=39) received the same teachers, instruction, and flipped-classroom methodology as the experimental group (n=42), but without the AFS; the experimental group received weekly predictions and personalized feedback generated from a deep learning model trained on prior student data and interpreted by GPT-4. The groups were not equivalently formed at baseline, and the paper reports a significant initial knowledge difference favoring the control group, so this is a quasi-experimental comparison rather than a randomized trial.

Results showed higher quiz scores, recorded-session engagement, live-session participation, forum activity, and portfolio scores in the experimental group, while average practice scores did not significantly differ. The authors conclude that continuous predictive feedback paired with an LLM can improve engagement and several performance indicators, and they argue that the system may scale individualized monitoring and support for larger cohorts. However, the study is in a higher-education/vocational arts context, not K-12 mathematics, and the paper’s strongest evidence is for engagement and course-performance metrics rather than specific learning gains on standardized academic tests.

finding.finding_summary: The experimental group outperformed the control group on quiz scores and portfolio assessment scores after receiving weekly predictive feedback via the AFS. Quiz scores averaged 0.81 (SD=0.18) for the experimental group versus 0.67 (SD=0.19) for the control group, with t=3.23, p<0.01, Cohen’s d=0.74. Portfolio assessment scores were also higher in the experimental group (0.73, SD=0.26) than in the control group (0.69, SD=0.19), although this difference was not statistically significant (t=0.69, p=0.49, d=0.16).
finding.measure: Quiz scores and portfolio assessment scores
finding.effect_size: d=0.74 for quiz scores; d=0.16 for portfolio scores
finding.std_deviation: Quiz SDs: 0.18 experimental, 0.19 control; Portfolio SDs: 0.26 experimental, 0.19 control

finding.finding_summary: The AFS was associated with higher student engagement across multiple measures. Recorded session engagement was 0.84 (SD=0.22) in the experimental group compared with 0.65 (SD=0.12) in the control group, t=4.33, p<0.01, d=0.99. Live session participation was 0.61 (SD=0.25) versus 0.42 (SD=0.17), t=3.62, p<0.01, d=0.83, and forum activity was 0.62 (SD=0.37) versus 0.37 (SD=0.23), t=3.47, p<0.01, d=0.80. These are large engagement effects, indicating improved participation and involvement under continuous feedback.
finding.measure: Recorded session engagement, live session participation, forum activity
finding.std_deviation: Recorded session SDs: 0.22 experimental, 0.12 control; Live participation SDs: 0.25 experimental, 0.17 control; Forum activity SDs: 0.37 experimental, 0.23 control

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that the predictive-feedback workflow scales individualized monitoring and reduces the burden of manual tracking and intervention. Although no formal workload metric was reported, the system was described as enabling weekly automated prediction, JSON generation, and delivery of personalized messages to hundreds of students simultaneously, with the authors emphasizing time and resource savings for educators.
finding.measure: Scalability of monitoring and feedback delivery; educator workload implications
finding.study_size: n=81 in the comparison, with an additional production cohort of 116 mentioned

paper_profiles.title: Secondary Education (High School) in China
paper_profiles.venue: Education in China and the World
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This book chapter provides a descriptive and comparative overview of China’s general upper secondary education system, focusing on educational effectiveness, resource allocation, and indicators of school quality. Rather than evaluating a specific intervention, it synthesizes official statistics and international datasets from OECD, PISA 2018, China’s Ministry of Education, and other national sources to characterize trends in enrollment, graduation, staffing, infrastructure, and student outcomes.

The chapter’s central question is how China’s high school system compares internationally on key measures of access, resources, and educational performance. It reports that China has very high gross enrollment and graduation rates, strong PISA performance in reading, mathematics, and science, favorable student–teacher ratios, high teacher credential levels, and substantial digital infrastructure, while also noting lower per-student expenditure and relatively low proportions of teachers with master’s degrees compared with some peers.

Because the chapter is a policy-oriented descriptive analysis rather than an intervention study, it does not test AI tutoring or compare instructional conditions. Its main conclusion is that China’s high school education has achieved broad access and strong academic outcomes, but continued improvement is needed in funding, advanced teacher qualifications, and some aspects of educational quality and equity. The chapter also argues for ongoing development of differentiated, high-quality high school education supported by policy reform and infrastructure investment.

finding.finding_summary: Chinese high school students scored an average of 630 points in mathematics on PISA 2018, placing China first among the compared countries. The chapter interprets this as evidence of strong mathematical reasoning and problem-solving skills, with China outperforming peers such as the ROK (545) and Japan (540).
finding.measure: PISA 2018 mathematics score

finding.finding_summary: Chinese high school students averaged 598 points in reading on PISA 2018, the highest among the compared countries. The chapter states that this reflects strong reading comprehension and interpretation skills, with performance above France (536), Japan (517), the U.S. (514), and the ROK (533).
finding.measure: PISA 2018 reading score

finding.finding_summary: Chinese high school students scored an average of 631 points in science on PISA 2018, ranking first among the countries compared. The chapter interprets this as strong science literacy and the ability to apply scientific concepts to complex scenarios; the U.S. scored 510 and Japan 540 for comparison.
finding.measure: PISA 2018 science score

finding.finding_summary: The chapter reports mixed non-cognitive results from PISA 2018. China scored relatively poorly on growth mindset (0.29, last among the core countries) and resilience (0.02, fifth among the six core countries analyzed), but showed a relative strength in mastery goal orientation (0.13, second among the six core countries).
finding.measure: PISA 2018 student questionnaire scales: growth mindset, resilience, mastery goal orientation

finding.finding_summary: The chapter presents mixed evidence on durable skills measured through PISA school-climate and non-cognitive scales. Chinese students showed positive scores for student cooperation (0.19), teacher support (0.25), and adaptive instruction (0.27), suggesting a supportive classroom climate, but the discussion also notes weaker growth mindset and resilience, indicating uneven development of collaboration-related and adaptive learning skills.
finding.measure: PISA 2018 school climate scales and related non-cognitive indicators

finding.finding_summary: At the system level, the chapter finds high and improving Chinese high school access, completion, staffing, and infrastructure. It reports a gross enrollment rate of 56% in 2020, a graduation rate of 98.3%, a student–teacher ratio of 12.8 in 2021, teacher bachelor’s-degree attainment near 98.7% in 2021, and strong digital infrastructure (e.g., Wi-Fi coverage 76.3%).
finding.measure: Enrollment, graduation, staffing, infrastructure, and expenditure indicators from OECD/MOE/NBS/PISA

finding.finding_summary: The chapter suggests improving resource allocation efficiency through a decreasing student–teacher ratio and rising per-student expenditure. China’s student–teacher ratio fell from 13.4 in 2017 to 12.8 in 2021, while per-student expenditure rose from USD 3,618 in 2017 to USD 6,180 in 2022, indicating better resourcing and potentially more individualized support.
finding.measure: Student–teacher ratio and per-student expenditure

paper_profiles.title: Institutional Support for Academic Engagement in Online and Blended Learning Environments: Exploring Affective, Behavioral, and Cognitive Dimensions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how a university can measure and model student academic engagement in online and blended learning environments, using the Academic Communities of Engagement (ACE) framework as the basis for instrument development. The authors address a measurement problem: how to capture affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement, and how to assess the institutional support structures that may facilitate those forms of engagement.

The study was conducted at a private, not-for-profit university in Colombia with 1,295 students (1,165 undergraduate and 130 graduate) enrolled in online, blended, live-remote, and fully asynchronous courses during the COVID-19 period. The researchers developed and translated the ACE-HE survey, then used confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling to test the engagement and support models. The measurement models fit well, and the structural model showed a very strong positive relationship between overall institutional support for academic engagement and academic engagement (β = 0.915, p < .001). However, when support and engagement dimensions were tested separately, only affective support directly predicted its matching engagement dimension; behavioral and cognitive support did not directly predict their corresponding engagement dimensions, though affective support also predicted behavioral and cognitive engagement.

Overall, the paper concludes that the ACE framework is useful for measuring engagement in online/blended higher education, but that its support-to-engagement relationships may be more interconnected and less one-to-one than originally theorized. The authors argue for expanding ACE to include school/institutional support structures and environmental barriers, and they suggest that institutions should consider supports beyond individual courses, such as technical help, advising, and other academic resources.

finding.finding_summary: The study found strong evidence that institutional support for academic engagement was positively associated with academic engagement overall (β = 0.915, p < .001, n = 1,253). In the separate dimension model, support for affective engagement was strongly and positively related to affective engagement (β = 1.163, p < .001), and also positively predicted behavioral engagement (β = 0.802, p < .001) and cognitive engagement (β = 0.589, p < .001).
finding.measure: ACE-HE survey measures of affective, behavioral, and cognitive engagement; structural equation modeling of engagement constructs

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that the Institutional Support for Academic Engagement model had good fit and that institutional support structures were meaningfully associated with student engagement in the university context (β = 0.915, p < .001, n = 1,253). The authors conclude that institutions can play an important role in supporting online and blended student engagement through course and non-course support structures, and they propose an expanded ACE framework that includes the school/institutional community.
finding.measure: Structural equation modeling of institutional support for academic engagement; CFA/SEM fit statistics

paper_profiles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: Computer-Assisted Learning and AI-guided Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews causal and quasi-causal evidence on computer-assisted learning (CAL) and AI-guided tutoring in education, with a strong emphasis on mathematics, and then presents new observational evidence on the diffusion of generative AI in Italy. The review asks when AI-enabled learning tools improve achievement, how implementation conditions shape results, and whether these technologies can reduce or widen educational inequalities. It situates generative AI within the broader CAL literature, arguing that the educational value of AI depends heavily on pedagogy, teacher support, and implementation fidelity rather than on access to technology alone.

The empirical review synthesizes several K-12 and secondary-school studies comparing CAL or AI tutoring to traditional instruction, no intervention, or alternative tutoring models. Across cited experiments, well-designed CAL and AI-supported interventions often produce positive math gains, especially when paired with teacher coaching, structured scaffolding, or human tutoring; however, answer-giving AI can suppress learning relative to no AI access. The paper also highlights implementation and equity concerns such as digital divides, cognitive offloading, and variable uptake across regions.

The paper’s original empirical contribution is an observational study using weekly region-level Google Trends data on ChatGPT searches across Italian regions. It finds that adoption was initially concentrated in higher-income regions and later diffused as digital infrastructure improved, but notable regional disparities persisted. The authors conclude that equitable benefits from AI in education require targeted policy, infrastructure investment, and pedagogical integration, because technological availability alone is insufficient to ensure learning gains or equal access.

finding.finding_summary: The paper synthesizes multiple studies showing that CAL and AI tutoring often improve mathematics achievement, but effects depend strongly on design and implementation. Reported effects range from no significant effect in some software-based interventions to positive gains such as d=0.15 to 0.56, including Büchel et al. (2022) with +0.21 SD and +0.24 SD for CAL arms, Hirata (2022) with +0.56 SD short-term gains, Oreopoulos et al. (2024) with +0.12 to +0.22 SD, and Bastani et al. (2024) where GPT-Tutor improved practice performance (+0.361) while GPT-Base hurt later test performance (-0.054).
finding.measure: Math test scores, arithmetic scores, standardized math achievement, exercise/test performance
finding.study_size: multiple_studies_reported; key examples include n=6,400, n=870, n=3,200, and n=477
finding.effect_size: d=0.12 to d=0.56; some findings reported as +0.21 SD, +0.24 SD, +0.36 SD, -0.054
finding.std_deviation: reported in SD for several studies; otherwise not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies literacy-related gains in a generative AI intervention that targeted English alongside digital and AI skills. In De Simone et al. (2025), students receiving Copilot-based tutoring improved by +0.23 SD in English and +0.31 SD overall, indicating that AI-supported tutoring can improve language-related academic outcomes in low-income secondary settings when paired with teacher supervision.
finding.measure: Standardized English test
finding.study_size: n=414 complete cases (447 participants; 857 eligible students)

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports gains in engagement-related outcomes in studies where students or tutors used AI-supported systems. Thomas et al. (2024) found statistically significant improvements in engagement alongside achievement for hybrid tutoring versus adaptive software alone, and Wang et al. (2024) found tutors with Tutor CoPilot used more effective pedagogical strategies, which likely supported more engaged tutoring interactions. The paper also notes that some AI designs may reduce engagement through passive answer-seeking behavior, so the overall picture is mixed across interventions.
finding.measure: Engagement measures, tutoring interaction quality, classroom participation proxies
finding.study_size: approximately n=500 across three quasi-experimental studies; n=1,800 students in Tutor CoPilot RCT

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively discusses metacognition and self-regulation as outcomes of generative AI tutoring. Fan et al. (2024), reviewed in the paper, found that ChatGPT improved the immediate quality of a writing product but was associated with lower use of metacognitive strategies such as planning, monitoring, and self-evaluation, suggesting cognitive offloading and weaker durable learning processes. This is presented as evidence that AI can boost short-term performance while potentially harming deeper learning behaviors.
finding.measure: Metacognitive strategy use, self-regulated learning behaviors, writing task quality

finding.finding_summary: A central finding of the paper is that AI adoption in education is shaped by regional inequality and digital infrastructure rather than technology access alone. Using weekly Google Trends data on ChatGPT searches in Italy, the authors find adoption was initially concentrated in higher-income regions and then diffused as infrastructure improved, but persistent regional disparities remained, implying that AI can reinforce or reflect existing structural divides without targeted policy support.
finding.measure: Weekly regional Google Trends search intensity for ChatGPT in education/employment category

paper_profiles.title: The Impact of AI-Based Learning on Academic Performance
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examines whether AI-assisted personalised learning improves academic performance compared with traditional instruction in Portuguese secondary school science classes. The authors focus on a practical classroom question: whether generative AI and related AI learning tools can produce better learning gains than standard teacher-led methods in real school settings.

Using a non-randomised two-shot pre-test/post-test quasi-experimental design, the study compared two naturally formed Grade 10 groups in a public secondary school in central Portugal. The experimental group received AI-assisted instruction through platforms including Brisk Teaching, Khanmigo, ChatGPT 4.0 Turbo, and Quizizz AI, while the control group followed conventional teaching methods such as lectures, textbook work, and teacher-led questioning. The intervention covered two science units: Energy in the Ecosystem and Heredity and Variation, with achievement measured by a 40-item curriculum-aligned test and learner factors measured through Likert-scale questionnaires.

Results showed that both groups improved from pre-test to post-test, but the AI-supported group improved substantially more. Pre-test differences between groups were not statistically significant, while post-test scores were significantly higher in the AI group. The authors also report strong positive learner perceptions related to engagement, prior knowledge, and learning preferences, suggesting that AI-based personalised instruction was associated with higher motivation and comprehension. Overall, the paper concludes that AI-driven personalised learning can be an effective approach for improving STEM learning outcomes in secondary education, though the study remains quasi-experimental and context-specific.

finding.finding_summary: Students in the AI-driven personalised learning group achieved significantly higher post-test performance than the traditional instruction group on two science units, Energy in the Ecosystem and Heredity and Variation. In the AI group, mean scores increased from 15.60 to 33.20 on Unit 3 and from 15.17 to 36.37 on Unit 4; the corresponding between-group post-test comparisons were significant (t=5.0570 and t=6.2887, p=0.0001).
finding.measure: 40-item multiple-choice achievement test aligned to the science curriculum units
finding.std_deviation: SD=4.21 pre / 3.48 post (Unit 3 AI); SD=3.06 pre / 4.92 post (Unit 4 AI); SD=5.14 pre / 4.84 post (Unit 3 control); SD=3.95 pre / 4.93 post (Unit 4 control)

finding.finding_summary: The study found strong positive learner perceptions of AI-supported instruction for engagement and motivation. The overall engagement mean was 4.48/5 and was interpreted as 'Very Highly Influenced,' with the highest item being timely AI feedback (M=4.80) and students reporting that AI-adapted personalized learning paths were more engaging than traditional methods (M=4.57).
finding.measure: Student engagement Likert-scale questionnaire

finding.finding_summary: The paper also reports a positive association between AI-based learning and students' comprehension and collaboration-related preferences, but this is secondary to the achievement and engagement outcomes. Students rated peer collaboration positively (M=4.58) and showed high endorsement of AI-supported personalized learning as helpful for adapting to strengths and weaknesses, suggesting potential support for collaborative and self-monitoring habits.
finding.measure: Learning preferences questionnaire items and engagement survey responses

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a PRISMA-based systematic review of artificial intelligence (AI) research in higher education from 2016 to 2022. The authors ask where the research was conducted, who authored it, what academic levels and subject areas were studied, and how AI was being used across higher education settings.

The review screened 371 records and included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles. The evidence base is largely descriptive and bibliometric rather than intervention-based: it maps countries, author affiliations, academic levels, subject domains, intended users, and functional uses of AI such as assessment/evaluation, prediction, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning.

The sample was dominated by undergraduate studies, with language learning, computer science, and engineering most common. The review concludes that AIEd research in higher education grew sharply in 2021–2022, shifted geographically toward China, and increasingly involved education faculty. It also notes that many uses of AI remain traditional—especially assessment and prediction—and calls for more research on understudied populations, graduate learners, and more innovative uses such as ChatGPT.

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI in higher education is commonly used to improve efficiency in assessment, prediction, and student-data management. Across 138 studies, the most frequent functional uses included assessment/evaluation and predicting, with automatic assessment appearing in 26 studies and managing student learning in 19 studies, suggesting AI is often used to reduce grading and analysis workload rather than to measure learning gains directly.
finding.measure: Systematic review coding of functional uses of AI across included studies

paper_profiles.title: The Effect of a One-on-One Dialogue-Based Mathematical Intelligent Tutoring System for Learning Equivalent Fraction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether a one-on-one dialogue-based mathematical intelligent tutoring system (ITS) can improve elementary students’ learning of equivalent fractions. The study was motivated by the limited number of mathematics ITSs in the literature and by the potential of dialogue-based agents to provide interactive, adaptive tutoring that more closely resembles classroom instruction.

The authors developed an ITS with a talking-head interface in which a computer agent asks scripted questions, detects errors and misconceptions from student responses, and provides adaptive guidance or feedback. The system was designed around 4th-grade equivalent-fraction content in Taiwan. A quasi-experimental study compared 39 students using the ITS with 37 students receiving traditional classroom instruction over two hours, with pretest and post-test parallel measures of equivalent fraction and a learning-interest questionnaire.

Results indicated that both groups improved significantly from pretest to post-test on equivalent-fraction achievement, but the ITS group improved significantly more than the traditional instruction group. The paper also reports significant gains for the ITS group across genders and ability levels. Learning interest increased in both groups, but there was no significant difference between the ITS and control conditions on interest. Overall, the study suggests that a dialogue-based math ITS can support elementary students’ fraction learning, though it did not clearly outperform teacher-led instruction on motivation.

finding.finding_summary: In a quasi-experiment with 76 fourth-grade students (experimental n=39, control n=37), both the ITS and traditional instruction improved equivalent-fraction achievement, but the dialogue-based ITS produced significantly better learning effectiveness than classroom instruction. The paper reports significant pretest-to-posttest gains on parallel equivalent-fraction tests, though no exact effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Parallel pretest/post-test equivalent-fraction achievement tests

finding.finding_summary: Learning interest increased significantly in both the experimental and control groups, indicating that instruction of either type could improve interest in equivalent-fraction learning. However, there was no significant difference between the ITS and traditional instruction conditions on interest, so the intervention did not show a clear motivational advantage.
finding.measure: Learning interest questionnaire administered pre- and post-intervention

paper_profiles.title: Flipped classroom improves student learning in health professions education: a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This meta-analysis asks whether flipped classroom instruction improves student learning compared with traditional classroom teaching in health professions education. The authors note that student perceptions of flipped classrooms had often been positive, but evidence on actual learning outcomes had not been synthesized in a meta-analysis focused on objective performance measures.

The review included 28 comparative studies published in peer-reviewed journals from 2012 to 2017, covering medical, pharmacy, nursing, dental, public health, and related learners. Included studies had between-subject comparisons of flipped versus traditional instruction, used pre-class video lectures plus face-to-face class meetings, and measured learning with objective assessments such as exams or post-tests. The pooled result showed a significant advantage for flipped classrooms overall (SMD = 0.33, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.46, p < 0.001), with substantial heterogeneity but no evidence of publication bias.

Moderator analyses suggested the flipped classroom effect was robust across research designs, student types, and several implementation features. The one instructional feature associated with a larger effect was the use of quizzes at the start of in-class sessions to check understanding of pre-class materials (SMD = 0.56 vs. 0.26 without quizzes). The paper also found that most students in the included preference surveys favored flipped classrooms over traditional classes. No long-term retention studies were included, and the paper explicitly calls for future longitudinal research on retention.

finding.finding_summary: Across 28 comparative studies (total n=4,715; 2,295 flipped, 2,420 traditional), flipped classrooms produced a significant improvement in objective student learning outcomes versus traditional classrooms. The pooled standardized mean difference was SMD = 0.33 (95% CI 0.21 to 0.46, p < 0.001), indicating a small-to-moderate positive effect on achievement/test performance.
finding.measure: Objective learning performance, including exam scores and post-test scores

finding.finding_summary: The review found that student preference generally favored the flipped classroom approach. In five survey-based studies, 228 of 320 respondents (71%) preferred flipped classrooms over traditional classrooms, while 92 (29%) preferred traditional instruction.
finding.measure: Student preference survey questionnaires

paper_profiles.title: SMRC: Aligning Large Language Models with Student Reasoning for Mathematical Error Correction
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of correcting mathematical errors made by students in a way that preserves the student’s original reasoning path, rather than simply producing a correct final answer. The authors argue that educationally useful feedback should be “teacher-style”: it should both fix the error and maintain continuity with the learner’s valid steps, supporting cognitive development and reducing confusion.

To address this, the paper proposes SMRC (Student Mathematical Reasoning Correction), a framework that combines Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with a reward model trained to score reasoning steps. The reward model is built from a constructed benchmark dataset, MSEB, which contains 158 real high-school student solution records across algebra, geometry, matrices, and trigonometry. The system uses breadth-first search, outcome-based reward propagation, and pruning to guide correction generation while preserving correct steps.

The paper evaluates SMRC on ProcessBench, MR-GSM8K, and MSEB using metrics for answer accuracy (ACC) and correct-step retention rate (CSRR). Results show that SMRC generally outperforms baseline methods on MR-GSM8K and MSEB, with especially strong gains on the MSEB benchmark. However, the paper is primarily a systems/methods paper rather than a causal study of student learning outcomes, and the evidence is limited to benchmark performance on mathematical error-correction tasks.

finding.finding_summary: SMRC improved mathematical error-correction performance on benchmark tasks, especially on MR-GSM8K and MSEB. On MSEB, SMRC achieved ACC=40.1 and CSRR=73.7 (HM=51.8), outperforming the compared baselines; on MR-GSM8K it achieved ACC=91.4 and CSRR=94.5 (HM=92.9). The study does not report student learning gains, but it does report direct benchmark gains on mathematical reasoning correction and step retention.
finding.measure: Benchmark correction accuracy (ACC), correct step retention rate (CSRR), and harmonic mean (HM) on mathematical reasoning correction tasks
finding.study_size: MSEB n=158; ProcessBench and MR-GSM8K study size not_reported in the paper text provided

paper_profiles.title: Alignment of Large Language Models with Constrained Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper studies constrained alignment for large language models, asking whether practical parameter-space optimization methods can find optimal policies when multiple objectives and safety-style constraints must be satisfied. The authors frame the problem as maximizing a primary reward while enforcing secondary utility constraints, then analyze the gap between the idealized distribution-space solution and what can be achieved by an LLM parameterization.

To address this, they propose Constrained Alignment via Iterative Dualization (CAID), an iterative dual-based method that alternates between updating the dual variables and re-optimizing the model under the current Lagrangian. The paper provides theoretical guarantees for primal-dual gap, reward optimality, and constraint satisfaction under explicit assumptions, and then evaluates the method on two RLHF-style benchmarks: PKU-SafeRLHF and Anthropic HH-RLHF.

Empirically, the method improves constraint satisfaction and the trade-off between helpfulness and safety compared with one-shot alignment, including in a multi-constraint setting involving harmlessness and humor. The paper is not an education study and does not examine K-12 learners, instructional interventions, or student outcomes; its relevance is methodological, concerning constrained optimization for LLM alignment rather than classroom AI use.

paper_profiles.title: Learning Elementary Cellular Automata with Transformers
paper_profiles.venue: NeurIPS 2024 Workshop on Mathematical Reasoning and AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether Transformer models can learn and generalize the rules governing elementary cellular automata (ECA), a simplified mathematical dynamical system. The author frames the work as a test of whether Transformers can abstract fixed-arity Boolean rules from observed sequences and use that abstraction for next-state prediction, multi-step planning, and autoregressive rollout.

The study trains a 4-layer, 8-head Transformer encoder on synthetic ECA trajectories generated from random initial states and randomly sampled local rules. Several training formulations are compared: predicting the next state (O-S), predicting multiple future states (O-O), predicting the next state plus the rule (O-SR), and predicting the next state given the rule (RO-S). The dataset uses lattice size W=20 and neighborhood radius r=2, with 9.5×10^5 training samples and 10^5 test samples, where test rules are unseen during training.

Results show that the model achieves high accuracy on next-state prediction and can generalize to unseen Boolean rules, but performance drops sharply when asked to plan multiple steps ahead without intermediate context. Adding future-state prediction or explicit rule prediction improves longer-horizon performance, and increasing model depth substantially improves multi-step prediction. The paper concludes that Transformers can learn abstract rule structure in this synthetic setting, but their ability to propagate state over longer horizons is limited unless training objectives or architecture provide additional support.

finding.finding_summary: The Transformer learns the underlying ECA rule dynamics well enough to generalize across unseen Boolean functions of fixed arity. On next-state prediction (O-S), average per-bit accuracy reached about 0.96 on the main setting (input orbit length 10), indicating strong performance on the synthetic mathematical prediction task.
finding.measure: Average per-bit accuracy on next-state prediction for Elementary Cellular Automata trajectories
finding.study_size: n=9.5×10^5 training samples; n=10^5 test samples

paper_profiles.title: Designing Service Systems from Textual Evidence
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a service-operations problem: how to choose the best configuration among alternatives when the main evidence of performance is textual rather than scalar. The authors focus on settings where a cheap large-language-model (LLM) judge can score text automatically, but those scores may be biased in configuration- and instance-dependent ways, while human expert audits are accurate but expensive.

To solve this, the paper formulates configuration selection as a fixed-confidence best-arm identification problem with always-available proxy scores and selectively acquired human audits. It develops an inverse-propensity-weighted estimator and anytime-valid confidence sequences, then builds the PP-LUCB algorithm, which jointly chooses what to evaluate and when to audit. The method is designed to remain valid under adaptive sampling, selective auditing, and delayed human feedback.

The paper evaluates the framework in synthetic experiments and real service-system case studies using live LLM APIs, including customer-support classification and queue-design tasks. The main conclusion is that selective auditing guided by residual uncertainty can substantially reduce audit cost while still correctly identifying the best configuration, and that the approach remains statistically valid even when audit outcomes are delayed. The study is about adult/operational decision-making rather than K-12 education, and it does not investigate student learning outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Right Question is Already Half the Answer: Fully Unsupervised LLM Reasoning Incentivization
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can be trained to reason better without any labeled reasoning traces, golden answers, or pretrained reward models. The authors propose Entropy Minimized Policy Optimization (EMPO), a reinforcement-learning method that uses semantic entropy over clustered model outputs as an intrinsic reward signal, with the goal of favoring semantically consistent responses on unlabeled questions.

The method is evaluated on adult-oriented mathematical reasoning benchmarks and free-form natural reasoning benchmarks using Qwen2.5 Base models (and additional Llama3 experiments in the appendix). For math, the paper trains on 20,000 prompts from NuminaMath-CoT and reports pass@1 accuracy gains on benchmarks such as MATH, Minerva Math, OlympiadBench, AIME24, and AMC23; for natural reasoning it reports gains on MMLU-Pro and GPQA. The main conclusion is that fully unsupervised RL can substantially improve benchmark accuracy, and that the gains appear to come primarily from better elicitation and selection of pre-existing reasoning paths rather than creation of fundamentally new reasoning abilities.

finding.finding_summary: EMPO improved pass@1 accuracy on multiple math benchmarks for adult-scale base LLMs. For Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, average accuracy increased from 28.1% to 42.1%; for Qwen2.5-Math-7B, average accuracy increased from 30.7% to 48.1% on MATH, Minerva Math, OlympiadBench, AIME24, and AMC23. These results are benchmark accuracy improvements rather than student-learning effects.
finding.measure: Pass@1 accuracy on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (MATH, Minerva Math, OlympiadBench, AIME24, AMC23)

paper_profiles.title: FedMOA: Federated GRPO for Personalized Reasoning LLMs under Heterogeneous Rewards
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of training large language models with federated reinforcement learning when clients have heterogeneous reward functions and limited privacy-preserving access to data. The authors argue that standard federated extensions of GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) struggle with imbalanced multi-objective optimization, unstable training, and high communication/computation costs.

To address this, the paper proposes FedMOA, a federated GRPO framework that combines client-side adaptive objective weighting via hypergradient descent with server-side task-aware, accuracy-aware aggregation. Each client dynamically reweights objectives such as accuracy, format, and tag-count rewards during local training, while the server aggregates updates based on task clusters and progress proxies derived from adapted accuracy weights.

Experiments are conducted on mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, including GSM8K, MATH, MBPP, and HumanEval, using a Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct model in simulated federated settings with homogeneous and heterogeneous data/reward configurations. The paper concludes that FedMOA consistently improves global accuracy and more balanced multi-objective rewards relative to a naive federated GRPO baseline, with especially strong gains under heterogeneous settings. However, the study does not involve K-12 learners or educational interventions; its educational relevance is indirect and centered on math reasoning benchmarks rather than classroom settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved performance on math reasoning benchmarks, especially GSM8K and MATH, when using FedMOA instead of the federated GRPO baseline. In the Homo+Heter setting, GSM8K accuracy increased from 72.9% to 74.9%, and MATH accuracy increased from 65.8% to 67.0%; in the Heter+Heter setting, MATH accuracy increased from 62.6% to 64.8% (n=not_reported, effect sizes not reported).
finding.measure: Benchmark accuracy on GSM8K and MATH

paper_profiles.title: PRAGMA-VL: Towards a Pragmatic Arbitration of Safety and Helpfulness in MLLMs
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a safety-alignment problem in multimodal large language models (MLLMs): how to dynamically balance safety and helpfulness rather than applying a fixed refusal policy. The authors argue that static alignment methods can be over-cautious on benign queries or overly permissive on risky ones, especially when visual and textual inputs interact in complex ways.

To address this, they propose Pragma-VL, an end-to-end alignment framework with three stages: a contextual data augmentation pipeline (PragmaSafe) that creates helpfulness/harmlessness labels and context-dependent weights; a cold-start pre-alignment stage that improves visual risk perception using risk-aware contrastive learning plus risk-aware supervised fine-tuning; and a parallel reward model trained with joint Bradley-Terry and MSE losses to produce context-aware rewards for GRPO policy optimization. The evaluation is conducted on two open-source multimodal models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Llava-1.5-7B) across multiple safety benchmarks and general ability benchmarks.

The reported results show improved safety-helpfulness balance relative to several baselines, with gains on benchmark win rates and reduced attack success rates, while preserving or slightly improving general capabilities such as MathVista, ScienceQA, and VQAv2. The paper is primarily a systems/alignment methods paper for adult MLLM users and model builders; it does not study K-12 educational outcomes or student learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports improved alignment efficiency in the sense of more effective safety-helpfulness arbitration in MLLMs, but this is a model-training and inference efficiency claim rather than a human workflow productivity outcome. Pragma-VL outperforms baselines on preference-accuracy metrics in reward-model evaluation (e.g., Weighted Acc. 96.3% and 98.7% on the Qwen2.5-VL-7B parallel model at ∆≥2 and ∆≥4, respectively), indicating a more reliable reward-model pipeline.
finding.measure: Reward-model preference accuracy on PragmaSafe validation set

paper_profiles.title: Designing for human–AI complementarity in K-12 education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a case study on designing and evaluating Lumilo, mixed-reality smart glasses intended to help teachers better support students using AI tutoring software in K-12 classrooms. The broader problem is that, while AI tutors can personalize instruction, the role of teachers in these environments is under-studied, and existing support tools often fail to present information in ways teachers can act on effectively.

The authors describe a participatory, human-centered design process involving teachers, including classroom observations, co-design activities, replay enactments, and iterative prototyping. Lumilo was designed to show teachers real-time analytics about students’ learning, metacognition, and behavior while preserving teachers’ ability to monitor the classroom naturally. The prototype was then evaluated in a field study with 343 middle school students in 18 classrooms across 4 schools/districts, using a pre/post linear equation-solving task and random assignment of classrooms to three conditions: no glasses, glasses without analytics, and glasses plus analytics.

The main finding is that teacher use of Lumilo improved student learning relative to business-as-usual AI-supported classrooms, and the analytics-enhanced version outperformed the stripped-down glasses condition as well. The effects were strongest for students who entered with lower pretest knowledge, suggesting that the tool helped teachers direct attention more effectively to students who needed it most and reduced the usual “rich get richer” pattern seen in AI-supported classrooms. The study concludes that well-designed human–AI partnerships can improve learning in real classrooms, especially when teacher-facing analytics are used to guide targeted support.

finding.finding_summary: In a field experiment on linear equation solving, students learned more when teachers used Lumilo, a mixed-reality teacher awareness tool, than in business-as-usual AI-supported classrooms. The study analyzed posttest learning gains for 286 students (from 343 initially enrolled; 57 absent/excluded) across 18 classrooms, 8 teachers, and 4 schools/districts, and found an additional benefit from the analytics-enabled version over the reduced-glasses condition.
finding.measure: Pre/post test scores on linear equation solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that Lumilo changed teacher attention allocation in ways that favored lower-knowledge students, which in turn helped reduce inequitable 'rich get richer' learning patterns. Although the study did not directly measure student motivation or engagement with a standardized instrument, it did observe teachers giving brief encouragement and reflective prompts, and it frames these as mechanisms that may support student persistence and learning during AI tutoring.
finding.measure: Teacher time allocation; classroom observations of teacher interactions

finding.finding_summary: The paper provides evidence that teachers used Lumilo to support student reflection and metacognitive prompting during AI-tutoring sessions. Observations showed teachers often asked students to explain next steps or justify actions (for example, 'So what should you do next?' and 'Why did you subtract x from the right side?'), indicating a positive effect on metacognitive engagement rather than only content coaching.
finding.measure: Classroom observation of teacher-student interactions during AI tutoring

finding.finding_summary: Lumilo improved teachers' ability to locate and assist students in real time, with teachers spending an average of about 24 seconds per visit and directing more of their attention to students with lower initial knowledge. The study also reports that the tool helped teachers decide whom to help and when, suggesting a productivity and orchestration benefit in classroom management.
finding.measure: Teacher attention allocation/time spent per student visit; classroom orchestration behavior
finding.study_size: n=14 teachers in pilots; n=8 teachers in field evaluation

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that human-centered, participatory design can produce more effective AI-supported classroom systems than technology-driven tool development alone. This is a case study of a school-based intervention rather than a policy study, but it does offer evidence that teacher-AI partnership design can improve outcomes in real K-12 settings and may inform broader adoption and implementation practices.
finding.measure: Field implementation and deployment of Lumilo in K-12 classrooms

paper_profiles.title: How Do AI Companies “Fine-Tune” Policy? Examining Regulatory Capture in AI Governance
paper_profiles.venue: AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how AI companies and related industry actors may influence AI policy in ways that could amount to regulatory capture. The authors develop a framework for identifying capture in AI governance, distinguishing between captured policy outcomes (policy content, enforcement, and governance structures) and mechanisms of influence (personal engagement, incentive shaping, information capture, cultural capture, and indirect capture).

The study is based on 17 semi-structured expert interviews with AI policy experts in the United States, United Kingdom, and European Union, supplemented by observational data and a scoping review of AI governance literature. Interviewees described concerns that industry influence is most visible in agenda-setting, advocacy, donations/gifts, revolving-door hiring, and academic capture, and that captured outcomes would more likely involve weak or absent regulation than over-regulation. The paper concludes that AI governance is vulnerable to undue industry influence and recommends transparency, stronger public-sector capacity, independent funding, and procedural safeguards to mitigate capture.

This is not a study of AI tutoring, K-12 instruction, learning outcomes, or student achievement. It is a qualitative policy/governance paper focused on industry influence in AI regulation rather than educational use of generative AI.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds substantial perceived industry influence on AI policymaking, but the experts interviewed generally did not believe US AI policy was already fully captured. Across 17 interviews, respondents identified agenda-setting (15), advocacy (13), academic capture (10), and information management (9) as key mechanisms, while expressing concern that these mechanisms could produce weak, absent, or unevenly enforced regulation.
finding.measure: Expert interview reports of AI policy outcomes and influence mechanisms

paper_profiles.title: Safe, Untrusted, “Proof-Carrying” AI Agents: toward the agentic lakehouse
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper argues that programmable lakehouse systems can provide the right abstractions for safe, agentic AI workflows over sensitive data infrastructure. The core problem is how to let AI agents automate high-stakes data engineering tasks—specifically repairing broken data pipelines—without compromising trust, correctness, reproducibility, or governance.

The authors present Bauplan as a case study of a programmable lakehouse in which the full data lifecycle is exposed through code-based APIs, declarative I/O, and transactional branch-then-merge workflows. They show how these abstractions reduce the attack surface for untrusted agents, support isolated execution, and enable human review before production changes are merged. The paper then describes a proof-of-concept agentic loop using MCP tools, smolagents, and LLMs to repair a faulty pipeline under a verifier-based “proof-checking” step.

The paper is not an educational study and does not involve K-12 learners, instruction, or achievement outcomes. It is a systems/AI-infrastructure paper aimed at data engineers and platform builders, demonstrating feasibility through a prototype rather than a formal experimental benchmark. Its main conclusion is that safe-by-design agentic automation is plausible in a programmable lakehouse, but broader scalability, model robustness, and infrastructure evolution remain open problems.

paper_profiles.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Conversational AI
paper_profiles.venue: ICTIR’ 17 Workshop on Search-Oriented Conversational AI (SCAI’ 2017)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual survey of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for conversational AI. It explains basic reinforcement learning concepts, contrasts reinforcement learning with supervised learning, and discusses why reward design, goal trade-offs, and evaluation are difficult in dialogue systems.

The paper reviews several DRL and deep learning conversational models, including sequence-to-sequence models, persona-based models, and dialogue management approaches, and briefly notes how these ideas connect to applications in domains such as healthcare, banking, and education. In the education discussion, the paper mentions conversational tutoring systems such as AutoTutor as an example of dialogue-based learning technology, but it does not present a study of educational outcomes.

Overall, the paper argues that DRL is promising for conversational agents because it can support trial-and-error learning, strategic dialogue, and more human-like interaction. Its main contribution is synthesis and conceptual discussion rather than empirical evaluation, and it highlights open research challenges such as sparse rewards, multiple objectives, coherent dialogue generation, and evaluation metrics.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses conversational AI systems for dialogue generation and language interaction, but it does not report any empirical educational outcomes for speaking or listening. No sample, effect size, or measured language-fluency outcome is provided; the discussion is purely conceptual.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper mentions user experience, personalization, and evaluation of conversational agents, which are related to engagement and experience, but it does not empirically measure motivation, persistence, or self-regulation. No quantitative outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper references conversational coherence, strategic dialogue, and planning in reinforcement learning, but these are discussed as design challenges rather than measured learning outcomes. No empirical evidence is reported for critical thinking, metacognition, or collaboration.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: Expert-Guided LLM Reasoning for Battery Discovery: From AI-Driven Hypothesis to Synthesis and Characterization
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is about battery materials discovery, not education. It introduces ChatBattery, an expert-guided framework for using large language models (LLMs) to generate, evaluate, and refine hypotheses for optimizing lithium-ion battery cathode materials. The work combines LLM-based hypothesis generation with domain-specific search, ranking, computational validation, and human expert oversight.

The authors apply ChatBattery to the optimization of the NMC811 cathode material and report a complete cycle from AI-generated candidate design to synthesis and characterization. Using the framework, they identify three novel cathode compositions (NMC-SiMg, NMC-SiCa, and NMC-MgB), each showing higher reversible capacity than NMC811. The paper also reports DFT/MACE-MP computational validation and wet-lab synthesis results, concluding that expert-guided LLM reasoning can accelerate scientific discovery in materials science. However, the paper does not study any K-12 education outcomes or generative AI tutoring.

paper_profiles.title: Multimodal Conversational AI: A Survey of Datasets and Approaches
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper surveys the research landscape for multimodal conversational AI, defining the problem of building conversational systems that can understand and respond using multiple modalities such as text, images, audio, video, dialogue history, and action. The authors motivate multimodal conversation as an extension of traditional conversational AI, where language-only systems are limited by their inability to use nonlinguistic cues that humans routinely leverage in interaction.

The paper organizes the field into five technical subproblems: representation, fusion, translation, alignment, and co-learning. It then reviews representative datasets and state-of-the-art approaches for each area, including visual question answering, visual dialogue, image-grounded conversation, video question answering, and multimodal navigation/dialogue tasks. The discussion emphasizes that many existing datasets and models are still simplifications of true multimodal conversation, often relying on short dialogues, limited modalities, and task formulations that do not fully capture long-term conversational dependency or personality dynamics.

The main conclusion is that multimodal conversational AI remains an open research challenge, and progress will require both richer datasets and better learning objectives that more directly model conversation across modalities. The paper highlights multimodal co-learning as a promising future direction because it can exploit cross-modal synergies to improve resource-poor modalities using resource-rich ones. This is a survey paper and does not report original human-subject experiments or educational outcomes.

paper_profiles.title: Expansive Participatory AI: Supporting Dreaming within Inequitable Institutions
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how participatory AI (PAI) and co-design processes can better support youth in imagining socially just futures within existing institutions, with a particular focus on schooling. The authors argue that many participatory design efforts remain constrained by institutional norms and technocentric assumptions, which can limit the ability of impacted communities to envision more expansive possibilities for AI and education.

To address this, the paper proposes design principles for "desettling" inequitable institutional practices during co-design, emphasizing that AI should be framed as a means to an end, that feasibility constraints should be temporarily removed to support dreaming, and that facilitators should embrace contradictory and evolving youth perspectives. The paper illustrates these principles through a Learning Futures Workshop with high-school-aged youth, where participants first imagined ideal collaborative spaces outside school, then used junk materials to build fantastical spaces, and finally considered how AI might help realize those dreams in classrooms.

The main conclusion is that this workshop format helped youth reimagine classroom goals beyond work alone and opened space for expansive technological ideas, including dream-based AI tools. The study is conceptual and qualitative rather than evaluative: it does not test educational outcomes or compare interventions, but instead offers a framework and case study showing how participatory AI processes can surface youth aspirations and challenge the grammar of schooling.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that expansive participatory AI co-design can help participants interrogate and reshape inequitable institutional norms, especially the "grammar of schooling." In the workshop case study with high-school-aged youth, the process supported reimagining classroom goals and opening space for alternative institutional possibilities, but no quantitative effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Youth co-design reflections and workshop-generated ideas about institutional goals and classroom collaboration

paper_profiles.title: Supporting Data-Frame Dynamics in AI-assisted Decision Making
paper_profiles.venue: ACM Workshop on Human-AI Interaction for Augmented Reasoning (AIREASONING-2025-01)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a human-AI decision support problem: current AI systems often provide static recommendations or explanations, but do not adequately support the dynamic, iterative way people refine evidence and hypotheses during complex decision making. The authors frame this limitation using data-frame theory and evaluative AI, arguing that effective decision support should let both humans and AI update evidence, retrieve alternative hypotheses, and rescore competing explanations over time.

To operationalize this idea, the paper proposes a mixed-initiative collaboration framework in which AI and users jointly participate in three functions: evidence extraction, hypothesis retrieval, and hypothesis scoring. The paper illustrates the framework with a proof-of-concept skin cancer diagnosis prototype based on a concept bottleneck model and dermoscopy concepts from the derm7pt dataset. The interface lets users refine extracted evidence, add or remove hypotheses, and inspect or adjust supporting and contradicting evidence.

The paper is conceptual and design-oriented rather than an educational intervention study. It does not evaluate outcomes on learners or classroom contexts; instead, it argues that the framework could improve collaborative decision making and potentially reduce cognitive burden and overreliance in high-stakes domains. The authors conclude that the prototype demonstrates feasibility and that future user studies with dermatologists are needed to assess effectiveness and tradeoffs.

paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines what K-12 learning design should look like when AI is introduced as a collaborative learning partner in classrooms. The authors focus on a gap in the AIED literature: there is little empirical work describing how teachers think student-AI collaboration (SAC) should be designed across curriculum, interaction, environment, and change over time.

The study is based on in-depth semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AI in education, drawn from primary and secondary schools involved in software education, AI pilot schools, or AI convergence high schools. Using a hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis, the authors developed a student-AI collaboration model and identified teachers’ priorities for SAC: capacity building and subject-matter knowledge as learning goals; interdisciplinary, authentic, and creative tasks; process-oriented and collaboration assessment; and supports such as AI principles, data literacy, error analysis, AI ethics, and scaffolding from AI itself.

The findings also emphasize the importance of flexible learning spaces, robust digital infrastructure, system-level policy support, teacher capacity building, collaborative school culture, and a safe-to-fail climate. Teachers anticipated SAC would evolve through three stages: learn about AI, learn from AI, and learn together.
