Overall, the paper argues that effective SAC depends not only on classroom-level task design, but also on institutional and cultural conditions that support sustained human-AI collaboration in education.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that SAC should develop durable skills such as critical thinking, creativity, problem-solving, reflection, collaboration, and communication. The study is qualitative and does not report effect sizes, but the central finding is that these skills were viewed as primary learning goals of student-AI collaboration across the 10 interviewed teachers.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about intended learning goals and skills for SAC

finding.finding_summary: Teachers identified social-emotional development as an important aim of SAC, including engagement, motivation, persistence, coping with uncertainty, and a positive attitude toward failure and debugging. The study also emphasized gamification and AI designed to encourage students to try again when they struggle, but no quantitative effect estimates were reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about motivation, engagement, persistence, and attitudes toward failure

finding.finding_summary: The paper found strong teacher support for system-level conditions needed for SAC, including national AIED policy, governance and coordination mechanisms, teacher professional development, flexible school structures, collaborative school culture, and safe-to-fail environments. These were reported as prerequisites for successful implementation rather than measured outcomes, so no statistical effects are available.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on policy, governance, school organization, and culture

paper_profiles.title: A critical evaluation, challenges, and future perspectives of using artificial intelligence and emerging technologies in smart classrooms
paper_profiles.population: Not population-specific; general K-12 and higher-education smart classroom literature
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative literature review of artificial intelligence and emerging technologies in smart classrooms. It surveys major technology areas used in smart classroom settings, including classroom management systems (e.g., computer vision for attendance and behavior recognition, smart environments), teaching aids (robotics, chatbots, VR/AR/MR), e-learning platforms, all-screen technologies, and automated performance assessment.

The paper does not test a single intervention or report primary empirical data; instead, it synthesizes prior studies to discuss potential benefits, limitations, and future directions for AI-enabled smart classrooms. Its main conclusion is that AI can improve engagement, personalization, monitoring, and assessment, but adoption is constrained by cost, privacy and ethics concerns, bias, lack of integration, and teacher readiness. The review also highlights that some technologies may be especially useful for remote learning, special needs support, and adaptive instruction, though the paper itself does not present subgroup-specific empirical results.

Because the article is broad and conceptual, it is best understood as a technology survey and critical discussion rather than an outcome study of student achievement. It is aimed primarily at educators and AI practitioners interested in the opportunities and challenges of implementing AI in educational environments.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI-enabled smart classroom tools can automate or streamline attendance recognition, behavior monitoring, performance assessment, plagiarism checking, and feedback generation, reducing teacher workload and time spent on routine tasks. No single pooled effect size is reported because this is a narrative review rather than an empirical evaluation.
finding.measure: teacher workload; automation of attendance, assessment, and feedback tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes prior work suggesting that AI-enhanced smart classroom technologies can improve student engagement, motivation, attention, and self-regulation by providing interactive, immersive, and adaptive experiences. The review cites studies on engagement estimation and notes that systems can detect boredom, disaffection, or lack of attention, but it does not report a synthesized quantitative effect.
finding.measure: student engagement, motivation, attention, behavioral disaffection

finding.finding_summary: The review emphasizes institutional-level implications of AI adoption in schools, including privacy, ethics, bias, GDPR compliance, security risks, teacher training needs, and the need for integrated infrastructure. It presents these as both opportunities and threats for school systems, but no empirical institutional outcome data or effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: privacy/security concerns, governance, adoption barriers, infrastructure integration

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses literature suggesting that immersive and collaborative technologies such as VR/AR/MR and smart classroom systems can support collaboration, communication, and problem solving. These claims are synthesized from prior studies rather than directly tested in the review itself, and no effect sizes are reported.
finding.measure: collaborative and communicative skills; problem solving

paper_profiles.title: Co-Designing a Real-Time Classroom Orchestration Tool to Support Teacher–AI Complementarity
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to design real-time classroom orchestration tools that help teachers manage AI-enhanced K–12 math classrooms more effectively. Rather than studying a student-facing tutor, the paper asks what kinds of information teachers need during sessions with intelligent tutoring systems, and how that information should be delivered so that human teachers and AI systems complement one another.

The intervention/approach is an iterative co-design process for Lumilo, a mixed-reality wearable awareness tool (smart glasses / heads-up display) for teachers. Across multiple formative studies, the authors used generative card sorting, directed storytelling interviews, speed-dating with storyboard concepts, low-fidelity and mid-fidelity prototyping, and replay-based simulation to elicit teacher needs and refine analytics displays. The work involved 10 middle-school math teachers in early design studies and 16 middle-school math teachers in later prototyping, across multiple schools and districts, all in the context of AI-enhanced math instruction and intelligent tutoring systems.

The main conclusions are that teachers strongly value real-time, actionable awareness of student thought processes, stuckness, misconceptions, off-task behavior, and class-level patterns, but they prefer tools that support rather than override teacher judgment. Teachers rejected designs that felt like automation of their instructional decisions, and instead favored wearable displays that keep attention on the classroom and provide concise, selective, and privacy-sensitive information. The paper’s contribution is primarily methodological and design-oriented: it offers an end-to-end case study of co-design for learning analytics tools and a set of recommendations for future teacher-AI complementarity systems.

finding.finding_summary: Across multiple co-design studies with middle-school math teachers (n=10 in initial needs studies; n=16 in later prototyping studies), teachers reported that real-time analytics could help them prioritize who to help, when to intervene, and how to reduce monitoring and orchestration burden in AI-enhanced classrooms. The paper does not report quantitative effect sizes; the evidence is qualitative, but consistently points to perceived gains in teacher efficiency and classroom management.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported orchestration needs, perceived usefulness of real-time analytics, and design feedback during interviews, card sorts, speed-dating, and prototyping sessions

finding.finding_summary: Teachers wanted real-time indicators of student motivation, frustration, off-task behavior, and who is 'almost there,' because they believed these cues would help them respond to student needs and maintain engagement. The paper reports these as design requirements and preferences rather than measured student outcomes, so no quantitative effect is available.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported desire for analytics about student motivation, frustration, engagement, and behavioral state

finding.finding_summary: Teachers repeatedly emphasized the value of seeing students' thought processes, solution paths, misconceptions, and sequences of prior states, which would support real-time diagnosis and instructional decision-making. The study is qualitative and reports no effect sizes, but it clearly centers on metacognitive/diagnostic information and teacher decision support rather than direct student learning gains.
finding.measure: Teacher preferences for analytics revealing student reasoning, misconceptions, and solution-path sequences

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence-based language learning: illuminating the impact on speaking skills and self-regulation in Chinese EFL context
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This study examined whether AI-based language instruction improves second language speaking performance and self-regulation among Chinese EFL learners. The authors framed the work as addressing a gap in the literature on how AI affects both speaking outcomes and self-regulated learning in an EFL setting.

The intervention used Duolingo’s AI-driven speaking features, including speech recognition, personalized feedback, prompts, and gamified practice. Ninety-three intermediate-level Chinese EFL students were randomly assigned to an AI-based course or a traditional speaking course over 13 weeks, with speaking anxiety, global English proficiency, and pretest performance controlled in the analyses.

Results showed that the AI group improved significantly more than the control group on all speaking subskills measured—fluency, vocabulary, accuracy, and pronunciation—as well as self-regulation. The study also found that students with higher initial vocabulary benefitted more from the course, while speaking anxiety negatively affected fluency and pronunciation. Overall, the paper concludes that AI-supported speaking practice can enhance oral language development and foster self-regulatory processes in EFL learners.

finding.finding_summary: The AI-based Duolingo speaking intervention significantly improved L2 speaking outcomes relative to the traditional course. For fluency specifically, the course effect was positive and statistically significant (B=0.65, SE=0.24, p=0.006) after controlling for pretest, English proficiency, and speaking anxiety.
finding.measure: IELTS speaking fluency/coherence score

finding.finding_summary: The intervention also improved learners’ self-regulation. The AI group scored significantly higher than the control group on the Self-Regulated Language Learning Questionnaire after the 13-week treatment (B=0.51, SE=0.22, p=0.018).
finding.measure: Self-Regulated Language Learning Questionnaire (SRLLQ)

finding.finding_summary: The study measured self-regulation using the SRLLQ and interpreted the findings as evidence that AI-supported instruction fostered metacognitive and self-monitoring processes. Although self-regulation is the central outcome reported in the paper, the improvement was positive and statistically significant (B=0.51, SE=0.22, p=0.018).
finding.measure: Self-regulated language learning (including internal motivation, external motivation, cognitive strategies, metacognitive strategies, and evaluation)

finding.finding_summary: The intervention improved additional speaking subskills beyond fluency. Vocabulary increased significantly in the AI group (B=0.57, SE=0.29, p=0.034), accuracy improved (B=0.46, SE=0.23, p=0.013), and pronunciation improved (B=0.42, SE=0.21, p=0.025). A pretest-by-course interaction was significant only for vocabulary (B=0.41, p=0.046), indicating students with higher initial vocabulary benefitted more.
finding.measure: IELTS speaking sub-scores: vocabulary, grammatical accuracy, pronunciation

paper_profiles.title: A systematic review of literature reviews on artificial intelligence in education (AIED): a roadmap to a future research agenda
paper_profiles.population: Not population-specific; synthesis of AIED literature reviews across K-12, higher education, special education, early childhood, and lifelong learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper does not evaluate a single AI intervention in classrooms. Instead, it conducts a systematic review of literature reviews on artificial intelligence in education, aiming to synthesize the broader AIED review literature and map trends, stakeholders, educational levels, subject areas, methods, technologies, advantages, and challenges.

The authors screened major education/technology databases and included 143 eligible review articles. Using a technology-enhanced learning framework, they coded the reviews by publication trends, participant groups, educational levels, disciplines, review type, objectives, AI techniques, and reported benefits/challenges. The synthesis shows that AIED review work is concentrated in China and the U.S., heavily focused on higher education and on students/teachers, with comparatively little attention to special education, administrators, and policymakers.

The paper concludes that AIED literature is dominated by systematic reviews, with machine learning, generative AI/LLMs, intelligent tutoring systems, and chatbots emerging as key techniques. Commonly cited benefits include personalized learning, improved teaching/learning quality, and better assessment support, while major challenges include data privacy, lack of AI training, design difficulty, limited humanity/personalization, and concerns about inclusion and reliability. The article is primarily a roadmap and research-agenda paper rather than an outcomes study of effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: Across 143 reviewed literature reviews, AI in education was most often described as improving assessment/support systems and reducing workload through automation, personalized recommendations, and chatbot/AI tutor assistance. The synthesis reports that assessment support was the most frequently cited advantage (n=38), alongside teaching and learning support (n=95) and decreased work stress (n=4), but it does not provide pooled effect sizes or causal estimates.
finding.measure: Reported advantages/challenges in literature reviews; especially assessment support, workload reduction, and administrative/teaching efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper identifies field-level patterns and institutional gaps rather than learner-level effects. It reports that AIED research is concentrated in China and the U.S., mostly in higher education, and underrepresents special education, administrators, and policymakers; it also highlights governance concerns such as data privacy, inclusion/equality, and legal responsibility.
finding.measure: Geographic distribution, stakeholder coverage, educational level coverage, and reported ethical/governance challenges in the review corpus

paper_profiles.title: The Potential Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Equity and Inclusion in Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This OECD working paper examines how artificial intelligence may affect equity and inclusion in education, with a focus on school education. Rather than evaluating a single intervention, it synthesizes existing literature and policy guidance on learner-centred, teacher-led, and institutional AI tools, considering both opportunities and risks for different student groups and education systems.

The paper discusses how AI tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, AI-enabled simulations, chatbots, and administrative systems may support adaptive learning, accessibility, teacher workload reduction, and institutional decision making. It also highlights major concerns, including unequal access, techno-ableism, algorithmic bias, socio-emotional trade-offs, privacy, and commercial influence. The paper concludes that evidence on learning and equity effects remains limited and uneven, and that more robust research and stronger governance are needed before AI adoption can be assumed to improve inclusion or achievement.

Because the paper is a desk-based review and policy analysis, it does not present original empirical estimates for a specific K-12 mathematics subgroup intervention. Its main contribution is conceptual and descriptive: mapping AI use cases to equity/inclusion concerns and identifying evidence gaps, especially around heterogeneous effects for diverse learners and the need for stronger evaluation designs.

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies potential academic benefits of learner-centred AI tools, especially intelligent tutoring systems and AI-enabled simulations, but emphasizes that the evidence base is limited and uneven. It cites emerging studies suggesting some gains for disadvantaged students and ethnic minorities, while also noting a recent meta-analysis reporting mixed results and insufficient evidence on heterogeneous effects.
finding.measure: Academic outcomes reported across prior studies of intelligent tutoring systems and related AI learning tools

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools such as chatbots and simulations may support engagement, motivation, and well-being, but it also warns that reduced human interaction could negatively affect socio-emotional development. It presents these effects as plausible and context-dependent rather than established by robust new evidence in this paper.
finding.measure: Engagement, motivation, mental health, and social interaction outcomes discussed across prior studies

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the review is that AI can improve operational efficiency by reducing teacher workload and streamlining administrative or instructional tasks. Examples include AI-supported assessment, classroom management, curation of learning materials, and data-based decision making, although the paper does not report new effect estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, administrative task efficiency, and instructional support

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can influence institutional systems through admissions, student-risk identification, and governance of educational services, but stresses that unchecked adoption may widen inequities between schools and education systems. It frames the overall institutional impact as contingent on policy, oversight, privacy protections, and resource distribution.
finding.measure: Institutional decision-making, admissions processes, and system-level equity/inclusion considerations

paper_profiles.title: Distributed agency in second language learning and teaching through generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This column argues that generative AI is reshaping second language learning and teaching by changing how agency is distributed between learners, teachers, and AI systems. Rather than presenting an intervention study, it synthesizes early examples and emerging research on tools such as ChatGPT, AI writing assistants, and custom GPT-based tutors to show how these systems can support language practice, writing development, feedback, and personalized learning.

The paper is framed around applied linguistics and ecological theories, especially sociomaterialism and relational pedagogy. It emphasizes that AI can expand learner and teacher agency when used critically and thoughtfully, but that its usefulness is limited by hallucinations, weak pragmatic sensitivity, bias, and broader ethical and access issues. The author also stresses that AI should not be treated as a simple replacement for human interaction: collaborative human-to-human communication remains essential for pragmatic competence, cultural learning, and authentic social development.

The paper focuses on language learning in general rather than a specific K-12 or mathematics context, and it does not report original empirical data. Its main contribution is conceptual: it proposes that learners and teachers develop critical AI literacy and use AI as a partner in iterative, reflective, and ethically informed language work. The column concludes that AI will likely become a pervasive companion in language education, but its educational value depends on context, access, and how human and machine agency are structured.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not report an original empirical study of literacy outcomes; instead, it discusses how generative AI may support language writing tasks such as brainstorming, drafting, revising, grammar checking, and feedback. Claims about improved writing are illustrative and drawn from cited studies, but no effect size, sample, or literacy outcome is reported in this paper itself.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses AI-supported oral and written conversation practice in second language learning, including voice chatbots and conversational agents, but it does not present empirical evidence on speaking or listening outcomes. No direct measure of fluency, sample size, or effect estimate is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively discusses critical thinking, metacognition, and prompt refinement as important learner skills in effective AI use, especially through iterative prompting and reflective use of outputs. However, these are conceptual recommendations rather than measured outcomes, and no empirical effect is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The article addresses institutional and governance issues around AI access, commercial control, fairness, ethics, and educational policy responses, arguing for critical AI literacy and thoughtful integration rather than bans. These are normative and theoretical claims; no institutional outcome is measured.
finding.measure: not_reported

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: All educational levels (K-12, tertiary, professional development)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the emerging role of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT and GPT-3, in education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes early research and provides an argument-based overview of how LLMs may support learning and teaching, while also raising concerns about bias, privacy, copyright, misuse, overreliance, and unequal access.

The paper discusses potential uses across learner and teacher contexts, including automated quiz generation, feedback, explanations, personalized practice, tutoring support, lesson planning, and assessment assistance. It also considers broader opportunities for immersive technologies and inclusive education, noting that LLMs could support learners with disabilities and multilingual access, but only with careful human oversight and pedagogical framing.

The central contribution is conceptual and normative: the authors argue that LLMs could meaningfully enhance education if integrated responsibly, but that current systems are brittle and can reproduce unfairness or misinformation. The paper concludes with mitigation strategies and calls for further empirical research, especially on trustworthy, ethical, and equitable deployment in educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can support reading and writing by generating summaries, explanations, grammar/style suggestions, and reading-comprehension questions. These claims are conceptual and illustrated with examples rather than tested empirically, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLMs can assist language learning through conversation practice, pronunciation support, translations, and grammar/vocabulary explanations. However, this is a position-based claim without direct empirical evaluation in the paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper notes that middle and high school students may benefit from LLM-generated practice problems, quizzes, and step-by-step explanations for mathematics learning, and it references automatic math word-problem generation as an application area. No direct mathematics outcome was measured in this paper.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes that LLMs may reduce teacher workload by automating quiz creation, feedback generation, assessment support, and lesson-planning tasks. Examples cited in the review include reduced grading effort in large courses (up to 85% in a cited study), but the paper itself does not present new empirical data.
finding.measure: Teacher time/workload, automated feedback and assessment efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the institutional and policy challenge of responsibly integrating LLMs into education. It argues that schools and systems need governance around copyright, privacy, bias mitigation, cost, academic integrity, multilingual fairness, and sustainable use; these are presented as risks and implementation requirements rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy, fairness, and integrity considerations

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs may improve student engagement, curiosity, and willingness to participate by providing interactive dialogue, prompts, and personalized support. These are conceptual claims supported by cited examples, not direct findings from the position paper itself.
finding.measure: Student engagement, curiosity, participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly frames LLMs as tools that can support critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and fact-checking, but also warns that overreliance may weaken those same skills. This is a conceptual and cautionary synthesis rather than a direct empirical test, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, fact-checking

paper_profiles.title: Language Models Are Multilingual Chain-of-Thought Reasoners
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models can perform grade-school mathematics and other reasoning tasks across multiple languages. The central question is how multilingual chain-of-thought prompting affects performance on math word problems and related benchmarks, especially in languages that are underrepresented in pretraining data.

The authors introduce MGSM, a benchmark created by manually translating 250 GSM8K grade-school math problems into ten typologically diverse languages. They evaluate GPT-3 and PaLM under several prompting strategies: direct answer prediction, native-language chain-of-thought, English chain-of-thought, and translate-to-English then solve. They also extend the analysis to XCOPA and XL-WiC to test broader multilingual reasoning and semantic judgment.

The paper is not a K-12 intervention study; it is a model evaluation study. Its main conclusion is that large models, especially PaLM-540B, show strong multilingual reasoning abilities and that English chain-of-thought prompting is often as good as or better than native-language reasoning. For MGSM, performance improves with scale and with chain-of-thought prompting, and the authors report little dependence on pretraining language frequency. The work is relevant to multilingual math tutoring only indirectly, because it studies model capability rather than student outcomes or classroom implementation.

finding.finding_summary: Large language models solved grade-school math word problems substantially better when prompted with chain-of-thought than with direct answers. On MGSM (n=250 translated GSM8K items across 10 languages), PaLM-540B reached 55.0% accuracy with NATIVE-EXEMPLARS + TRANSLATE-EN, 51.3% with EN-COT, 48.1% with NATIVE-COT, and 18.6% with DIRECT; GPT-3 text-davinci-002 reached 45.6% with TRANSLATE-EN and 11.7% with DIRECT. The authors conclude that multilingual arithmetic reasoning is an emergent ability that improves with scale and is relatively strong even in underrepresented languages such as Bengali and Swahili.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Multilingual Grade School Math (MGSM) grade-school math word problems

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual Catchword article that explains what generative AI is, how it works, and why it matters for business and information systems research. Rather than evaluating a specific system or intervention, the authors present a structured overview of generative AI at the model, system, application, and socio-technical levels, with examples drawn from large language models, image generation, and conversational agents.

The paper also discusses four major limitations of current generative AI: incorrect outputs, bias and fairness concerns, copyright violation, and environmental costs. It then outlines future research directions across BISE subfields, including human-computer interaction and education, where generative AI could support digital teaching assistants, supplemental learning materials, prompt engineering, and guidance for verifying model outputs. Because this is a conceptual agenda-setting article, it does not study a K-12 population, test an intervention, or report empirical outcomes.

For education specifically, the paper argues that generative AI may reshape teaching and assessment by enabling conversational tutors and individualized learning supports, but it offers these as implications and research questions rather than empirical findings. No subgroup analyses, student outcome data, or mathematics tutoring results are reported.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI could substantially reshape educational institutions by changing assessment practices, teaching workflows, and governance around AI use, but it provides no empirical evaluation. In education, the authors propose that schools and educators will need new guidelines for prompt use, verification of outputs, and appropriate reliance on generative AI systems, alongside digital teaching assistants and supplemental materials.
finding.measure: Conceptual discussion of educational governance, assessment, and institutional change

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests generative AI could improve efficiency by automating content creation, summarization, knowledge retrieval, and the production of teaching materials, which may reduce educator workload. However, these claims are illustrative rather than empirically tested, and no sample, effect size, or measured productivity outcome is reported.
finding.measure: Conceptual claims about automation of content creation and teaching-material production

paper_profiles.title: TurkishMMLU: Measuring Massive Multitask Language Understanding in Turkish
paper_profiles.venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces TurkishMMLU, a large benchmark for evaluating large language models (LLMs) on Turkish-language multiple-choice question answering. The motivation is that existing multilingual benchmarks often rely on machine translation, which can introduce errors and miss cultural nuance; the authors instead build a manually curated, curriculum-aligned resource from Turkish high-school exam-preparation materials.

TurkishMMLU contains 10,032 questions across nine high-school subjects, spanning mathematics, natural sciences, Turkish language and literature, history, geography, philosophy, and religion/ethics. Each item includes a correctness ratio derived from student performance on the source platform, allowing the authors to analyze question difficulty. They also create a 900-question subsample (TurkishMMLUsub) for cheaper evaluation and test more than 40 open- and closed-source LLMs under zero-shot, 5-shot, and 5-shot chain-of-thought prompting.

The paper finds that closed-source models, especially GPT-4o, achieve the strongest overall performance, while newer open-source models such as Llama-3 70B-Instruct substantially outperform older open models. Mathematics is the hardest subject category, and performance declines consistently as question difficulty increases. Few-shot prompting usually helps, chain-of-thought helps mainly on mathematics and natural sciences, and the authors show that results on the smaller subsample correlate almost perfectly with the full benchmark (Pearson r=0.999). The study is therefore primarily a benchmark and model-comparison paper rather than an intervention study in education.

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics was the hardest category for almost all models, and performance improved with few-shot prompting and especially with chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting on math items. In the 5-shot CoT setting, GPT-4o reached 88.2% overall on TurkishMMLUsub and improved by +25.0 points on mathematics relative to its non-CoT few-shot result; however, many other models below 60% in the non-CoT setting performed worse with CoT.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy on mathematics questions in TurkishMMLU / TurkishMMLUsub
finding.study_size: n=10,032 total questions; n=900 in TurkishMMLUsub

finding.finding_summary: The benchmark directly evaluates broad academic knowledge beyond math and science, including Turkish language and literature, history, geography, philosophy, and religion/ethics. Across subject categories, the easiest domain was Social Sciences and Humanities, while models showed large variation by subject; GPT-4o led with 83.1% 5-shot accuracy on TurkishMMLUsub and Llama-3 70B-IT was the strongest open model at 67.3%.
finding.measure: Multiple-choice accuracy across subject categories and overall macro-average
finding.study_size: n=10,032 total questions; n=900 in TurkishMMLUsub

finding.finding_summary: The paper uses question difficulty and chain-of-thought prompting as proxies for reasoning demands and finds that model performance consistently decreases as difficulty increases, with significant positive point-biserial correlations for all models (all p < 0.001). This indicates that harder items requiring more reasoning or multi-step inference are systematically more challenging, and CoT sometimes improves performance, especially in mathematics, but not consistently across subjects.
finding.measure: Point-biserial correlation between model correctness and question difficulty; accuracy under chain-of-thought prompting
finding.study_size: 32 open-source models for subsample/full-set correlation; selected models for difficulty analysis
finding.effect_size: rpb=0.130 to 0.287 depending on model; Pearson r=0.999 between TurkishMMLUsub and TurkishMMLU

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.population: Not reported (general education; K-12 discussed in review context)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines the educational potential of artificial intelligence, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. The paper asks how AI tools can support teaching and learning, what benefits they may provide, and what ethical, practical, and pedagogical concerns arise when integrating them into education.

The article does not test an intervention with participants; instead, it synthesizes prior literature on AI in education, including intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, automated assessment, and personalized learning platforms. It discusses applications across educational settings and briefly references prior studies involving students with learning disabilities, language learning, motivation, and anxiety, but these are cited as supporting literature rather than being analyzed directly in the paper.

The main conclusion is that AI tools such as ChatGPT may improve personalization, feedback, engagement, and some forms of instructional support, while also raising substantial concerns about bias, privacy, reliability, academic integrity, and teacher preparation. The authors argue that effective and ethical use of AI in education requires careful design, teacher support, and further research rather than uncritical adoption.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can reduce repetitive work for teachers and administrators by automating grading, feedback, and some student-support tasks. No original effect estimate is reported; this is a literature-based claim illustrated with examples such as automated scoring and assignment feedback systems.
finding.measure: teacher workload / administrative task burden

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI can improve learning outcomes through personalized instruction, tailored learning paths, and instant feedback across subject areas. However, it does not report original empirical data; the claim is supported by cited prior studies and examples of AI tutoring and adaptive platforms.
finding.measure: learning outcomes / academic performance

finding.finding_summary: The article highlights reported benefits for motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduced anxiety, especially in personalized AI-supported environments. It cites prior studies (e.g., AI math tutor and robot-supported learning) but provides no new sample, effect size, or confidence interval itself.
finding.measure: motivation, engagement, confidence, anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI can support critical thinking, creativity, self-reflection, and self-directed learning by giving individualized feedback and prompts. These are conceptual conclusions drawn from the literature rather than findings from an original study.
finding.measure: critical thinking, creativity, self-regulation, self-directed learning

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.population: Not specified (broad education context; includes examples from undergraduate, vocational, and high school settings)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper examines the promise and risks of artificial intelligence in education, arguing that AI can simultaneously enhance learning and erode important cognitive processes. Using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory as interpretive lenses, the authors discuss how AI tools such as adaptive learning systems, chatbots, and intelligent tutoring systems may reduce extraneous cognitive load and improve access to personalized instruction, while also potentially encouraging cognitive offloading, reduced retention, and weaker higher-order thinking.

The paper is not an empirical study of one intervention. Instead, it synthesizes prior studies and illustrative examples across higher education, vocational education, language learning, and STEM to make a conceptual case for balanced AI integration. The authors emphasize that AI should complement, not replace, human instruction, and that instructional design should preserve active engagement, reflection, autonomy, and critical thinking.

Its main conclusion is that AI in education has a paradoxical character: it can act as both a cognitive amplifier and a cognitive inhibitor depending on how it is implemented. The paper recommends pedagogically informed adoption, teacher guidance, periodic AI-free practice, and fairness-aware design to avoid overreliance, motivation loss, and bias. No original dataset or statistical analysis is reported.

finding.finding_summary: Across the cited literature, AI is presented as having both benefits and risks for durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, and creativity. The paper argues that AI-supported learning can improve fluency, flexibility, and elaboration in idea generation, but may also increase cognitive fixation, lower creative confidence, and weaken independent reasoning when students over-rely on AI outputs; no new effect size is reported in this opinion piece.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and higher-order thinking outcomes as discussed across prior studies

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can support competence through customized learning but may undermine autonomy and relatedness if students become dependent on AI and receive too little human interaction. It also notes that overreliance on AI may reduce motivation and engagement, but these claims are conceptual and synthesized from cited sources rather than newly estimated in this article.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, autonomy, and relatedness as discussed in relation to AI use

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI use in STEM and language learning more broadly, including examples from adaptive learning and English-language software. It summarizes cited evidence suggesting AI can improve procedural performance and communicative competence/fluency, while also potentially weakening conceptual understanding when learners rely on AI too heavily; however, this article itself reports no original academic achievement data.
finding.measure: Procedural performance, concept understanding, and language learning performance as discussed from cited studies

paper_profiles.title: Can LLMs Solve Longer Math Word Problems Better?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) are able to solve math word problems equally well when the contextual narratives are longer. The authors argue that existing benchmarks such as GSM8K mainly contain concise problems, so they create E-GSM by extending GSM8K grade-school math word problems into longer narratives while preserving the original conditions and answers.

The paper studies two main interventions: a prompting strategy for proprietary LLMs called Condition-Retrieving Instruction (CoRe), and an auxiliary fine-tuning task for open-source LLMs called extension. CoRe first asks the model to identify the key conditions and goal before solving, while extension uses additional long-context training data derived from repeated problem expansions. The experiments evaluate four proprietary models and four open-source models on E-GSM, and also test generalization on MAWPS, SVAMP, and GSM-IC.

Results show that all models perform worse as context length increases, indicating a clear long-context reasoning weakness. CoRe improves accuracy and robustness for proprietary models, and extension consistently improves open-source models, with especially large gains for longer problems. The authors further analyze informativeness and missing-step metrics and conclude that the main gains come from improved reasoning pathways rather than improved semantic understanding. Because the paper is benchmark- and evaluation-focused rather than a K-12 classroom study, it does not examine student subgroup effects such as special education, multilingual learners, English learners, or students with low prior achievement.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that LLM accuracy on grade-school math word problems declines as context length increases, but the proposed methods improve performance. On E-GSM, CoRe improves proprietary-model accuracy in higher rounds (e.g., GPT-3.5-turbo Acc4 from 64.42% to 69.76%), and extension improves open-source models (e.g., LLaMA-2-7B Acc4 from 38.95% to 48.13%).
finding.measure: Accuracy on extended grade-school math word problems (E-GSM), including Acc0-Acc4, CoLeG-E, and CoLeG-R
finding.study_size: n=1319 original questions plus extended variants across 5 rounds; model evaluations on 4 proprietary and 4 open-source LLMs

paper_profiles.title: BanglaMATH: A Bangla benchmark dataset for testing LLM mathematical reasoning at grades 6, 7, and 8
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper introduces BanglaMATH, a new benchmark dataset of 1.7k Bangla math word problems collected from Bangladeshi elementary-school workbooks and exam materials. The central question is whether large language models can perform mathematical reasoning in Bangla, a low-resource language that is underrepresented in existing math benchmarks, which are overwhelmingly English-based.

The study evaluates several general-purpose LLMs in a zero-shot setting on grade 6, 7, and 8 problems spanning arithmetic, algebra, geometry, and logical reasoning. Problems are annotated with grade level, reasoning steps, and number of digits, enabling analysis by grade and complexity. The authors also test robustness by adding distractor information and assess language bias by translating a subset of problems into English.

Results show that only Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek V3 achieve consistently strong performance, with accuracy at or above 80% across the three grade levels. Accuracy drops as grade level, arithmetic complexity, and reasoning complexity increase. Both top models are vulnerable to irrelevant distractors, and both perform better on English translations than on Bangla, suggesting a substantial language bias. The paper’s main contribution is a benchmark and diagnostic analysis, not a learning intervention, and it concludes that current LLMs remain limited for equitable multilingual mathematical reasoning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper finds that LLM mathematical performance is strong only for some models and conditions, but generally declines with increasing grade and problem complexity. Gemini 2.5 Flash and DeepSeek V3 reach ≥80% accuracy across grades 6-8, while other models perform worse; for example, GPT-4 remains below 70% across grades and accuracy drops below 50% for problems requiring four or more reasoning steps.
finding.measure: Accuracy on Bangla elementary math word problems by grade, digit count, and reasoning-step complexity
finding.study_size: n=1,703 problems overall; n=60 for distractor and translation subsets

paper_profiles.title: Language Models Are Multilingual Chain-of-Thought Reasoners
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (benchmark evaluation on grade-school math and multilingual reasoning; no human K-12 participant sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language models can perform chain-of-thought reasoning in multilingual settings, especially on arithmetic and commonsense reasoning tasks. The authors introduce MGSM, a benchmark created by manually translating 250 GSM8K grade-school math problems into ten typologically diverse languages, and then evaluate GPT-3 and PaLM under several prompting strategies: direct answer prediction, chain-of-thought in the native language, chain-of-thought in English, and translate-to-English with English reasoning.

The paper is not an intervention study with K-12 learners; instead, it is a model evaluation paper focused on multilingual benchmark performance. For MGSM, the models show clear gains from chain-of-thought prompting over direct prediction, and the largest model (PaLM-540B) reaches 55.0% average accuracy with translated-English prompting and 51.3% with English chain-of-thought under native-language exemplars. Performance is strong even in underrepresented languages such as Bengali and Swahili, and English chain-of-thought often matches or exceeds native-language reasoning. The authors also extend the analysis to XCOPA and XL-WiC, where multilingual chain-of-thought sometimes improves reasoning performance, though not consistently on all tasks.

finding.finding_summary: On the MGSM grade-school math benchmark (n=250 translated problems across 11 languages including English), chain-of-thought prompting substantially improved accuracy over direct answer prediction. For PaLM-540B, accuracy rose from 18.6% with DIRECT to 48.1% with NATIVE-COT, 51.3% with EN-COT, and 55.0% with TRANSLATE-EN; for GPT-3 text-davinci-002, accuracy rose from 11.7% to 26.4%, 31.6%, and 45.6%, respectively.
finding.measure: Accuracy on MGSM grade-school math word problems

paper_profiles.title: Diffusion Models for Generative Artificial Intelligence: An Introduction for Applied Mathematicians
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a mathematically oriented introduction to diffusion models for generative artificial intelligence. Rather than evaluating an educational intervention, it explains the forward noising and reverse denoising processes used in diffusion-based image generation, derives the relevant probability expressions, and shows how these models can be trained and sampled with simple algorithms.

The authors target advanced undergraduate and postgraduate students in mathematics and related disciplines, with the stated goal of providing accessible derivations, computational examples, and code. The paper uses MNIST digit generation as an illustrative example and discusses broader issues such as evaluation metrics, computational cost, ethics, privacy, bias, and the relation of diffusion models to PDEs.

The paper does not study K-12 learners, tutoring systems, or mathematics achievement outcomes. It is a conceptual/tutorial article about the mathematical foundations of diffusion models, not an empirical education study. As such, there are no subgroup effects, no special education or multilingual learner analyses, and no instructional impact estimates reported.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 Mathematics Educators (Elementary, Middle, and High School contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks how K-12 mathematics educators evaluate lesson plans generated by generative AI models compared with human-created curriculum materials, and whether those preferences vary by grade level and lesson-plan component. The authors frame the work as an exploratory comparative study of educator decision-making in AI-assisted lesson planning rather than a student outcome study.

The study compares three sources of mathematics lesson plans: a customized prompt-based GPT-4 system, a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model, and human curriculum designer lesson plans retrieved from open educational repositories. Twenty experienced K-12 math educators participated in pairwise blinded evaluations of 529 lesson-plan pairs across warm-up, main task, cool-down, and overall quality measures, with 2,979 optional comments also collected for thematic analysis. Quantitative analysis used pairwise preference counts and bootstrapped estimates, while qualitative analysis used LDA topic modeling and manual coding.

Overall, educators still preferred human-created plans for warm-ups, main tasks, and overall quality, especially in elementary settings, but GenAI plans were comparatively stronger for cool-down/reflection activities. Preferences also shifted by grade level: human-authored plans dominated in elementary school, while AI-generated plans became more competitive in middle school and, in some comparisons, high school. The authors conclude that GenAI appears most useful as an assistive tool for structured lesson components and summarization, but human curriculum expertise remains important for pedagogy, differentiation, and student discourse.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that educators saw GenAI as a useful assistive tool for lesson planning, with AI-generated plans often praised for structure and adaptability. Although human-created plans were still preferred overall, the authors conclude that GenAI can reduce educator cognitive load and workload by supporting structured lesson-plan drafting, especially for cool-down sections and other more templated components.
finding.measure: Educator preferences and qualitative comments about lesson-plan usefulness, structure, and workload reduction
finding.study_size: n=16 educators (529 evaluated lesson-plan pairs; 2116 total measure-level evaluations)

finding.finding_summary: Educators consistently favored human-authored lesson plans for fostering student discourse, collaboration, and differentiated support, but preferred GenAI outputs for some structured components such as cool-downs. Qualitative themes indicated that human plans better supported group work and meaningful discussion, while AI plans were seen as more structured but less deep in facilitating interactive learning.
finding.measure: Pairwise educator preferences and comment themes on group work, student discourse, and cognitive demand

finding.finding_summary: Educators emphasized engagement, scaffolding, and developmentally appropriate warm-ups, especially in elementary grades, and preferred human-authored plans for these purposes. The paper does not measure student social-emotional outcomes directly; instead, it reports educator perceptions that human plans better supported engagement while GenAI was stronger in more structured wrap-up activities.
finding.measure: Educator preferences regarding warm-up relevance, engagement, and overall lesson appeal

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that GenAI could support a human-AI collaborative model for curriculum development and responsible AI integration in K-12 education. Their findings are presented as evidence to inform adoption decisions, tool design, and educator workflow integration rather than as direct policy evaluation.
finding.measure: Educator preferences and thematic feedback about AI integration in lesson planning

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual discussion and case-study-based reflection on how artificial intelligence, especially ChatGPT and other large language models, should be integrated into education. The paper focuses on three proposed competencies for the AI era: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It argues that schools and universities need more than simple AI bans or permissive policies; they need structured guidance, training, and a culture of responsible AI use.

The paper draws primarily on informal discussions and teaching experience at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, combined with a narrative literature review. The case context is higher education, with the author suggesting the ideas may also be useful for children and K-12 settings, but no K-12 intervention or empirical study is conducted. The article describes institutional AI guidelines, examples of classroom uses of AI, and a set of proposed AI literacy course components and prompting techniques.

Its main conclusion is that effective AI use in education depends on teaching students to understand AI’s limitations, to prompt it strategically, and to critically evaluate outputs rather than accept them uncritically. The article is normative rather than experimental: it does not test an intervention or report causal effects, but instead proposes practical recommendations for educators and institutions navigating generative AI adoption.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that prompt engineering and AI literacy can support critical thinking by encouraging students to question, compare, and evaluate AI outputs rather than relying on them passively. However, this is a conceptual claim grounded in examples and literature discussion, not an empirical effect estimate, and no study-level outcome data are reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, reflective evaluation of AI outputs, and prompt-engineering skill development

finding.finding_summary: The article proposes institutional AI guidelines, workshops, regular updates, dedicated budgets, and paid expert positions as ways to build an AI-supportive culture in the university. These recommendations are intended to improve governance, transparency, and responsible AI use across the institution, but no empirical institutional outcome measures are reported.
finding.measure: Institutional AI policy/guidelines, training structures, and governance practices

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that AI tools can help teachers with time-consuming tasks such as curriculum creation, case-study generation, and classroom design, thereby improving efficiency and sparing teacher workload. These are presented as practical possibilities rather than measured outcomes, and the article provides no quantitative evidence of workload reduction.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, curriculum development efficiency, and task automation potential

paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper investigates what K-12 learning design should look like when AI is introduced as a collaborative learning agent, rather than simply a tool for delivering content or feedback. The authors focus on student-AI collaboration (SAC) and ask what curriculum, interaction supports, learning environments, and developmental stages are needed to make such collaboration effective in schools.

The study uses in-depth semi-structured interviews with 10 Korean leading teachers in AI in Education (5 primary, 5 secondary) drawn from SW leading schools, AI pilot schools, and AI convergence curriculum-oriented high schools. Using hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis, the authors derive a four-part SAC model covering curriculum, student-AI interaction, environment, and evolution over time. Teachers emphasized capacity building, subject-matter knowledge, interdisciplinary and authentic tasks, process-oriented and collaboration assessment, instruction on AI principles and data literacy, AI ethics and everyday AI experiences, intuitive interfaces, flexible physical/digital learning environments, systematic policy support, and a culture of collaboration and safe-to-fail learning. The paper concludes with a staged view of SAC development: students first learn about AI, then learn from AI, and eventually learn together with AI.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers perceived student-AI collaboration as supporting higher-order and durable skills, especially critical thinking, creativity, analytical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, leadership, and reflection. The evidence is qualitative and based on interviews with 10 teachers (n=10), who described SAC as helping students become more future-proof and able to work productively with AI.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on higher-order thinking, collaboration, leadership, reflection, and problem-solving in SAC

finding.finding_summary: Teachers argued that SAC should strengthen motivation, engagement, persistence, and willingness to retry after failure. They specifically highlighted gamification, educationally meaningful socio-emotional interaction, AI ethics education, and safe-to-fail classroom culture as supports for sustaining participation and reducing fear of failure. No quantitative effect sizes were reported because the study is qualitative (n=10).
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on engagement, motivation, persistence, affective support, and safe-to-fail culture

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed SAC could improve subject-matter knowledge building across domains by helping students organize, link, retrieve, and apply content knowledge to authentic and creative tasks. The paper does not report student outcome data; rather, it synthesizes teacher views from interviews with 10 Korean AIED teachers on how SAC should be designed to deepen subject understanding.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on subject-matter knowledge building and application in authentic tasks

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the institutional conditions needed for SAC, including systematic AIED policy, governance and coordination mechanisms, teacher capacity building, flexible school systems, collaborative school culture, and safe-to-fail environments. The evidence is qualitative and drawn from interviews with 10 teachers, who consistently emphasized policy and institutional support as prerequisites for implementation.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes on policy, governance, teacher training, school system flexibility, and collaborative culture

paper_profiles.title: Teacher’s Perceptions of Using an Artificial Intelligence-Based Educational Tool for Scientific Writing
paper_profiles.population: Adult (K-12 STEM teachers in a doctoral course)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 STEM teachers perceived an AI-enhanced scaffolding system for scientific writing after using it themselves. The authors focus on whether hands-on interaction with an AI-based tool changes teachers’ views about AI’s instructional value, what benefits they perceive, and what concerns they raise about classroom implementation.

The intervention was an artificial intelligence-enhanced scaffolding system (AISS) built on GPT-2. Teachers first read about AI in education and discussed related literature, then completed a writing activity in which they used the system to draft and revise a short scientific essay in response to an authentic air-quality problem. The AI provided generated text that functioned as conceptual and strategic scaffolding, including expert modeling, immediate feedback, and individualized suggestions. Data came from interview transcripts and log files, and were analyzed thematically.

Participants were nine STEM teachers from K-12 schools in the southeastern United States, all with at least 10 years of teaching experience and none with prior experience using educational AI. The study found broadly positive perceptions: teachers saw the system as useful for expert modeling, stronger evidence-based writing, reasoning, and higher-order thinking, especially for middle and high school students. They also expressed concerns about reduced teacher roles, transparency of AI decisions, and the accuracy and validity of AI-generated support. The paper concludes that direct experience with AI scaffolding can increase teachers’ receptivity to AI in STEM education and can inform future implementation guidelines.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that the AISS improved scientific writing support by generating well-written sentences and paragraphs that served as exemplary models. The tool was perceived as helping users strengthen claims and organize writing logically; no quantitative effect size was reported because this was a qualitative perception study (n=9).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of AI-supported scientific writing quality, sentence structure, and paragraph sequencing

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently described the system as supporting reasoning, argumentation, higher-order thinking, and self-directed learning. They said the AI prompted them to compare options, justify claims with evidence, and reflect on their thinking, but the study did not report quantitative effect sizes (n=9).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of reasoning, argumentation, higher-order thinking, and self-reflection during scientific writing

finding.finding_summary: The AI scaffold was viewed as helpful for constructing evidence-based scientific claims and for supporting problem solving in an authentic air-quality task. Teachers emphasized that the system expanded the scope of evidence considered and guided them toward stronger claims, but no quantitative effect size was reported (n=9).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of evidence-based scientific writing and problem solving in an authentic STEM writing task

finding.finding_summary: Teachers noted that the system produced immediate responses and individualized support, which they saw as more efficient than waiting for human feedback. However, they also worried about the need to review AI output for accuracy and appropriateness, so the efficiency benefit was perceived rather than measured quantitatively (n=9).
finding.measure: Teacher perceptions of immediacy, individualized support, and review burden associated with AI scaffolding

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a review paper that surveys the emerging literature on artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT. Rather than testing a specific intervention, it synthesizes conceptual and prior empirical work on how AI tools are being used to support teaching, learning, feedback, assessment, and administrative tasks.

The paper discusses potential benefits for students, teachers, and administrators, including personalized learning, instant feedback, improved motivation and engagement, reduced teacher workload, and support for assessment and student monitoring. It also highlights important ethical and practical concerns such as bias, privacy, reliability, academic integrity, and the need for teacher training and supervision.

The context is broad and not limited to a particular grade band or subject area. Although the paper references educational applications that include mathematics tutoring and K-12-related AI work, it does not report a primary empirical study or a mechanism experiment. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT and related AI systems have substantial promise in education, but effective and responsible use will require careful design, pedagogical alignment, and policy/ethical safeguards.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI chatbots can reduce teacher administrative workload by automating grading, scoring, feedback, and student-question answering. This is presented as a synthesis claim from prior literature rather than a single evaluated intervention; no primary sample size, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload; automated grading/scoring/feedback efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI-supported learning can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce learning anxiety. These outcomes are discussed across cited studies, but this paper itself does not report a new experiment or pooled estimate; no study size or effect size is provided.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, confidence, anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes that AI tools can improve general academic performance and learning outcomes through personalized instruction and feedback. However, these claims are broad and secondary, with no original outcome measurement reported in this review article.
finding.measure: General academic performance / learning outcomes

paper_profiles.title: Interacting with educational chatbots: A systematic review
paper_profiles.population: Mixed (K-12, higher education, and other learners across reviewed studies)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the lack of synthesis on how educational chatbots are designed, deployed, and evaluated in prior education research. The authors systematically review 36 peer-reviewed studies published from 2011 to 2021, organizing them along seven dimensions: field of application, platform, educational role, interaction style, design principles, empirical evidence, and limitations.

The review finds that educational chatbots are most often used in computer science and general education, and are most commonly web-based and chatbot-driven. Across the reviewed studies, chatbots primarily serve as teaching agents or peer agents, with design principles including personalized learning, experiential learning, collaborative learning, affective learning, learning by teaching, and scaffolding.

Empirical evidence in the reviewed literature is mixed but generally positive: many studies report improved learning, engagement, or satisfaction, often in experiments with relatively small samples, though some studies find no sustained engagement or only limited effects. The paper concludes that educational chatbots are promising but that future work should improve dataset quality, usability, and attention to interaction style and design principles.

finding.finding_summary: The review includes two mathematics chatbot studies, especially a teachable-agent mathematics chatbot in Matsuda et al. (2013). In the summarized experiment (n=183), the paper reports improved learning with p < 0.001 after students interacted with the chatbot while solving mathematical equations and steps.
finding.measure: Learning performance on mathematics tasks / post-test outcomes in a teachable-agent equation-solving context

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, chatbots often improved engagement, interest in learning, subjective satisfaction, and motivation, though one longitudinal study found declining interest over time. Examples include improved engagement in Ruan et al. (2021) with p < 0.0001 (n=56) and improved subjective satisfaction in Tegos et al. (2020) with p = 0.03 (n=56).
finding.measure: Engagement, interest in learning, subjective satisfaction, motivation, and sustained communication interest
finding.study_size: multiple studies; e.g., n=56, n=122, n=34

finding.finding_summary: The review reports gains in more durable learning-related skills such as formal argumentation quality, collaboration, and reflective learning. For example, Wambsganss et al. (2021) found that chatbot-based adaptive tutoring improved the convincingness and formal argumentation quality of student writing (n=55, p < 0.05), and other reviewed studies used collaborative and scaffolded discussion formats to support critical thinking.
finding.measure: Argumentation quality, collaborative discussion quality, reflection, and problem-solving processes

finding.finding_summary: The review includes language-learning chatbots and writing-related tutoring applications, though literacy is not the central focus of the paper. A notable example is Wambsganss et al. (2021), where chatbot-based adaptive tutoring improved formal argumentation in writing tasks (n=55, p < 0.05), indicating positive effects on writing-related literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: Writing quality / formal argumentation in text production

finding.finding_summary: Several reviewed studies concern foreign-language learning, including one experiment using a user-driven chatbot in English learning. The review reports improved engagement in Ruan et al. (2021) (n=56, p < 0.0001) and describes language-learning chatbots as supporting oral interaction and feedback, although direct fluency gains are not consistently quantified in the review.
finding.measure: Foreign-language learning engagement and conversational practice quality

paper_profiles.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to induce stronger reasoning behavior in large language models without relying on supervised human-written reasoning traces. The authors ask whether pure reinforcement learning, using only correctness-based rewards, can incentivize emergent reasoning patterns such as self-reflection, verification, and longer chain-of-thought generation.

The approach trains DeepSeek-R1-Zero on top of DeepSeek-V3-Base using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with rule-based rewards for mathematical, coding, and logical reasoning tasks. A later multi-stage pipeline (DeepSeek-R1) adds cold-start data, rejection sampling, supervised fine-tuning, preference rewards, and language-consistency rewards to improve readability and alignment while retaining reasoning gains.

The study is not an education intervention and does not involve students or classrooms; its evaluation context is benchmark reasoning tasks, including mathematics, code, STEM, and general instruction-following benchmarks. The main conclusion is that outcome-based RL can substantially improve verifiable reasoning performance, especially on math and coding tasks, and that reasoning behaviors like reflection and longer deliberation can emerge organically from the reward structure. The paper also reports that adding human-aligned constraints and non-reasoning data improves general usability, though some alignment steps slightly reduce pure reasoning performance in intermediate stages.

finding.finding_summary: Pure RL substantially improved performance on mathematical reasoning benchmarks. DeepSeek-R1-Zero’s AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 77.9% during training, and the final DeepSeek-R1 reached 79.8% on AIME 2024 and 97.3% on MATH-500 pass@1.
finding.measure: AIME 2024 pass@1; MATH-500 pass@1

paper_profiles.title: Reflection on whether Chat GPT should be banned by academia from the perspective of education and teaching
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion-based essay that argues against a blanket academic ban on ChatGPT and similar generative AI tools, while also acknowledging substantial risks to academic integrity, privacy, bias, and over-reliance. Rather than reporting an empirical study, the author synthesizes prior literature and public examples to make a normative case for regulation, guided use, and educational adaptation.

The central claim is that generative AI should be integrated into education and teaching in a controlled way instead of simply prohibited. The paper discusses how ChatGPT may support learning, personalized tutoring, content generation, and teacher efficiency, but it also emphasizes that schools and governments should establish rules, supervision, and assessment changes to reduce misuse and preserve academic integrity.

The paper is framed around K-12 and higher education broadly, with repeated references to school policy, classroom use, and teacher guidance. It does not present original data, experimental manipulation, or direct measurement of student outcomes; instead, it draws on examples from universities, school systems, and prior studies to support its arguments.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI should not be universally banned in academia; instead, it should be regulated through institutional policies, teacher supervision, and revised assessment practices. This is a conceptual argument rather than an empirical test, so no effect size, sample size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: policy and governance recommendations regarding ChatGPT use in education

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that education should increasingly prioritize critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and self-directed learning in response to generative AI. This is presented as a normative recommendation, not an outcome measured in participants, so no empirical effect estimates are reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem analysis, problem-solving, self-direction (conceptual educational goals)

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims ChatGPT can reduce teacher and researcher workload by helping generate text, answer questions, and support educational management, thereby improving efficiency. However, the article provides no original empirical evaluation of workload or productivity, and no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: teacher/researcher workload and educational task efficiency

paper_profiles.title: The effect of ChatGPT on students’ learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking: insights from a meta-analysis
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether ChatGPT improves student learning outcomes and under what conditions its effects are strongest. The authors argue that prior experimental findings are mixed, so they conduct a PRISMA-based meta-analysis to synthesize evidence from 51 quasi-experimental and experimental studies published between November 2022 and February 2025.

The meta-analysis covers 72 independent effect sizes on three outcomes: learning performance, learning perception, and higher-order thinking. Across the included studies, ChatGPT showed a large positive effect on learning performance (g=0.867) and moderate positive effects on learning perception (g=0.456) and higher-order thinking (g=0.457). Moderation analyses found that effects varied by course type, learning model, duration, and in some cases the role ChatGPT played; for example, learning performance was strongest in problem-based learning and in 4–8 week interventions, while higher-order thinking was strongest when ChatGPT acted as an intelligent tutor.

The evidence base includes secondary and college studies, with most included samples from college settings and STEM, language/writing, or skills/competencies courses. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support learning when used with appropriate scaffolds and instructional framing, but that benefits depend on implementation details rather than the tool alone. Because the review is limited to experiments that compare ChatGPT-based instruction against non-ChatGPT controls, it is relevant to causal evidence on GenAI tutoring, though it does not isolate prompt-engineering or guardrail mechanisms in the way a dedicated mechanism experiment would.

finding.finding_summary: Across 44 independent studies, ChatGPT had a large positive effect on learning performance (Hedges’s g=0.867, 95% CI [0.683, 1.052]). Performance was typically measured with post-test or exam scores, and the effect was robust in sensitivity analyses.
finding.measure: Learning performance tests/exams (post-test or comparable achievement measures)

finding.finding_summary: Across 19 independent studies, ChatGPT had a moderate positive effect on learning perception (g=0.456, 95% CI [0.287, 0.625]). The paper reports this outcome as being assessed primarily through scales and questionnaires, and the effect was stronger in longer interventions (>8 weeks).
finding.measure: Learning perception scales/questionnaires

finding.finding_summary: Across 9 independent studies, ChatGPT had a moderate positive effect on higher-order thinking (g=0.457, 95% CI [0.255, 0.650]). The included measures were primarily scales and questionnaires, and the strongest effects were observed when ChatGPT served as an intelligent tutor.
finding.measure: Higher-order thinking scales/questionnaires

paper_profiles.title: AI to the rescue: Exploring the potential of ChatGPT as a teacher ally for workload relief and burnout prevention
paper_profiles.venue: Research and Practice in Technology Enhanced Learning
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI, specifically ChatGPT, can function as a teacher assistant to reduce workload and help prevent burnout in secondary education. The authors begin from a literature review showing that lesson planning and content development are among the most time-consuming non-teaching tasks for teachers and major contributors to burnout, then explore whether ChatGPT can generate usable lesson plans and supporting materials aligned to instructional frameworks.

The study tests ChatGPT with prompts for math, science, and English lesson planning for students aged 12-15 and 16-18, using the 5Es instructional model as an evaluation lens.
