finding.finding_summary: Student survey outcomes were mixed and not statistically significant. The paper reports small positive and negative estimates across measures such as whether the tutor cared about understanding, cared about how well the student did in math, whether the student felt they could learn math when it is hard, and session/tutor ratings, with no significant treatment effects.
finding.measure: Student post-session survey ratings (5-point scales)

finding.finding_summary: Tutor CoPilot changed tutor pedagogical behavior in ways aligned with deeper learning and comprehension. Using classifiers over 550,000+ messages, the authors found treatment tutors were significantly more likely to use high-quality strategies such as prompting students to explain and asking questions to guide thinking, and less likely to give away answers or solution strategies. Some of these strategy shifts were described as approximately 2 standard deviations more frequent on a log-odds scale.
finding.measure: Tutor chat strategy usage / pedagogical language inferred from NLP classifiers
finding.effect_size: approximately 2 standard deviations more frequent on a log-odds scale for some strategies

finding.finding_summary: The system was designed and reported as a low-cost way to scale expertise in real time. The paper estimates Tutor CoPilot cost about $20 per tutor annually based on observed usage, and tutors reported it was helpful for generating well-phrased explanations and on-the-spot hints, though some suggestions needed simplification for grade level.
finding.measure: Estimated annual per-tutor cost; tutor interview feedback on usability
finding.study_size: n=20 interviewees (approximate); usage-based cost estimate from study sample

paper_profiles.title: Improving Student Learning with Hybrid Human-AI Tutoring: A Three-Study Quasi-Experimental Investigation
paper_profiles.venue: LAK '24: Proceedings of the 14th Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether a hybrid human-AI tutoring model can improve middle school mathematics learning relative to math software alone, and whether its benefits differ by students’ prior achievement. The authors argue that AI can handle adaptive math instruction while human tutors provide motivational, relational, and targeted support, potentially expanding access to effective tutoring for low-income students during the school day.

To examine this, the authors report three quasi-experimental field studies in urban, predominantly low-income middle schools in Pennsylvania and California. Across sites, students used different adaptive math programs (IXL, i-Ready, and MATHia) either alone or with remote human tutoring; one site also compared software-only, software plus math teacher support, and software plus teacher plus tutor support, and another site tested a dashboard-guided tutoring prototype with changing tutor-student ratios. The samples included 125 students at Site 1, 385 students at Site 2, and 75 students at Site 3.

The main findings are that adding human support to math software increased student engagement and some intermediate learning outcomes, including time spent, questions answered, skills proficient, and lesson/workspace completion. Effects were especially strong for lower-pretest or below-grade-level students, while higher-performing students sometimes benefited less or even appeared to slow in the round-robin tutoring condition. The study concludes that hybrid human-AI tutoring is promising for improving learning opportunities in K-12 math, but that dashboard-guided targeting and better tutor allocation may further improve equity and effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: Across three quasi-experimental site studies, adding human tutoring support to adaptive math software improved math-learning process and intermediate performance outcomes. In Site 1, the hybrid human-AI condition significantly increased time spent, questions answered, and skills proficient relative to software only (e.g., time spent β=0.202, 95% CI [0.057, 0.347]; skills proficient also increased), and in Site 2 students completed more lessons during tutoring (β=2.44e-01, 95% CI [0.106, 0.381]). In Site 3, improving tutor access from about 1:8 to 1:4 increased MATHia progress by 0.36 workspaces per hour (95% CI [0.02, 0.70]).
finding.measure: IXL time spent, questions answered, skills proficient; i-Ready lessons passed; MATHia workspaces completed per hour

finding.finding_summary: The study directly interprets increased time on task and engagement with math software as evidence of improved student participation and engagement under hybrid tutoring. In Site 2, average time on task increased from 24 minutes per week before tutoring to 33 minutes during tutoring, and the authors repeatedly describe these changes as gains in engagement and learning opportunities rather than test-score gains.
finding.measure: Time on task / time spent using math software

finding.finding_summary: The intervention is explicitly framed as a scalable way to increase tutor efficiency and the effective use of tutor time, especially through dashboards and lower tutor-student ratios. In Site 3, moving from about 1:8 to 1:4 tutors per student increased the rate of MATHia progress by 0.36 workspaces per hour, indicating higher productivity per hour of software use.
finding.measure: Workspaces completed per hour; tutor-student ratio; time spent per session

paper_profiles.title: Learning gain differences between ChatGPT and human tutor generated algebra hints
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether hints generated by ChatGPT can support algebra learning as effectively as human-authored tutor hints inside an adaptive tutoring system. The authors frame the problem as a scalability question for educational content production: if large language models can produce effective worked-solution hints, they may reduce the cost of authoring tutoring content.

To test this, they ran an online randomized experiment with 77 Amazon Mechanical Turk participants using Open Adaptive Tutor (OATutor). Participants were randomly assigned to either manually authored human tutor hints or ChatGPT-generated hints, and to one of two algebra lessons: Elementary Algebra or Intermediate Algebra. Each condition included a pre-test, five-item acquisition phase, and post-test.

The study found that 70% of ChatGPT-generated hints passed quality checks, but the rest were rejected because they contained incorrect work or an incorrect answer. Both the human and ChatGPT conditions showed positive learning gains, but only the human-hint conditions had statistically significant pre-to-post improvement. In both algebra lessons, human-authored hints produced significantly larger learning gains than ChatGPT-generated hints. The authors conclude that, in this setup, ChatGPT hints were not yet a substitute for human-authored instructional content and still required human supervision.

finding.finding_summary: In a randomized comparison of algebra hints, human-authored hints outperformed ChatGPT-generated hints on learning gain in both topic areas. Across the two lessons, both conditions produced positive gains, but only the control condition (human hints) showed statistically significant pre-to-post improvement (Elementary Algebra p=0.0219; Intermediate Algebra p=0.0213), while the ChatGPT condition did not (p=0.1427 and p=0.7912, respectively).
finding.measure: Pre-test to post-test learning gains on algebra problems/lesson assessments
finding.study_size: n=77 total; Elementary n=40 (control 19, experiment 21); Intermediate n=37 (control 17, experiment 20)

paper_profiles.title: Educators’ Perceptions of Large Language Models as Tutors: Comparing Human and AI Tutors in a Blind Text-only Setting
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether large language model (LLM) tutors can match or outperform human tutors on key tutoring qualities in a blind, text-only comparison. Rather than measuring student learning gains, the authors focus on perceived engagement, empathy, scaffolding, and conciseness in tutoring dialogues around grade-school math word problems.

The study compares paired tutoring snippets drawn from MathDial (human tutor conversations with AI-simulated students) and MWPTutor (an LLM-based tutor with guardrails for correctness). Thirty-five annotators with teaching experience, plus three LLM judges, reviewed 210 paired dialogs truncated to the first five turns and selected which tutor was better on each metric. The paper reports that annotators generally preferred MWPTutor over MathDial on all four metrics, with statistically significant differences for conciseness, empathy, and scaffolding, but not engagement.

The context is K-12 mathematics tutoring, specifically grade-school math word problems, but the study is not a learner-outcome evaluation and does not involve real students receiving instruction. Its main conclusion is that, in this constrained text-only setting, LLM tutors can be perceived as at least as good as human tutors on several subjective tutoring qualities, though the authors caution that the setting is limited and that human and LLM judgments are not perfectly aligned.

finding.finding_summary: This study directly compares tutoring quality in grade-school math word-problem conversations between a human tutor condition (MathDial) and an LLM tutor condition (MWPTutor). Human annotators with teaching experience judged MWPTutor better on scaffolding in the majority of pairs, with the paper reporting a significant advantage for MWPTutor (t=3.16, p<0.001; mean score=0.55, SD=2.51; 5 annotators per pair across 210 pairs).
finding.measure: Blind pairwise human ratings of tutoring conversations on math word-problem tutoring quality, especially scaffolding in grade-school mathematics

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly evaluates perceived engagement and empathy in math tutoring dialogues. Human annotators preferred MWPTutor on empathy with a significant difference (t=3.36, p<0.001; mean score=0.65, SD=2.81) and on engagement the direction favored MWPTutor but was not statistically significant (t=1.32, p=0.09; mean score=0.25, SD=2.72).
finding.measure: Blind pairwise human ratings of engagement and empathy in tutoring conversations

finding.finding_summary: The paper treats conciseness as a tutoring-efficiency metric and finds MWPTutor preferred over MathDial on conciseness. Human annotators gave a significant advantage to MWPTutor (t=3.65, p<0.001; mean score=0.55, SD=2.19), suggesting that the LLM tutor was perceived as making progress more efficiently in the truncated dialog snippets.
finding.measure: Blind pairwise human ratings of conciseness of tutoring conversations

finding.finding_summary: Scaffolding is analyzed as a pedagogical process supporting independent problem solving, which overlaps with durable-skills-related instructional support. In the paired-dialog comparison, MWPTutor was judged better at scaffolding than MathDial, with a statistically significant advantage (t=3.16, p<0.001; mean score=0.55, SD=2.51).
finding.measure: Blind pairwise human ratings of scaffolding in tutoring conversations

finding.finding_summary: Although the paper’s empirical setting is mathematics tutoring, it does not measure math achievement outcomes; instead it studies qualitative tutor performance. The paper reports that LLM-based tutoring transcripts were preferred over human tutoring transcripts across most rubric dimensions, but this outcome assignment is only marginal because the study is about tutoring communication quality rather than a separate academic content outcome.
finding.measure: Perceived quality of tutoring dialogue in grade-school math word problems

paper_profiles.title: Integrating AI Tutors in a Programming Course
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the 1st ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference (SIGCSE Virtual 2024)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines the deployment of RAGMan, an LLM-powered tutoring framework, in an introductory undergraduate programming course. The system was configured as five homework-specific AI tutors for the course’s Workout Projects (WPs), using retrieval-augmented generation, instructor-authored prompts, and guardrails intended to prevent the tutors from giving direct solutions or code. The authors describe how students used the tutors, how well the tutors responded, how students perceived the tool, and whether any grade differences appeared between the 2024 cohort that had access to AI tutors and a comparable 2023 cohort that did not.

The study is an exploratory, non-randomized classroom deployment in ICS32 at a large U.S. public university, with 455 enrolled students. Data sources included 2,072 logged conversations (4,769 message pairs; 671 conversations and 3,164 message pairs after cleaning), a voluntary end-of-course survey with an 88% response rate, and anonymized final grades. The tutors answered 98% of in-scope questions well and 94% of all sampled responses were rated good; among survey respondents who used the tutors, 79% said the tutors positively affected learning and 78% reported that they helped their learning.

The grade comparison between the AI-tutor cohort and the prior year’s cohort suggested some positive institutional and student-outcome changes, but the authors explicitly caution that causation cannot be inferred. Relative to the prior year, the 2024 cohort had significantly fewer failures and a higher share of B grades, while A grades showed a small decline. The paper concludes that AI tutors may support student success and learning in programming courses, but that the evidence is observational and limited to one course offering.

finding.finding_summary: Among survey respondents who used the AI tutors, 79% reported that the tutors had a positive impact on their learning process, and the authors also report that 78% felt the tutors helped their learning. Students particularly valued the judgment-free environment and step-by-step guidance, suggesting improved confidence and comfort in asking questions.
finding.measure: End-of-course student survey on perceived helpfulness and learning impact
finding.study_size: n=survey respondents not_reported (88% response rate); 79% reported using at least one AI tool

finding.finding_summary: The tutors were designed to nudge students toward problem-solving rather than provide direct solutions, and student feedback emphasized step-by-step guidance that supported understanding of programming concepts. However, the paper does not report a direct validated measure of critical thinking or metacognition, so the evidence is indirect and based mainly on self-report and interaction analysis.
finding.measure: Student survey responses and qualitative analysis of tutor interactions
finding.study_size: n=671 cleaned conversations; survey sample size not_reported

finding.finding_summary: In the programming course context, the AI tutors were associated with improved course outcomes in the workout projects and final grade distribution, including fewer failures and more B grades in the 2024 cohort than in the 2023 cohort. The authors report statistically significant differences in combined WP grades (p=0.012) and in the lower tail of final letter grades, but they caution that the study design does not support causal claims.
finding.measure: Workout Project grades, combined WP grade, final exam grades, and final course letter grades
finding.study_size: 2023 cohort n=359; 2024 cohort n=455 enrolled, with final grade comparison reported for cohorts

finding.finding_summary: The system provided scalable, on-demand support in a large introductory course, with about half of students engaging the tutors and 2,072 conversations logged across the deployment. The paper presents the tutors as a mechanism for extending instructional support without additional staff load, but it does not directly measure instructor workload or productivity.
finding.measure: Usage logs of AI tutor conversations and message pairs
finding.study_size: n=2,072 conversations; 4,769 message pairs (3,164 message pairs after cleaning)

finding.finding_summary: The deployment suggests that a guardrailed LLM tutoring system can be integrated into an existing large undergraduate course with limited disruption, and the authors frame the results as evidence that such tools may help institutions scale support. The study is not a policy evaluation, but it reports course-level outcome shifts and adoption patterns that have institutional relevance.
finding.measure: Class deployment, usage adoption, and comparative course outcomes across two cohorts
finding.study_size: n=455 enrollment in the AI-tutor cohort; comparison with previous year cohort

paper_profiles.title: The Path to Conversational AI Tutors: Integrating Tutoring Best Practices and Targeted Technologies to Produce Scalable AI Agents
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual review and design framework for conversational AI tutors. It asks what generative AI tutoring systems should keep from legacy intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), what should change because of generative AI’s new capabilities, and what should be centered as uniquely enabled by conversational interaction. Rather than testing a single intervention, it synthesizes research on human tutoring, prior ITS, and emerging generative AI tools to propose a keep-change-center-study framework for future tutor design.

The paper argues that effective tutoring depends on three broad ingredients: pedagogical scaffolding, motivational support, and interpersonal rapport. It reviews evidence that legacy ITS technologies such as knowledge tracing, knowledge graphs, and affect detection remain valuable, while generative AI adds new affordances for real-time content generation, dialogic feedback, and more flexible student-driven interaction. The authors also emphasize limitations of current large language models, including hallucinations, over-helpfulness, and weak diagnosis of student knowledge, and argue these must be addressed through hybrid human-AI architectures.

Because the paper is not an empirical evaluation of a deployed K-12 system, it does not provide head-to-head outcome evidence for generative AI math tutoring versus non-generative adaptive software or teacher-led tutoring. Its main conclusion is that conversational AI tutors may eventually achieve scalable, high-quality tutoring if they integrate proven ITS components with conversational generative AI, but substantial further efficacy testing is still needed. The paper mainly serves as a research agenda and design rationale rather than as an outcomes study.

paper_profiles.title: Towards Educator-Driven Tutor Authoring: Generative AI Approaches for Creating Intelligent Tutor Interfaces
paper_profiles.venue: Proceedings of the Eleventh ACM Conference on Learning @ Scale (L@S ’24)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical barrier in the adoption of intelligent tutoring systems: while ITSs can provide personalized and adaptive learning support, building them typically requires specialized programming and design expertise. The authors focus on the user interface authoring problem, asking how generative AI can help educators create tutor interfaces more efficiently without taking away their ability to control the design process.

The proposed solution extends the Apprentice Tutor Builder with GPT-4–based generation. Educators provide high-level requirements, and the system generates either a full tutor interface or reusable interface components using a compact domain-specific language, prompt engineering, and design constraints. The paper presents a small-scale comparison against a prior version of the builder, comparing time and keystrokes needed to build two example interfaces: a simple sequential-problem tutor and a more complex arithmetic equation solver. Using AI assistance reduced interface-building time for both tasks, with a larger gain for the complex interface (68% time reduction versus 23% for the simple interface). Keystrokes were also reduced (31% and 47%, respectively). The authors conclude that generative AI may improve tutor-authoring efficiency, especially for more complex interfaces, but they emphasize that larger and more controlled studies are needed to evaluate interface quality, usability, and educational effectiveness.

finding.finding_summary: A small-scale comparison found that AI assistance reduced the time required to build both tutor interfaces. For the simple interface, time decreased from 187 s to 143 s (23% reduction) and keystrokes from 184 to 126 (31% reduction); for the complex arithmetic equation solver, time decreased from 372 s to 116 s (68% reduction) and keystrokes from 141 to 74 (47% reduction).
finding.measure: Time to build tutor interfaces; keystrokes required
finding.study_size: n=4 team members (compared against prior ATB reports)

paper_profiles.title: Generative AI for Programming Education: Benchmarking ChatGPT, GPT-4, and Human Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper benchmarks generative AI models for introductory programming education, asking how well ChatGPT and GPT-4 can play roles similar to a tutor, assistant, or peer in common coding-help scenarios. The authors evaluate six scenarios: program repair, hint generation, grading feedback, pair programming, contextualized explanation, and task synthesis.

The study uses five introductory Python programming problems from GeeksforGeeks and 25 real-world buggy student-style programs derived from them. For each scenario, ChatGPT, GPT-4, and a human-tutor baseline are compared using expert annotations and scenario-specific metrics such as correctness, edit distance, grading agreement, and whether generated hints/explanations are complete and comprehensible. The evaluation shows GPT-4 consistently outperforms ChatGPT and often approaches human tutors, especially on program repair, pair programming, and contextualized explanation.

At the same time, GPT-4 still falls well short of human tutors on harder pedagogical tasks, especially grading feedback and task synthesis. The paper concludes that generative AI is promising for programming education but still unreliable in scenarios requiring deeper bug diagnosis, fine-grained judgment, or generation of high-quality instructional tasks.

finding.finding_summary: Across six introductory Python programming scenarios, GPT-4 substantially outperformed ChatGPT and often approached human tutor performance. On program repair, GPT-4 achieved 88.0% correctness versus 68.0% for ChatGPT and 100.0% for tutors (n=25 instances per scenario), while on pair programming it reached 64.0% overall versus 38.0% for ChatGPT and 82.0% for tutors.
finding.measure: Scenario-specific correctness/overall quality metrics for programming tasks (e.g., Correct, Overall, Match)

paper_profiles.title: How to Build an Adaptive AI Tutor for Any Course Using Knowledge Graph-Enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses a practical problem in AI tutoring: standard large-language-model-based tutoring systems can hallucinate facts and often fail to preserve conceptual relationships between course ideas. The authors propose Knowledge Graph-enhanced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (KG-RAG), which combines an LLM, retrieval-augmented generation, and a knowledge graph to improve answer completeness, precision, and conceptual coherence.

The system is implemented with DeepSeek-V3 and evaluated in the context of a finance course. The main empirical study involved 76 first-year university students who were randomly assigned to either standard RAG tutoring or KG-RAG tutoring after a 3-hour self-study period and a 45-minute interactive session. The KG-RAG group outperformed the standard RAG group on a 10-point multiple-choice assessment (M=6.37, SD=1.92 vs. M=4.71, SD=1.93; t=-3.75, p=0.00035, Cohen’s d=0.86), and students also reported positive perceptions of relevance, usability, and learning support.

The paper concludes that KG-RAG can improve the quality of AI tutoring responses by grounding generation in structured domain knowledge rather than only semantic similarity retrieval. It emphasizes that the approach may be cost-effective and globally deployable, but it is evaluated on a relatively small undergraduate sample in a finance setting rather than K-12 mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: In a controlled experiment with first-year university students (n=76), KG-RAG tutoring produced significantly higher post-intervention quiz scores than standard RAG tutoring. The KG-RAG group scored M=6.37 (SD=1.92) versus M=4.71 (SD=1.93) on a 10-point assessment, with t=-3.75, p=0.00035, and Cohen’s d=0.86.
finding.measure: 10-point multiple-choice assessment on finance course content

finding.finding_summary: Student feedback suggested the AI tutor was perceived as relevant, easy to use, and helpful for understanding, with several Likert-scale items showing statistically significant positive ratings. For example, relevance averaged M=4.18 (SD=0.78, p<.001), ease of use M=3.68 (SD=0.81, p<.001), and perceived improvement in understanding M=3.42 (SD=1.02, p=0.003) among n=76 participants.
finding.measure: Student feedback Likert-scale survey
finding.std_deviation: Relevance SD=0.78; understanding SD=1.02; ease of use SD=0.81

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that participants felt their understanding improved after using KG-RAG, suggesting gains in comprehension and learning support rather than only short-term answer quality. The understanding item was significantly above the neutral midpoint (M=3.42, SD=1.02, p=0.003), though the study did not directly measure metacognition or critical thinking.
finding.measure: Self-reported understanding improvement on Likert-scale survey

paper_profiles.title: LLM-Powered AI Tutors with Personas for d/Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing Online Learners
paper_profiles.venue: ACM conference paper (manuscript submitted to ACM; arXiv preprint)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how d/Deaf and Hard-of-Hearing (DHH) learners perceive and interact with LLM-powered AI tutors that are given different personas tied to varying levels of experience in DHH education. The authors ask whether persona background information changes users’ expectations, trust, questioning behavior, and perceived accessibility of the tutor during online learning.

To study this, the authors built a prototype side-by-side video-and-chat interface using GPT-4o and four AI tutors: a baseline ChatGPT tutor and three role-playing tutors with different personas (one without DHH-specific background, one DHH access specialist, and one associated with a DHH-centric university). Sixteen DHH participants, recruited from mainstream and DHH-centric universities, watched a 15-minute AR technology video and interacted with each tutor, followed by semi-structured interviews. The study used qualitative thematic analysis of interviews and interaction logs.

Findings show that DHH learners did use the personas to ask DHH-related questions, and they judged tutors by their perceived knowledge of the DHH community and their position within it. Participants often preferred tutors they believed would better understand DHH concerns, but they also worried about transparency, representation, and whether the personas accurately reflected community membership. Accessibility preferences were mixed: participants wanted sign-language support, more control over response length and detail, and sometimes preferred warm, supportive dialogue while others preferred direct, impersonal answers. Overall, the paper concludes that LLM personas can shape interaction and trust for DHH learners, but current systems lack multimodal sign-language support and need more transparent, culturally situated persona design.

finding.finding_summary: The study centered on how DHH learners engaged with an AR technology learning video through LLM-powered tutors, but it did not test learning gains. Participants asked content questions about AR and said the tutors sometimes helped them understand concepts better, yet the evidence is qualitative and based on perceptions rather than measured learning outcomes (n=16).
finding.measure: Qualitative interview feedback and interaction logs about AR video learning

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported that some personas, especially Casey, felt warm, supportive, and more engaging, which made them more willing to continue the conversation. Others preferred ChatGPT’s direct tone, indicating mixed but generally positive effects on engagement and comfort rather than a uniform outcome (n=16).
finding.measure: Interview-reported engagement, trust, comfort, and willingness to continue interaction

finding.finding_summary: The tutors elicited questioning, reflection, and follow-up reasoning, especially when Jamie asked questions back to participants. Learners reported that this made the interaction feel more conversational and helped them think more deeply about the topic, but the paper provides qualitative evidence only (n=16).
finding.measure: Qualitative reports of follow-up questioning, reflection, and conversational engagement

paper_profiles.title: Do Hackers Dream of Electric Teachers?: A Large-Scale, In-Situ Evaluation of Cybersecurity Student Behaviors and Performance with AI Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how undergraduate cybersecurity students use an embedded generative AI tutor while solving hands-on, CTF-style challenges in an upper-division course. The study asks what kinds of questions students ask, how conversational patterns relate to challenge completion, and how students perceive the tutor’s usefulness compared with human support.

The intervention is SENSAI, an LLM-based, context-aware tutoring system integrated into a semester-long required cybersecurity course. The tutor used GPT-4o and received the student’s conversation history plus live terminal/file context, but it did not have access to solutions; it was designed to act as a Socratic mentor. The sample included 309 students in a 15-week course, with 142,526 tutor queries across 25,261 conversations and survey data from end-of-semester reflections.

The authors identify several dominant query families (e.g., debugging, implementation help, conceptual understanding, and direction requests) and derive short, reactive, and proactive conversation styles. They report that conversation style significantly predicts challenge completion and that the relationship varies by module difficulty. Short conversations had the highest completion rates, proactive conversations were somewhat lower, and reactive conversations were lowest across most modules; differences widened as tasks became more advanced. Students appreciated the tutor’s availability but rated it below human TAs and said it was less useful on harder material. The paper concludes that AI tutors can support practice-based learning in cybersecurity, but should complement rather than replace human assistance, and students should be taught effective ways to interact with them.

finding.finding_summary: The study focuses on cybersecurity task performance in an undergraduate course using a generative AI tutor. Across 25,261 conversations from 309 students, short conversations had the highest overall challenge completion rate (94.6%), followed by proactive conversations (90.7%) and reactive conversations (87.5%); the style effect was significant and varied by module (likelihood ratio test χ²=168.18, p<.001; interaction χ²(16)=46.67, p<.001).
finding.measure: Challenge completion rate across cybersecurity CTF-style course modules
finding.effect_size: OR ranged from 0.27 to 0.61 for reactive vs. short in most modules; proactive vs. short OR ranged from 0.39 to 0.66 in six modules

finding.finding_summary: Students reported valuing the tutor’s availability and said it helped them move past being stuck, but also reported that its usefulness declined on harder material. Compared with human TAs, students rated the AI tutor below TAs overall, suggesting it supported access and persistence but with limits in perceived helpfulness.
finding.measure: End-of-semester reflection survey on tutor utility, trust, and comparison to teaching assistants
finding.study_size: n=293 survey responses (with 150+ coded open responses; 309 participants in study cohort)

paper_profiles.title: Using Large Language Models to Provide Explanatory Feedback to Human Tutors
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This workshop paper addresses how to use large language models (LLMs) to provide real-time corrective and explanatory feedback to human tutors in an online lesson about giving students effective praise. The authors frame the problem as one of automatically classifying tutor responses into effective versus ineffective praise and then identifying the exact phrases that should be highlighted in explanatory feedback.

The paper studies tutor responses from a scenario-based training lesson, "Giving Effective Praise," with 65 volunteer tutors and 129 annotated responses. The authors fine-tune BERT for two tasks: binary/multi-label classification of praise types (Effort vs. Outcome) and named entity recognition (NER) to locate the relevant praise spans for templated feedback. Results show substantially better performance for identifying effort-based praise than outcome-based praise (Effort F1=0.811; Outcome F1=0.350), while the NER model performs poorly overall (F1=0.202), though the authors argue it can still support partially correct feedback highlighting and true-negative detection.

Overall, the paper concludes that LLM-based methods can be useful for tutor training, especially for automatically identifying effort-based praise and for powering template-based explanatory feedback interfaces. However, the work is explicitly preliminary and emphasizes limitations from small, imbalanced data, suggesting future improvements via data augmentation, stronger evaluation metrics, and broader application across additional tutor lessons. It does not evaluate learner outcomes or compare against alternative tutoring systems in mathematics.

finding.finding_summary: The system shows promise for automating tutor feedback generation by classifying tutor praise responses and highlighting relevant spans for templated explanatory feedback. In the reported pilot results, BERT achieved F1=0.811 for identifying effort-based praise and the NER model achieved overall F1=0.202 on span labeling, suggesting partial feasibility for workflow support rather than demonstrated large-scale efficiency gains.
finding.measure: BERT classification accuracy/F1 for praise-type labeling; NER F1 for span identification
finding.std_deviation: 0.046 for Effort F1; 0.235 for Outcome F1; 0.039 for NER F1

finding.finding_summary: The paper’s main pedagogical target is tutor learning, specifically helping novice tutors learn to give effective praise through corrective and explanatory feedback. The reported model performance suggests the approach can support feedback about process-focused praise, but the study does not measure actual gains in tutor skill or reasoning.
finding.measure: Classification of effective vs. ineffective praise and NER-based identification of praise components

finding.finding_summary: The paper substantively concerns praise practices that support student motivation, effort attribution, and self-efficacy, but it evaluates tutor responses rather than direct learner social-emotional outcomes. The results indicate the system can identify effort-based praise (F1=0.811), which the authors position as the more productive praise type for encouraging motivation.
finding.measure: Detection of effort-based versus outcome-based praise in tutor responses
finding.std_deviation: 0.046 for Effort F1; 0.235 for Outcome F1

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a conceptual discussion of how artificial intelligence, especially chatbots and large language models such as ChatGPT, should be integrated into education. It argues that the most important competencies for students and educators in an AI-adopted world are AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking, and it positions these as essential for using AI responsibly rather than relying on it uncritically.

The paper is grounded in the author’s experience with AI implementation at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences (Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences) and is supplemented by a narrative literature review. It describes institutional tensions around banning versus allowing generative AI, proposes guidelines for transparent and ethical use, and recommends workshops, dedicated training, and institutional support for staff and students. The paper also surveys prompting techniques and frames them as pedagogical tools to improve learning, critical reflection, and understanding of AI limitations.

Although the article mentions possible relevance for children and classrooms more broadly, its concrete context, examples, and recommendations are primarily about higher education and adult learners. The piece does not evaluate a specific AI intervention with student outcome data; instead, it offers theoretical and practice-oriented guidance for AI adoption in educational settings. Its main conclusion is that schools and universities should build an AI culture that emphasizes informed use, transparency, and critical engagement.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that institutions need AI guidelines, workshops, budgeted support, and dedicated staff to manage generative AI responsibly, but it does not test these recommendations empirically. Its main institutional finding is that simple prohibition or unrestricted access are both problematic, and that a middle-ground governance approach is preferable.
finding.measure: Institutional policy/guideline discussion and case-based implementation at a university

finding.finding_summary: The paper makes critical thinking a central educational goal and argues that AI literacy and prompt engineering can strengthen students’ ability to evaluate AI outputs, question hallucinations, and avoid overreliance on machines. No quantitative effect size is reported because this is a conceptual and narrative discussion rather than an outcome study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, critical evaluation of AI outputs, and prompt engineering skill development

finding.finding_summary: The article claims AI can help teachers create case studies, curricula, and interactive classroom materials more efficiently, but it also notes that prompting can be time-consuming and that staff need training and support. These are presented as potential productivity gains rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, curriculum design efficiency, and classroom preparation

paper_profiles.title: Learning design to support student-AI collaboration: perspectives of leading teachers for AI in education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 teachers think student-AI collaboration (SAC) should be designed and supported in school learning environments. The authors ask what curriculum, interaction supports, learning environments, and developmental progression are needed when AI is treated as a collaborative learning agent rather than only as a tool or content area.

The study is based on semi-structured interviews with 10 leading Korean teachers involved in AI in education across primary and secondary schools. Using a hybrid inductive-deductive thematic analysis grounded in distributed cognition, the paper proposes a student-AI collaboration model with four components: curriculum, student-AI interaction, environment, and evolution over time.

Teachers argued that SAC should aim to build students’ higher-order cognitive capacities, social capacities, digital capacities, and subject-matter understanding. They also emphasized interdisciplinary learning, authentic and creative tasks, process-oriented and collaboration-focused assessment, AI principles/data literacy/error analysis, socio-emotional support, intuitive interfaces, flexible classrooms, strong digital infrastructure, systematic policy, teacher capacity building, collaborative school culture, and a safe-to-fail environment. The paper concludes that effective SAC requires coordinated changes across pedagogy, assessment, technology design, school organization, and policy rather than isolated classroom-level adoption of AI.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that student-AI collaboration should explicitly develop higher-order thinking, including computational thinking, critical thinking, creativity, analytical thinking, problem-solving, reflection, and collaboration. The evidence is qualitative and based on interviews with n=10 Korean leading teachers; no effect size or confidence interval was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about desired student competencies and SAC learning goals

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described SAC as supporting students’ motivation, persistence, engagement, confidence, and resilience, especially through gamification, educationally meaningful socio-emotional interaction, AI ethics instruction, and learning from failure. The study is based on qualitative interviews (n=10) and does not report quantitative outcome estimates.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about motivation, engagement, persistence, and safe-to-fail learning

finding.finding_summary: Teachers expected AI-supported learning platforms and interfaces to reduce repetitive teacher work by automating data handling and providing scaffolding, while also making task execution more efficient for students through intuitive interfaces and integrated digital tools. This is a qualitative finding from interviews with n=10 teachers; no quantitative productivity measure was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about workflow, automation, and platform integration

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the institutional conditions needed for SAC, including systematic AIED policy, governance and coordination mechanisms, flexible school systems, teacher capacity building, collaborative school culture, and safe-to-fail environments. These findings come from qualitative interviews with n=10 teachers and are not accompanied by quantitative effect sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher interview themes about policy, governance, school organization, and culture

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines the emergence of artificial intelligence in education, with particular attention to chatbots and ChatGPT, and asks how these tools may transform teaching and learning. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper synthesizes existing literature on AI applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessment, adaptive learning, and chatbot-based support, while also discussing ethical, practical, and pedagogical concerns.

The article is broad in scope and is not limited to a specific grade band, subject area, or student population, although it frequently references K-12 and higher education examples in the background literature. It argues that AI can potentially improve learning outcomes, motivation, personalized feedback, and teacher productivity, but emphasizes that responsible integration requires attention to bias, privacy, academic integrity, and teacher preparation. The paper concludes that AI and ChatGPT are promising educational tools, but that further empirical research is needed to determine when and how they improve learning in real educational settings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses mathematics-focused AI tutoring only as prior literature, citing an AI math tutor study that reportedly reduced student anxiety, but it does not present any original math outcome data or head-to-head comparisons. No effect size, sample size, or confidence interval is reported in this review article for mathematics performance.
finding.measure: math learning / math tutor anxiety (via cited prior studies, not original data)

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI tools can improve motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety, drawing on multiple cited studies rather than new empirical tests. For example, it notes that AI-based interventions have been reported to reduce anxiety among middle school students and to increase student motivation and learning interest, but no pooled effect size is calculated in this paper.
finding.measure: student motivation, engagement, confidence, and anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The article states that AI-supported learning can foster critical thinking, creativity, self-reflection, and self-directed learning by providing individualized guidance and feedback. These claims are synthesized from prior literature and are not based on an original evaluation in this paper, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: critical thinking, creativity, self-reflection, self-directed learning

finding.finding_summary: A central theme of the paper is that AI can reduce teacher and administrator workload by automating grading, scoring, feedback, and routine student support tasks. The article gives examples such as chatbots and automated grading systems, but it does not report original quantitative estimates of time savings or efficiency gains.
finding.measure: teacher workload, grading/scoring efficiency, administrative support

paper_profiles.title: Interacting with educational chatbots: A systematic review
paper_profiles.population: Undergraduate and other postsecondary learners; some K-12-adjacent/younger learners mentioned in the reviewed studies, but the review is not limited to K-12
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper addresses the broader question of how educational chatbots have been designed, deployed, and evaluated in prior research. The authors note that existing reviews had focused mainly on whether chatbots improve learning outcomes, but had not systematically examined interaction styles, educational roles, design principles, platforms, and empirical evidence across studies.

To answer this gap, the authors conducted a systematic review of 36 papers published between 2011 and 2021 from ACM Digital Library, Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and SpringerLink. The reviewed chatbots covered multiple subjects, with the largest share in computer science, followed by general education, language learning, and a small number in mathematics and other fields. Most chatbots were web-based and most often functioned as teaching agents; common interaction styles included chatbot-driven flow-based or intent-based conversations, though some user-driven systems were also identified.

The review found that educational chatbots were typically designed around personalized learning, experiential learning, social dialog, collaborative learning, affective learning, learning by teaching, or scaffolding. Across the reviewed empirical studies, the most common evaluations were experiments, evaluation studies, questionnaires, and focus groups, and the authors report that results generally point to improved learning, engagement, or satisfaction. Because this paper is a systematic review rather than a direct evaluation, it does not provide a single effect size; its main contribution is synthesis of the educational chatbot literature and identification of gaps, including limited evidence, design challenges, and the need for stronger empirical validation.

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies only two mathematics-focused chatbot studies out of 36, including the teachable agent SimStudent (Matsuda et al., 2013) and Rodrigo et al. (2012). In the reviewed experimental evidence, Matsuda et al. (n=183) reported improved learning with p < 0.001, while Rodrigo et al. (n=126) reported p = 0.65, indicating no statistically significant learning effect in that study.
finding.measure: Mathematics learning / problem-solving performance in chatbot-based tutoring and teachable-agent studies
finding.study_size: varies across included studies; key mathematics studies included n=183 and n=126

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed literature, chatbots were frequently associated with improved engagement, interest, motivation, and subjective satisfaction. In the experimental studies summarized by the review, several effects were statistically significant, including improved engagement in Ruan et al. (2021; n=56, p < 0.0001) and improved subjective satisfaction in Tegos et al. (2020; n=56, p = 0.03), while Fryer et al. (2017; n=122) found no evidence for sustained engagement.
finding.measure: Engagement, interest in learning, motivation, subjective satisfaction
finding.study_size: varies across included studies; examples include n=56, n=122

finding.finding_summary: The review reports evidence that some chatbots supported durable skills such as collaboration and argumentation. For example, collaborative-learning chatbot designs were included among the reviewed studies, and Wambsganss et al. (2021; n=55) found improved learning and better formal argumentation quality in the chatbot condition, compared with traditional instruction.
finding.measure: Formal argumentation quality, collaborative learning processes
finding.study_size: n=55 for the cited argumentation study

paper_profiles.title: Speculative Futures on ChatGPT and Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI): A Collective Reflection from the Educational Landscape
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper explores the promises and pitfalls of ChatGPT and generative AI in education through speculative future narratives rather than empirical testing. The authors ask what education might look like if conversational AI became deeply integrated into teaching, learning, assessment, and academic work, and they use fictional storytelling to surface both optimistic and cautionary possibilities.

The study is a global collective reflection written by a large, internationally diverse group of education scholars. It does not evaluate a specific intervention, compare AI tutoring to other instructional approaches, or report experimental outcomes. Instead, it examines broad educational implications of generative AI across contexts such as personalization, collaboration, assessment, accessibility, ethics, privacy, academic integrity, and the changing role of human educators.

The main conclusion is that generative AI can support learning, efficiency, and access, but it also introduces significant risks related to bias, inequity, surveillance, over-reliance, and dehumanization of education. The authors argue that the question is not simply whether AI should be used, but how, when, by whom, and for what purposes, with human agency and critical literacy remaining central.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that ChatGPT-like tools can support writing and language production by giving instant feedback, suggestions, summaries, and text-conversation practice. In the narratives, students use AI to write short stories, essays, and summaries, but no empirical effect sizes or controlled outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: Writing support, summaries, and text-based composition tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly presents generative AI as supporting speaking, listening, translation, pronunciation, and conversational practice. For example, fictional scenarios describe AI-mediated oral communication, real-time interpretation in over 100 languages, and holographic scholar interactions, but these are illustrative narratives rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Oral communication, pronunciation, translation, and conversational practice

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses AI as helping with broader academic tasks such as research assistance, knowledge retrieval, translation, and content synthesis across disciplines. These claims are speculative and narrative-based, not backed by direct quantitative evaluation.
finding.measure: Research assistance, knowledge synthesis, translation, and academic communication

finding.finding_summary: The narratives suggest AI may increase confidence, reduce frustration, and provide encouragement through personalized support, but they also warn about dependence and potential dehumanization. No formal measurement of motivation, engagement, or self-regulation is reported.
finding.measure: Confidence, frustration, encouragement, motivation, and engagement (narrative themes)

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI can support collaboration, critical thinking, problem solving, and creativity, but also risks weakening originality and over-reliance on machine-generated answers. These are conceptual claims drawn from speculative narratives rather than empirical assessment.
finding.measure: Collaboration, critical thinking, creativity, and problem-solving (conceptual/narrative)

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that ChatGPT can save educators time by helping with lesson planning, grading, writing emails, creating quizzes, summarizing concepts, and improving course outlines. The paper does not provide measured workload reductions, but it clearly frames efficiency gains as a major anticipated benefit.
finding.measure: Teacher time savings, lesson planning, grading, and content generation

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses heavily on institutional implications, including policy, academic integrity, access inequity, privacy, ethics, and the changing role of educators. It argues that schools and universities need new assessment strategies, AI literacy policies, and safeguards, but no empirical institutional outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, academic integrity, access, privacy, and institutional role change

paper_profiles.title: Teachers’ AI digital competencies and twenty-first century skills in the post-pandemic world
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This conceptual paper addresses the question of what AI-related digital competencies teachers need in the post-pandemic era, when online and blended teaching have increased the use of artificial intelligence in education. Rather than testing a classroom intervention, the authors review opportunities and challenges associated with AI-enabled educational tools and synthesize prior research and frameworks to propose a more comprehensive model of teacher AI competency.

The paper adapts and revises two existing frameworks—the European DigCompEdu framework and the P21 framework for twenty-first century learning—while also drawing on prior AI literacy work and TPACK-related thinking. It emphasizes that teachers need more than technical skill: they also need pedagogical, ethical, collaborative, and life/career-related competencies to use AI effectively for teaching, learning, assessment, and professional engagement.

The intended population is educators, especially teachers and teacher educators working in K-12 and higher education contexts, with a strong focus on online and blended learning environments during and after COVID-19. The article concludes that AI competency should be understood holistically, combining professional engagement, instructional design, content choices across disciplines, and student learning competencies. It offers a conceptual framework and recommendations for teacher preparation and professional development, but it does not report original empirical data on student outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools can reduce teacher workload and improve efficiency by automating repetitive tasks such as grading, feedback generation, administrative paperwork, and learning analytics. No original effect estimate is reported; the claims are synthesized from prior studies and examples (e.g., automated feedback, predictive models, dashboards).
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading/feedback efficiency, administrative task automation

finding.finding_summary: The article discusses AI-supported personalized learning as potentially improving student motivation, self-efficacy, and self-regulation in online learning environments. This is presented as a conceptual synthesis rather than a direct empirical test, so no sample size or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Student motivation, self-efficacy, self-regulation

finding.finding_summary: A central focus of the paper is the development of durable skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, communication, creativity, and problem solving in AI-rich learning environments. The authors argue that teacher AI competency should help foster these skills, but the paper provides no new empirical estimates or participant data.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, collaboration, communication, creativity, problem solving

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes that teacher AI digital competency should inform teacher education, professional development, school leadership, and educational standards. It argues for institutional frameworks and policy guidance for responsible AI integration, but does not evaluate policy outcomes empirically.
finding.measure: Teacher education frameworks, professional development, educational standards, institutional guidance

paper_profiles.title: Promises and challenges of generative artificial intelligence for human learning
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (conceptual perspective; no human participants studied)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This perspective paper examines how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may reshape human learning. Rather than reporting a single empirical study, it synthesizes literature across learning sciences, educational technology, and human-computer interaction to outline the main opportunities, risks, and research needs associated with GenAI in education.

The paper argues that GenAI may support learning by scaling personalized tutoring, diversifying learning resources, accelerating feedback, and enabling more authentic assessments. It uses examples such as ChatGPT-like tutors, AI-generated learning materials, multimodal feedback, and generative assessment agents to illustrate possible use cases, while emphasizing that the empirical base remains limited and mixed.

The article also highlights major challenges, including hallucinations, privacy and equity concerns, ethical issues, and disruption to traditional assessment. Its main conclusion is that GenAI should be integrated cautiously and in a human-centered way, with stronger evidence, AI literacy, and methodological rigor needed before broad educational claims can be made. Because it is a conceptual perspective, it does not provide direct head-to-head evidence for K-12 math tutoring versus peer tutoring, collaborative learning, or standard classroom instruction.

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review (review of reviews) that maps the scope, characteristics, quality, and findings of artificial intelligence in higher education research published between 2018 and July 2023. The authors ask what kinds of evidence syntheses have been conducted, where they were published, how collaborative they are, what technologies are used to conduct them, how strong the review methods are, and what AI applications and findings dominate the literature.

The review searched major databases and supplementary sources, ultimately including 66 evidence syntheses focused solely on higher education or continuing education. It classified reviews using an AI-in-education typology (e.g., profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, adaptive systems and personalisation) and appraised review quality with a DARE/AMSTAR-2-inspired checklist. Most included reviews were systematic reviews, usually published in journals, and a majority were by STEM-affiliated authors and conducted collaboratively, often within the same country.

The main substantive findings were that higher education AI evidence syntheses overwhelmingly focused on adaptive systems/personalisation and profiling/prediction, with fewer reviews on assessment/evaluation and very few on intelligent tutoring systems. The authors conclude that the field needs stronger methodological rigour, better reporting, more interdisciplinary collaboration, and more attention to ethics, transparency, and context. Because this paper is a tertiary review rather than a direct intervention study, it does not provide head-to-head causal evidence about learning outcomes for AI tutoring versus peer tutoring or standard instruction.

finding.finding_summary: This tertiary review found that AI in higher education evidence syntheses are concentrated in certain application areas and that the field has substantial reporting and methodological gaps. Across 66 reviews, 45.5% did not undertake any quality assessment, 51.5% did not report using digital synthesis tools, and 34.8% did not reflect on limitations, indicating a need for stronger governance, transparency, and rigor in the research base rather than a direct effect on institutions.
finding.measure: Quality assessment of review methods; reporting practices across included reviews

finding.finding_summary: The review suggests that evidence synthesis tools can improve efficiency and transparency in the review process, but adoption was limited. Only 12.1% (n=8) of reviews reported using evidence synthesis software with machine-learning functionality, while 16.7% used spreadsheets and 16.7% used reference-management software; the paper does not report an outcome effect size.
finding.measure: Use of review-management and evidence-synthesis tools

paper_profiles.title: Reflection on whether Chat GPT should be banned by academia from the perspective of education and teaching
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (non-empirical opinion essay; discusses K-12 and higher education broadly)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion essay that argues against a blanket academic ban on ChatGPT and similar generative AI tools, while also acknowledging academic integrity, privacy, bias, and overreliance risks. The author frames ChatGPT as part of a broader shift in artificial intelligence and digital transformation, emphasizing that education should adapt rather than attempt to prohibit these tools outright.

The article does not test an intervention or report original data. Instead, it synthesizes prior commentary and examples to make a normative case that schools should regulate and integrate ChatGPT responsibly, especially in ways that support personalized tutoring, more efficient learning, and educational reform. The paper discusses implications for K-12 schooling, higher education, assessment practices, and teacher practice, arguing that AI should be used to complement human thinking and support new educational goals such as critical thinking, collaboration, and adaptive learning.

The context is broad and international, with references to universities, school systems, and policy responses in several countries. The paper is primarily theoretical and policy-oriented, and its main conclusion is that AI tools like ChatGPT should not be banned wholesale but instead governed through clearer rules, assessment redesign, and responsible integration into teaching and learning.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that generative AI like ChatGPT could reshape school and university policies, curriculum design, assessment, and academic integrity practices, but it also raises concerns about plagiarism, privacy, bias, and overreliance. No original empirical evaluation is reported; the conclusions are normative and based on examples such as institutional bans and commentary rather than measured effects.
finding.measure: Policy and institutional responses to ChatGPT; academic integrity and governance considerations

finding.finding_summary: The article repeatedly argues that ChatGPT may support or weaken durable skills such as critical thinking, independent judgment, collaboration, and problem solving depending on how it is used. It does not provide empirical evidence; instead, it claims that overreliance could diminish thinking ability while careful integration could support higher-order skills and digital competence.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, independent thinking, collaboration, problem-solving, and self-direction (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses ChatGPT as a tool that can generate papers, abstracts, and text, and notes that it may help with writing-related tasks while also enabling plagiarism and academic misconduct. No study data are presented, so the article offers only a conceptual assessment of potential effects on writing rather than measured literacy outcomes.
finding.measure: Writing, paper/abstract generation, and academic writing quality (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The author claims ChatGPT can reduce workload, improve learning efficiency, assist with text generation and feedback, and help teachers manage and evaluate students more efficiently. These statements are illustrative and argumentative rather than empirical; no sample, comparison condition, or effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Workload reduction, task completion efficiency, and support for teaching/learning tasks

paper_profiles.title: The Perception by University Students of the Use of ChatGPT in Education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Emerging Technologies in Learning (iJET)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how university students perceive the use of ChatGPT in education, focusing on its perceived benefits, barriers, and possible ways to use it more responsibly and effectively. The study was motivated by the rapid emergence of ChatGPT and a noted gap in empirical research on students’ actual experiences with generative AI in learning contexts.

The researchers surveyed 200 Vietnamese university students who had used ChatGPT for academic purposes and conducted semi-structured interviews with 30 of them. Students generally viewed ChatGPT positively, reporting that it was easy to use and helpful for saving time, getting information across diverse fields, generating ideas, and receiving personalized tutoring and feedback. At the same time, they identified important limitations, especially concerns about reliability, inaccurate citations, weak handling of idioms and language nuances, and difficulty with complex mathematical formulas.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT can support learning as a consultant-like tool, but it should not be used uncritically or as a direct substitute for student work. Students recommended verifying ChatGPT outputs with reliable sources, using it as a reference rather than copying answers, providing clear usage guidelines, and promoting academic integrity. The study is descriptive and perception-based; it does not test learning outcomes or compare ChatGPT with other instructional methods.

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT was perceived as a useful study tool overall (mean=3.62/5, n=200), easy to use, and helpful for understanding theories, generating ideas, and supporting academic work. The survey showed a statistically significant above-average perception of use (one-sample t-test against 3.00: t=23.400, p=0.000), but this reflects attitudes rather than achievement gains.
finding.measure: Student perception survey of ChatGPT use as a study tool; Likert-scale items on usefulness, ease of use, and search functions

finding.finding_summary: Students perceived several motivational/affective and self-regulatory benefits, including saving time (mean=3.74), improving access to information, and receiving personalized tutoring and feedback (mean=3.56). The authors interpret these responses as indicating that ChatGPT can support learning efficiency and self-directed use, though no direct behavioral or achievement measure was collected.
finding.measure: Likert-scale perceptions of benefits including time saving, personalized tutoring/feedback, and adaptive learning

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT was viewed as helpful for brainstorming and illuminating ideas in writing, but students also noted concerns about overreliance and the need for critical evaluation of outputs. The study highlights both support for idea generation and concerns about critical thinking, source evaluation, and appropriate prompting, with no direct measured effect size.
finding.measure: Survey and interview perceptions of writing support, idea generation, and critical evaluation of AI output

finding.finding_summary: A recurring benefit was task efficiency: students most strongly agreed that ChatGPT could help save time (mean=3.74) and provide quick answers. Interviewees echoed that it returned information rapidly, suggesting perceived productivity gains, although the paper did not measure time savings objectively.
finding.measure: Likert-scale perception of time saving and quick response; interview reports

finding.finding_summary: Students identified a limitation in ChatGPT’s ability to handle difficult mathematical formulas (mean=3.72 as a barrier), indicating perceived weakness in mathematics-related use. This was discussed as a practical barrier rather than a tested effect on mathematics performance; no math achievement data were reported.
finding.measure: Likert-scale barrier item on inability to measure the value of difficult mathematical formulas

paper_profiles.title: Exploring the potential of artificial intelligence tools in educational measurement and assessment
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of how artificial intelligence tools, especially large language models such as ChatGPT, can be applied in educational measurement and assessment. It asks how AI might support different stages of assessment design and use, including test purpose specification, blueprint development, item generation, test instructions, item selection, administration, scoring, interpretation, analysis, and reporting.

The paper is not an empirical study of student outcomes; rather, it synthesizes potential applications and discusses benefits, limitations, and implementation challenges. It emphasizes that AI can improve efficiency, provide individualized feedback, and support assessment workflows, but it also raises concerns about bias, transparency, privacy, and overreliance on automation.

The context is broad educational assessment rather than a specific K-12 intervention or classroom setting. The paper argues that teachers remain essential in AI-based assessment for design, interpretation, ethical oversight, and instructional follow-up. It concludes that AI should augment, not replace, human judgment, and that successful adoption will require stakeholder participation, training, and transparent, ethical system design.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools and large language models can automate and speed up many assessment tasks, including item generation, scoring, reporting, and test administration. No empirical effect size is reported, but the review repeatedly claims that these tools can reduce teacher workload and save time by handling routine assessment functions more efficiently.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, assessment task efficiency, scoring/reporting speed

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on institutional implementation issues such as transparency, bias, privacy, stakeholder participation, training, and integration with existing assessment systems. It does not report empirical institutional outcomes, but it concludes that AI adoption in educational assessment could improve assessment systems if these governance and implementation challenges are addressed.
finding.measure: Implementation considerations, governance, transparency, privacy, stakeholder participation

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 mathematics educators and teachers; lesson plans spanning elementary, middle, and high school grades
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether K-12 mathematics educators prefer lesson plans created by human curriculum designers or generated by generative AI models. The motivating problem is that AI tools are increasingly used for lesson planning, but there is limited direct evidence on how educators judge their pedagogical quality across specific lesson components and grade bands.

The authors conducted a comparative user study using pairwise evaluations of lesson plans from three sources: a human curriculum designer database, a customized GPT-4 model, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model. Twenty experienced K-12 math educators reviewed 529 complete lesson-plan pairs (2,116 component-level evaluations) for warm-up, main task, cool-down, and overall quality, with qualitative comments collected for thematic analysis. The study focused exclusively on mathematics lesson plans aligned to Common Core State Standards and included elementary, middle, and high school contexts.

Results showed that human-authored plans were generally preferred overall and especially for warm-up, main tasks, student discourse, collaboration, and elementary-grade instruction. GenAI plans were comparatively stronger for cool-down/lesson wrap-up activities, with customized GPT-4 often preferred in that section, and LLaMA-2-13b fine-tuning showing more competitiveness in higher-grade content. The authors conclude that GenAI is best viewed as an assistive planning tool rather than a replacement for educator expertise, with human-AI collaboration recommended for lesson planning.

finding.finding_summary: The study directly examined K-12 mathematics lesson-plan preferences rather than student learning outcomes. Across 529 lesson-plan pairs from 20 experienced math educators, human-created plans were preferred overall (58.7% vs. CGPT-4; 53.6% vs. LLaMA-2-13b FT), but GenAI performed better on some components, especially cool-down activities where CGPT-4 was preferred 59.7% over human plans and LLaMA-2-13b FT was preferred 57.9% over human plans.
finding.measure: Educator binary preferences for mathematics lesson plans across warm-up, main task, cool-down, and overall quality
finding.study_size: n=20 educators; 529 lesson plan pairs; 2,116 component-level evaluations

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly identifies student engagement, discourse, and motivation-related features as key reasons educators preferred one lesson plan over another. Human-authored plans were favored for warm-up engagement and for fostering meaningful student discussion, while GenAI plans were praised for structured cool-downs and reflective closure; however, the study did not measure student affect directly.
finding.measure: Educator comments and preference judgments about engagement, student discourse, and lesson attractiveness

finding.finding_summary: Educators preferred human-authored plans for structured collaboration, meaningful student discourse, and differentiation, while GenAI was seen as stronger in structured content delivery and some higher-cognitive-demand high school tasks. The thematic analysis indicates that collaboration and discourse facilitation were central to why human plans were chosen, especially in elementary and middle school contexts.
finding.measure: Educator preferences and thematic coding of comments about group work, discourse, rigor, and lesson structure

finding.finding_summary: The study’s main implication is that GenAI can reduce educator workload by assisting with lesson planning, even though human-authored plans were preferred overall. The authors argue that customized GPT-4 and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b can generate competitive lesson plans, particularly for structured tasks, suggesting potential productivity gains in curriculum development.
finding.measure: Educator evaluations of lesson-plan usefulness and discussion of time/workload implications

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues for a human-AI collaborative model for curriculum development and suggests that GenAI should be integrated as an assistive tool rather than a replacement for professional curriculum designers. This is an institutional-level recommendation derived from comparative educator preferences and may inform school or district adoption decisions.
finding.measure: Qualitative conclusions about GenAI-human collaboration in K-12 lesson planning

paper_profiles.title: Facilitating student engagement through the flipped learning approach in K-12: A systematic review
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reviews K-12 research on flipped learning and asks how the approach affects student engagement, what technologies are used, and how the evidence is theoretically grounded. It is not a primary intervention study; instead, it synthesizes empirical studies published between 2012 and 2018 from seven databases, ultimately including 107 studies (journal articles, dissertations, book chapters, conference papers, and grey literature).

The review focuses on flipped learning, defined broadly as students receiving direct instruction or content outside class and using class time for active, collaborative work. The corpus was heavily concentrated in North American and Asian high school settings and most often in STEM, especially mathematics. The paper reports that flipped learning was generally associated with higher behavioural, affective, and cognitive engagement, with common indicators including increased peer interaction, enjoyment, participation, teacher interaction, confidence, and self-regulation.

The review also finds that teachers’ videos, learning management systems, and self-assessment quizzes were the most common technologies. However, the evidence base is methodologically uneven: many studies were short, had small samples, and only a minority defined engagement or used a theoretical framework. The authors conclude that flipped learning shows promising associations with engagement in K-12, but stronger, more rigorous, and more clearly reported studies are needed, especially outside high school STEM contexts.

finding.finding_summary: Mathematics was the most frequently studied subject in the corpus (38.3%, n=41), but the paper is a systematic review and does not pool a math achievement effect size. Across the included K-12 studies, flipped learning in math was generally reported as beneficial for student engagement and sometimes achievement, but the review emphasizes engagement rather than a direct causal estimate on math performance.
