finding.finding_summary: The article argues that LLMs can support higher-order skills such as prompt engineering, fact checking, editing, and debugging, and it warns that users must verify outputs critically. No empirical evaluation of these skills is provided in the paper.
finding.measure: Not reported; conceptual discussion of critical thinking, editing, and prompt engineering

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses institutional issues including plagiarism policy, authorship rules, disclosure requirements, grant review restrictions, bias governance, and equitable access to LLMs. It argues that institutions and journals should set clearer policies for responsible use, but no empirical institutional outcome is measured.
finding.measure: Not reported; policy and governance implications discussed qualitatively

paper_profiles.title: THE GRANTS REGISTER
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This document is a grants register listing funding opportunities from a variety of organizations and universities. It is not a research article and does not investigate an educational intervention, student outcome, or AI-related tutoring approach.

No empirical study is presented in the provided text. The content consists of administrative and eligibility information for fellowships, scholarships, and grants across multiple fields, including some education-related funding, but it does not report methods, participants, measures, or findings relevant to the requested sub-question on generative AI math tutoring or special populations in K-12 education.

paper_profiles.title: GPTs are GPTs: An Early Look at the Labor Market Impact Potential of Large Language Models
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This working paper asks how much of the U.S. labor market could be affected by large language models (LLMs) such as GPTs, and whether LLMs should be viewed as a general-purpose technology. Rather than studying adoption or realized productivity gains, the authors build a new exposure rubric to estimate which occupations and tasks are technically amenable to LLM assistance.

They apply the rubric to O*NET task and detailed work activity data for 1,016 occupations, using both human raters and GPT-4 to score whether an LLM or LLM-powered software could reduce task time by at least 50% while maintaining quality. The analysis is then aggregated to occupations and compared across wages, employment, job zones, and skill requirements. The paper finds broad exposure: roughly 15% of tasks are directly exposed, about 30% are exposed when complementary software is counted, and around 80% of workers are in occupations with at least 10% of tasks exposed.

The study is not an education intervention paper and does not examine K-12 students or tutoring outcomes. Its main conclusion is that LLMs have pervasive potential labor-market effects across many occupations, with higher exposure in jobs requiring writing, programming, and some higher-skill work, and lower exposure in science/critical-thinking-heavy and manual occupations. The paper positions LLMs as a candidate general-purpose technology whose impact may expand further through complementary software and systems design.

paper_profiles.title: The Promises and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence for Teachers: a Systematic Review of Research
paper_profiles.population: K-12 teachers (including pre-service and in-service; studies include elementary, primary, middle, and high school contexts)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper systematically reviews empirical research on how teachers use artificial intelligence (AI) in education and what roles teachers play in AI-related systems. The authors aim to clarify the promises and challenges of AI for teaching practice, focusing on the kinds of data collected from teachers, the roles teachers take in AI development and use, the benefits AI offers, the challenges teachers face, and the AI methods used in the reviewed studies.

The review screened Web of Science journal articles from the last 20 years up to September 14, 2020 and included 44 empirical studies, all in English, involving pre-service or in-service teachers in K-12 or related school contexts. The paper synthesizes patterns across these studies rather than evaluating a single intervention. It finds that teachers are used in AI research mainly as sources of training data, graders, and informants about student behavior, and that AI is most often used to support planning, monitoring/implementation, and assessment. The review also highlights recurring challenges such as limited algorithm reliability, weak technical capacity, and contextual limitations of AI systems, and it calls for broader teacher involvement and multimodal data in future AI development.

finding.finding_summary: Across the reviewed studies, AI was reported to reduce teacher workload by supporting timely monitoring, immediate feedback, intervention, and automated assessment. The review synthesized 44 studies and identified multiple efficiency-related benefits, including reduced burden through peer-tutor recommendation systems, automated essay scoring, and faster identification of students' needs; no single pooled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, monitoring efficiency, feedback timeliness, and automation of scoring/assessment

finding.finding_summary: The review found that AI-supported tools could increase student concentration monitoring, engagement-related observation, and teacher responsiveness during instruction, which may support more timely instructional adjustments. These findings were synthesized qualitatively from multiple studies, such as concentration detection and interaction analytics; no pooled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Engagement, concentration, and related learning-process indicators

finding.finding_summary: The review shows that AI was used to support non-domain-specific instructional tasks such as selecting readable texts, detecting authentic questions, and analyzing classroom interaction, but these were not evaluated as a single academic achievement outcome. The synthesis indicates that AI can support instructional decision-making and content selection in school subjects, though the paper does not report a pooled effect size.
finding.measure: Instructional support tasks and subject-specific classroom processes

paper_profiles.title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review of AI in higher education research. Rather than evaluating a single AI tool or classroom intervention, it maps and synthesizes 66 evidence syntheses published from January 2018 to July 2023, focusing on the scope, methods, quality, and main findings of AI-related reviews in higher education.

The review asks what kinds of evidence syntheses have been conducted, where they are published, who authors them, how collaborative the field is, what technologies are used to conduct reviews, and what the quality of this secondary research looks like. It also categorizes the substantive AI applications discussed in the reviews using a typology that includes profiling and prediction, intelligent tutoring systems, assessment and evaluation, and adaptive systems and personalisation.

The corpus is broad and mostly centers on general AI in higher education, with substantial attention to adaptive systems and personalisation and to profiling/prediction. The paper concludes that AIHEd review quality is improving overall but remains uneven, especially in reporting of screening reliability, exact search strings, data extraction details, and review limitations. It argues for more rigorous, transparent, ethically informed, and interdisciplinary AI research in higher education.

This study does not evaluate a K-12 tutoring intervention, and it does not report subgroup evidence for special education needs, multilingual learners, low prior achievement, or intervention-service participation. Its relevance to the retrieval question is therefore indirect only, through its broad discussion of AI tutoring and personalization in higher education.

finding.finding_summary: This tertiary review primarily examined the reporting and methodological quality of AI-in-higher-education evidence syntheses, not the effect of a student-facing intervention. It found that 51.5% of reviews did not report any digital evidence synthesis tool and 45.5% did not conduct a quality assessment, indicating workflow and reporting limitations rather than measured operational gains.
finding.measure: Review reporting quality and use of evidence synthesis tools

finding.finding_summary: The review identifies institutional and governance-level implications of AI in higher education, including uses for admissions, scheduling, retention, quality assurance, and analytics, but it does not test these outcomes experimentally. The authors conclude that future AIHEd work needs stronger ethical, methodological, and contextual grounding, reflecting a field-level call for improved research governance rather than an effect estimate.
finding.measure: Institutional use cases and review-level synthesis of AI applications

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing healthcare: the role of artificial intelligence in clinical practice
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is being applied in clinical practice and healthcare delivery. It synthesizes literature on AI methods such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and large language models across multiple healthcare functions, including diagnosis, treatment selection, dose optimization, patient monitoring, population health management, guideline development, virtual assistants, mental health support, and patient education.

The paper is not an empirical study of patients or learners; rather, it is a narrative/comprehensive review of indexed literature from PubMed/Medline, Scopus, and EMBASE. The authors argue that AI can improve accuracy, efficiency, cost-effectiveness, and decision-making while reducing human error and workload, but they also emphasize limitations such as bias, privacy/security concerns, hallucination, and the need for human oversight and regulation.

Although the introduction briefly references intelligent tutoring systems and student learning outcomes in math and science, the paper’s substantive focus is healthcare applications rather than education research. No K-12 intervention, learner subgroup analysis, or math tutoring evidence is reported. The main conclusion is that AI has broad promise for clinical practice, but responsible adoption requires strong governance, transparency, cybersecurity, and human expertise.

paper_profiles.title: Connecting Feedback to Choice: Understanding Educator Preferences in GenAI vs. Human-Created Lesson Plans in K-12 Education – A Comparative Analysis
paper_profiles.population: K-12 educators (elementary, middle, and high school mathematics teachers)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper asks whether educators prefer lesson plans created by generative AI models or by human curriculum designers, and which lesson-plan components and grade levels drive those preferences. It addresses a practical K-12 question: whether GenAI can support lesson planning, especially in mathematics, without sacrificing pedagogical quality.

The study compares three sources of lesson plans: a human curriculum designer database, a customized prompt-based GPT-4 model, and a fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b model. The authors created 400 math lesson-plan queries spanning K-12 grade levels and had 20 experienced mathematics educators evaluate paired lesson plans on warm-up, main task, cool-down, and overall quality using binary preference judgments, plus written comments. Four educators withdrew, leaving 16 educators and 529 complete lesson-plan pairs (2,116 measure-level evaluations) for analysis. Quantitative pairwise comparisons were complemented by bootstrapped aggregate analyses and qualitative thematic analysis of educator comments.

Overall, human-authored lesson plans were preferred for warm-up activities, main instructional tasks, and overall quality, especially in elementary grades, while GenAI—particularly customized GPT-4—performed better in cool-down/lesson wrap-up activities. Preferences shifted with grade level: human plans dominated in elementary school, AI became more competitive in middle school, and fine-tuned LLaMA-2-13b sometimes outperformed human plans in high school comparisons. Qualitative feedback suggested educators valued human plans for student discourse, collaborative learning, differentiation, and supports for multilingual learners and students with disabilities, whereas AI plans were praised for structure and concise summarization. The main conclusion is that GenAI is best viewed as a collaborative planning aid rather than a replacement for educator expertise.

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests GenAI can reduce educator lesson-planning burden by producing structured lesson plans that educators sometimes prefer, especially for cool-down activities. However, the study does not measure actual time savings or workload reduction directly; the conclusion is based on educator preference judgments and comments rather than a workload outcome measure.
finding.measure: Educator preferences for AI-generated vs. human-created lesson plans; qualitative comments about usability and planning support
finding.study_size: n=16 educators; 529 lesson-plan pairs; 2,116 measure-level evaluations

finding.finding_summary: Educators evaluated instructional features related to student discourse, group work, collaboration, scaffolding, and lesson coherence, which are durable-skill-relevant design elements. Human-created plans were preferred for fostering meaningful student discourse and structured collaboration, while GenAI plans were seen as stronger in structure and summarization but weaker in prompting interaction.
finding.measure: Binary preferences across lesson-plan components and thematic coding of comments on discourse, group work, and collaboration

finding.finding_summary: The study does not measure student motivation or engagement directly, but educators repeatedly cited engagement, warm-up relevance, and student interaction as reasons for preferring one lesson plan over another. Human-authored plans were especially favored in elementary grades for student engagement and developmentally appropriate warm-ups, while GenAI was more accepted for structured lesson conclusions.
finding.measure: Educator preference judgments and qualitative comments about engagement, warm-up relevance, and student interaction

finding.finding_summary: This is a K-12 mathematics lesson-plan study, and educators compared lesson plans built around Common Core math standards. Human-created plans were preferred overall for warm-ups, main tasks, and overall quality, while GenAI—especially customized GPT-4—was preferred for cool-downs and LLaMA-2-13b FT sometimes outperformed human plans in high school comparisons. The paper does not report student learning gains or achievement test scores; findings are about educator preference for math instructional quality rather than direct math outcomes.
finding.measure: Educator pairwise preferences for K-12 mathematics lesson plans aligned to CCSSM

paper_profiles.title: Multilingual Performance of a Multimodal Artificial Intelligence System on Multisubject Physics Concept Inventories
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines how well GPT-4o performs on a large set of validated physics concept inventories when the problems are presented as screenshots, so the model must process both text and visual information. The authors ask four main questions: how performance varies across physics subject areas, how performance changes across languages, how GPT-4o compares with published undergraduate post-instruction student scores, and how the presence of images affects answer accuracy.

The study uses 54 concept inventories from PhysPort spanning mechanics, electromagnetism, optics, astronomy, thermodynamics, quantum physics, mathematics, scientific reasoning, and laboratory skills. Inventories were presented as images in multiple languages; each item was submitted to GPT-4o three times, and responses were scored against answer keys. The analysis is descriptive rather than experimental, focusing on accuracy patterns across inventories, languages, and item types (text-only, image present but unnecessary, image required).

The main finding is that GPT-4o often matches or exceeds average undergraduate post-instruction performance, but performance is uneven across subjects and languages. The model performs best on thermodynamics, astronomy, reasoning, and relativity, and worst on laboratory skills and on items requiring visual interpretation. English is usually the best-performing language, and many non-English responses switch into English. The paper concludes that GPT-4o shows promise for physics education but has important limitations, especially with multimodal reasoning and cross-lingual robustness, and should not be treated as equivalent to human conceptual understanding.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4o performed comparatively well on scientific reasoning inventories, with reported English-language performance of 78.7% in the reasoning category. This places reasoning among the model’s stronger domains, though the paper does not report an effect size; the comparison is primarily descriptive against other categories and published undergraduate post-test averages.
finding.measure: Correct-response percentage on scientific reasoning concept inventories (e.g., Lawson Classroom Test of Scientific Reasoning, FORT, PIQL)

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4o did well on the mathematics-related concept inventories included in the dataset, with English performance reported around 71% on the CCI and 80% on PIQL, and good performance on TUV. The paper does not estimate an overall effect size, but results suggest the model can solve many conceptual mathematics items better than average undergraduate post-instruction performance.
finding.measure: Correct-response percentage on mathematics concept inventories (e.g., CCI, TUV, PIQL)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests GPT-4o may be useful as an educational support tool because it often outperformed average undergraduate post-instruction scores and could potentially assist with assessment, grading, feedback generation, and personalized instruction. However, these are inferential claims rather than direct productivity measurements, and the study does not quantify workload reduction or efficiency gains.
finding.measure: Qualitative/interpretive discussion of potential utility for automated grading, feedback, and instructional support

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that multilingual and multimodal AI systems may affect assessment validity, curriculum design, and educational equity, especially if performance varies across languages and visual formats. This is an institutional-level implication drawn from performance patterns, but the study does not directly measure policy or organizational outcomes.
finding.measure: Comparative performance across languages and image-based versus text-only items; implications for assessment and equity

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (position paper; discusses learners and teachers across primary, secondary, tertiary, and professional education)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the potential opportunities, risks, and implementation challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing an intervention, the authors synthesize early research and articulate how LLMs might support learning and teaching through content generation, feedback, tutoring, assessment, and other educational tasks.

The paper discusses applications across educational levels, with examples relevant to elementary, middle, high school, university, and professional learning. It also highlights specific use cases such as generating quizzes, explanations, practice problems, adaptive feedback, and math word problems, and notes that LLMs may be helpful for learners with disabilities when combined with other supports.

The main conclusion is that LLMs could meaningfully augment education, but only if deployed responsibly with strong human oversight, attention to bias and fairness, privacy and security protections, transparency, and pedagogical guidance. The paper is largely conceptual and does not report original empirical results; instead, it recommends further research and cautious adoption, especially to avoid overreliance, plagiarism, misinformation, and inequitable access.

finding.finding_summary: The paper does not evaluate a mathematics intervention empirically; it only notes that large language models can generate practice problems, explanations, step-by-step solutions, and math word problems for middle and high school learners. No sample sizes, effect sizes, or outcome measures are reported because the paper is a position paper rather than an empirical study.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by automating or assisting with lesson planning, quiz/question generation, feedback, assessment, and content creation. It cites prior studies suggesting efficiency gains such as reduced grading effort (e.g., up to 85% in a cited NLP-based feedback context), but the paper itself reports no original empirical data.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / grading effort / content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is the institutional and governance implications of LLM adoption in education, including copyright, bias, privacy, sustainability, fairness, and policy responses such as bans and oversight mechanisms. The paper is normative and conceptual, arguing that these systems can widen divides if poorly governed but could support equitable access if implemented responsibly.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, fairness, privacy, and institutional adoption considerations

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and collaboration when used as a supplement rather than a substitute for human learning. At the same time, it warns that overreliance may weaken these durable skills by making answers too easy to obtain and reducing independent inquiry.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, collaboration (conceptual claims and cited examples)

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs may improve engagement, participation, and curiosity, particularly through personalized tutoring, interactive dialogue, and curiosity-prompting agents. These claims are based on cited prior work and conceptual discussion rather than new empirical testing in this paper.
finding.measure: Student engagement, participation, curiosity, foreign-language anxiety (conceptual and cited evidence)

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a narrative review of the emerging literature on artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. The authors synthesize definitions, capabilities, educational applications, and risks of AI tools, especially generative AI systems that can produce human-like text, and they situate ChatGPT within broader AI-in-education (AIEd) paradigms.

The article does not test an intervention or report original participant data. Instead, it discusses how AI may support personalized learning, instant feedback, engagement, assessment, and teacher productivity, while also highlighting ethical concerns such as bias, privacy, academic integrity, and over-reliance on technology. It cites prior studies and reviews, including some on special education, reading comprehension, anxiety, and AI-supported language learning, to argue that AI has promise but requires careful implementation, teacher support, and policy attention.

Because the paper is an overview rather than an empirical study, it does not provide subgroup evidence for kindergarten through grade 12 students with special education needs, multilingual learners, low prior achievement, or intervention-service participation. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT and related AI tools could be valuable educational supports, but responsible use, equity, and human oversight are essential.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tools, including chatbots and automated grading systems, can reduce repetitive work for teachers and administrators by evaluating assignments, scoring responses, and providing feedback. No original data are reported, so this is a conceptual conclusion rather than an empirical result.
finding.measure: Teacher administrative workload / grading and feedback efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The review summarizes prior literature suggesting that AI-supported learning can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety, especially in personalized or interactive settings. It cites studies on AI math tutors, human-robot interaction, and chatbot-based learning, but the paper itself does not report new effect sizes or participant-level results.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, confidence, and anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The article notes that AI-based educational interventions have been reported to improve reading comprehension in students with dyslexia and that chatbots can support writing and punctuation learning. These are literature-based claims cited in the review, not findings from a new study in this paper.
finding.measure: Reading comprehension; writing/punctuation skills

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI and chatbot tools can support language learning by facilitating ongoing dialogue, communication practice, and pronunciation correction. It also cites a prior chatbot study for foreign language learning, but provides no original quantitative estimate in this article.
finding.measure: Language learning, dialogue practice, pronunciation correction

finding.finding_summary: Math tutoring is mentioned mainly as an example of AI-enabled personalized learning, and the paper cites prior work on an AI math tutor and math education reviews. However, this article does not evaluate a math tutoring intervention or report math outcome data itself.
finding.measure: Math learning / mathematics tutoring

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (opinion paper; synthesizes evidence across student populations, including undergraduate and secondary students)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper examines the promise and risks of artificial intelligence in education, arguing that AI can simultaneously enhance and erode learning. Using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory as its conceptual lens, the article discusses how AI may support personalization, efficiency, and accessibility while also increasing cognitive offloading, dependence, and reduced engagement in higher-order thinking.

The paper does not report a new empirical study; instead, it synthesizes prior literature and examples on memory retention, problem-solving, critical thinking, creativity, motivation, and language learning. It highlights that AI tools such as chatbots, adaptive systems, and tutoring platforms can improve some procedural and access-related outcomes, but overreliance may weaken retention, independent reasoning, and creative confidence. The authors conclude that AI should complement—not replace—human instruction, and they call for pedagogically informed, equity-aware implementation that preserves autonomy, competence, and active cognitive engagement.

Because the paper is an opinion piece, it does not focus on K-12 special education needs, multilingual learners, low prior achievement, or intervention-service participation as a studied subgroup; these topics are only mentioned indirectly in broader discussions of fairness, inclusion, and multilingual/multicultural inputs.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can increase competence and engagement through personalized support, but excessive dependence may reduce intrinsic motivation and relatedness. No original effect size is reported; the discussion is based on cited studies and theoretical reasoning rather than a new empirical analysis.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, and autonomy discussed conceptually

finding.finding_summary: The article centrally focuses on critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and creativity as key skills that AI may both support and erode. It cites prior studies suggesting AI can improve idea fluency/flexibility and procedural performance, but may also cause cognitive fixation, lower creative confidence, and reduced independent reasoning; no new effect sizes are reported in the paper itself.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, creative thinking, metacognition

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that AI can increase efficiency and reduce redundant work by automating lower-level tasks and personalizing instruction. These claims are conceptual and supported by cited examples rather than original data in this article, so no study-level effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Learning efficiency, reduction of redundant work, personalization

paper_profiles.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education: the state of the field
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a PRISMA-based systematic review of artificial intelligence (AI) research in higher education from 2016 through 2022. The authors ask how AI is being studied across countries, departments, academic levels, subject domains, intended users, and functional uses, aiming to update earlier reviews that ended around 2020.

The review included 138 peer-reviewed journal articles. It found that publications increased sharply in 2021–2022, that China surpassed the United States in number of studies, and that colleges of education became the most common first-author affiliation. Undergraduate students were the most frequently studied population, and language learning was the most common subject area.

Using grounded coding, the authors identified five major uses of AI in higher education: assessment/evaluation, predicting, AI assistants, intelligent tutoring systems, and managing student learning. The paper concludes that AI in higher education is still often used to augment existing practices rather than transform them, and it highlights gaps in research on graduate learners, instructors, managers, developing countries, and less-explored AI affordances such as newer tools like ChatGPT.

finding.finding_summary: Across 138 studies, AI in higher education was used most often for academic tasks such as assessment/evaluation, predicting academic performance, intelligent tutoring, and language-learning support. The review does not estimate a single intervention effect size; instead, it synthesizes how AI was applied and notes that many uses supported learning through feedback, prediction, and adaptive instruction.
finding.measure: Types and frequencies of AI uses in higher education studies

finding.finding_summary: Several included studies used AI to support student persistence, self-testing, immediate feedback, and emotion-related learning processes. For example, the review notes AI applications that provided personalized feedback, diagnosed student needs, and supported goal initiation, planning, action control, and emotion control, but the paper does not aggregate outcome effects across studies.
finding.measure: Student persistence, self-regulation, emotions, and engagement-related outcomes reported in primary studies

finding.finding_summary: The review reports AI uses that supported higher-order thinking, self-regulated learning, and diagnostic question answering, especially through intelligent tutoring systems and AI assistants. These applications were described as helping students plan, monitor, and respond to learning tasks, but no pooled effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Self-regulation, higher-order thinking, and related learning-process outcomes

finding.finding_summary: A major theme was efficiency gains, especially in automatic assessment/evaluation, question generation, and learning analytics. The review reports that automatic assessment reduced instructor grading time and that AI could help manage student data, sequence curriculum, and support instructional design, but it does not quantify a pooled effect.
finding.measure: Instructor workload, grading time, learning analytics, and instructional management processes

finding.finding_summary: The review found AI applications for institutional functions such as predicting dropout risk, admissions, student management, and big-data analysis for decision-making. These were presented as promising uses for organizational insight and student support, but the paper is descriptive and does not provide a causal estimate of institutional impact.
finding.measure: Admissions prediction, dropout prediction, student management, and institutional data analysis uses

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: A revolutionary tool for teaching and learning mathematics
paper_profiles.venue: EURASIA Journal of Mathematics, Science and Technology Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines early perceptions of ChatGPT as a tool for teaching and learning mathematics. The authors ask whether ChatGPT can support mathematics education, where it performs well, and where its limitations become apparent, especially in the context of mathematical problem solving and geometry.

The study uses a two-stage qualitative case study design. First, it conducts content analysis of 30 interviews with people who had discussed or used ChatGPT in mathematics-related contexts. Second, it performs a user-experience investigation in which three experienced educators tested ChatGPT across a set of math teaching scenarios, including solving equations, evaluating limits, derivatives, and geometry problems.

The paper concludes that ChatGPT is promising for quick explanations, example generation, and basic instructional support, particularly in geometry-oriented exposition. However, it also shows clear weaknesses: it can make calculation errors, mishandle algebra and calculus tasks, and lacks a deep conceptual understanding of mathematics or the ability to reliably detect and correct misconceptions. The authors recommend caution, verification of outputs, and development of guidelines for safe and responsible use in mathematics education.

finding.finding_summary: The study found that ChatGPT can provide step-by-step solutions and useful explanations for some mathematics tasks, but it also made clear errors on algebra, calculus, and geometry problems. In the user-experience scenarios, it gave incorrect answers for a linear equation, a cubic equation, a limit calculation, and a derivative evaluation, while performing better when explaining Pythagorean theorem examples and geometry concepts.
finding.measure: Accuracy and quality of ChatGPT responses to mathematics problems and explanations
finding.study_size: n=30 interviewees; n=3 educators testing scenarios

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper reports exploratory early experiments with a text-only, in-development version of GPT-4, arguing that it exhibits broad capabilities that may be indicative of a step toward artificial general intelligence. The authors probe the model with hand-designed prompts across many domains, including natural language, coding, mathematics, vision-like tasks via text representations, common-sense reasoning, theory of mind, tool use, and safety/bias scenarios. The paper is framed as a qualitative demonstration rather than a controlled evaluation, and the authors repeatedly note that results are preliminary and may differ from the final deployed model.

The paper’s central contribution is a set of curated examples showing GPT-4 producing fluent and often impressive outputs on tasks such as writing rhymed mathematical proofs, generating code for graphics, solving math problems, and answering common-sense questions. It also compares GPT-4 informally with ChatGPT, typically showing GPT-4 as more coherent, creative, or accurate on the showcased prompts. The authors emphasize that the model still has important limitations, including hallucinations, arithmetic mistakes, and weak planning, and they argue these limitations reflect broader challenges in moving from narrow AI to more generally intelligent systems.

Because the paper studies a general-purpose foundation model through illustrative prompts rather than a K-12 intervention, it does not directly examine student outcomes, tutoring effects, or subgroup impacts for learners with special education needs, multilingual learners, low prior achievement, or intervention-service participation. Its relevance to education research is primarily indirect, as a discussion of capabilities and limitations of GPT-4 that might inform future educational uses.

finding.finding_summary: The paper presents multiple illustrative examples in which GPT-4 solves mathematical tasks correctly, including a high-school level inverse-function problem yielding f(f(f(6))) = 4 and rhymed proofs about the infinitude of primes. These are not controlled experiments, but they show strong qualitative performance on discrete math reasoning tasks with no reported sample size or effect estimate.
finding.measure: Correctness on hand-designed mathematical reasoning prompts and problem-solving examples

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows GPT-4 producing outputs in non-mathematical academic/creative domains such as coding, literature, history, law, medicine, and art. Examples include writing Shakespeare-style proofs, generating TikZ/SVG code, and composing a Gandhi-style letter, suggesting broad cross-domain generative capability rather than measured learning gains.
finding.measure: Performance on interdisciplinary generation tasks (literary style transfer, coding, art generation, history-themed writing)

finding.finding_summary: The authors argue that GPT-4 demonstrates abilities associated with reasoning, abstraction, and some forms of common sense and theory-of-mind-style inference. These are illustrated through qualitative prompts rather than validated assessments, so the evidence is suggestive of stronger general reasoning but not a measured effect.
finding.measure: Qualitative demonstrations of reasoning, common sense, theory-of-mind, and explanation tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims GPT-4 can substantially accelerate or assist tasks such as coding, drafting, summarizing, and problem solving, including passing simulated LeetCode interview assessments. The evidence is anecdotal and benchmark-like rather than experimental, but the examples suggest meaningful productivity gains in content generation and programming workflows.
finding.measure: Task completion on coding/interview-style prompts and general generation efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of how Artificial Intelligence can be integrated into education, with emphasis on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. It is motivated by the rapid emergence of tools such as ChatGPT and by concerns that students and teachers may use them uncritically, misunderstand their limitations, or be unable to distinguish legitimate assistance from unethical substitution of student work.

The article draws on the author’s experience at a Swiss University of Applied Sciences, informal discussions with students and staff, and a narrative literature review. It describes the institution’s approach to AI guidelines for academic writing, including transparency requirements for documenting model use, how outputs were evaluated, and where AI was used in a manuscript. The paper then expands to broader suggestions for fostering an AI culture in higher education, such as workshops, regular updates, dedicated budgets, and paid expert positions.

A substantial portion of the paper argues that AI literacy should become a core educational skill, alongside prompt engineering and critical thinking, and outlines subcomponents of AI literacy and several prompting methods (e.g., zero-shot, chain-of-thought, self-consistency, tree-of-thought). The main conclusion is not that AI improves a particular measured outcome, but that schools and universities should proactively teach responsible, critical, and transparent AI use rather than banning or ignoring the technology.

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes that institutions can improve responsible AI use by implementing AI guidelines, workshops, regular updates, dedicated budgets, and paid expert roles. However, this is a conceptual recommendation based on a case discussion at one Swiss university and narrative literature review, not an empirical estimate of institutional change.
finding.measure: Institutional policy/guideline development and implementation recommendations

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking are key durable skills for modern education, and that prompt-engineering practice can help students evaluate AI outputs more critically. No direct student outcome data, sample size, or effect size is reported; the claim is theoretical and literature-based.
finding.measure: Critical thinking and AI literacy development

finding.finding_summary: The article suggests AI tools may help teachers create curricula, case studies, and classroom materials more efficiently, and may reduce some instructional planning burden when used as a sparring partner. These are illustrative examples and recommendations rather than tested productivity outcomes, so no effect size or sample size is reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload and curriculum/planning efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Photons = Tokens: The Physics of AI and the Economics of Knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper develops a conceptual and quantitative framework for thinking about the economics of large language model computation. It treats tokens as a physical quantity with thermodynamic cost and uses Landauer’s principle, Shannon capacity, and infrastructure data to estimate the supply, demand, and energy requirements of global AI token production.

The paper is not an educational intervention study. Instead, it analyzes the AI value chain from hardware to queries, arguing that token abundance does not eliminate constraints on agency, judgment, or the economic scarcity of worthwhile questions. It also derives a finite question budget under projected energy scenarios and discusses how value concentrates in the AI stack through transaction costs, Coasean firm boundaries, and durable-goods competition.

The paper is purely theoretical and policy/economics oriented, using arithmetic, illustrative calculations, and cited secondary data rather than original human-subject data. It does not study students, educators, or any K-12 educational outcome, and it contains no subgroup evidence relevant to generative AI math tutoring or special populations.

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: K-12 and higher education (general education contexts; not an empirical sample study)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper asks how large language models such as ChatGPT might be used in education and what risks and governance challenges they introduce. Rather than testing an intervention, it synthesizes early examples and research to outline possible educational applications for learners and teachers, including content generation, feedback, assessment support, tutoring, and personalized practice across school and postsecondary contexts.

The paper emphasizes that LLMs could support reading, writing, problem solving, language learning, and some mathematics-related activities, but only if used with caution. It argues that educational use requires strong human oversight, critical-thinking instruction, fact-checking strategies, privacy and security safeguards, bias mitigation, and policies to prevent misuse, overreliance, and inequitable access. The article is primarily conceptual and forward-looking, not an empirical evaluation of student outcomes or implementation effects.

For the K-12 context, the paper is best understood as a high-level review and position statement about responsible integration of generative AI into teaching and learning. It cites prior work suggesting possible uses in tutoring, quiz generation, and feedback, but it does not report original data on delayed retention, independent performance after AI removal, dosage, or teacher mediation in mathematics tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: This paper does not report an empirical test of AI mathematics tutoring outcomes; it only discusses mathematics as a potential application area for large language models. The discussion is conceptual and cites prior work on generating math word problems or practice problems, but provides no measured effect on math achievement, retention, or independent performance.
finding.measure: not_reported

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that large language models could reduce teacher workload by automating or semi-automating tasks such as quiz generation, feedback, lesson planning, and assessment. However, these are proposed benefits drawn from illustrative examples and cited studies, not original empirical findings from this paper.
finding.measure: teacher workload / task efficiency (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The central contribution is a set of governance, ethical, and implementation recommendations for integrating large language models into education responsibly. The paper emphasizes the need for human oversight, privacy and security controls, bias mitigation, transparent policies, and institutional strategies to address plagiarism, fairness, and access.
finding.measure: policy, governance, ethical and institutional implementation considerations

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs may support critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking when used as scaffolds, but also warns they may undermine these skills if learners over-rely on model output. No original data are reported; the finding is a conceptual balance of potential benefits and risks.
finding.measure: critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking (conceptual discussion)

finding.finding_summary: The paper states that LLMs may improve engagement, interaction, and curiosity in learning, and could support learners who experience anxiety or low willingness to communicate. These claims are descriptive and based on cited examples rather than new empirical data in this paper.
finding.measure: engagement, curiosity, willingness to communicate (conceptual discussion)

paper_profiles.title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) encode clinical knowledge and can answer medical questions accurately, safely, and helpfully. The authors construct MultiMedQA, a benchmark combining six existing medical question-answering datasets and a new consumer-health dataset (HealthSearchQA), and test PaLM, Flan-PaLM, and an instruction prompt-tuned variant, Med-PaLM, on multiple-choice and long-form medical question answering tasks.

The study examines both automated accuracy and human judgments from clinicians and lay users. On multiple-choice benchmarks, Flan-PaLM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, including 67.6% on MedQA, but human evaluation shows important gaps in scientific grounding, omitted content, inappropriate content, harm, and bias. Instruction prompt tuning substantially improves long-form answer quality for Med-PaLM, bringing performance closer to clinician responses on several axes, though it remains inferior to clinicians overall.

The paper’s main conclusion is that scale and instruction tuning improve medical question answering, but they do not by themselves make LLMs safe or clinician-level for real-world medical use. The authors argue that future medical LLMs need stronger grounding in authoritative sources, uncertainty communication, and guardrails to mitigate harm and over-reliance. This paper is about medical AI rather than K-12 education, so it does not provide direct evidence on tutoring, retention, or mathematics learning in school settings.

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.population: Not reported; broad education audience (primarily secondary and higher education examples)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is an opinion/review-style article that argues AI in education has a dual character: it can enhance learning through personalization and efficiency, but it can also erode memory, critical thinking, creativity, and motivation through cognitive offloading and overreliance. The authors frame the discussion using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory to explain why AI can reduce extraneous load while also weakening germane processing, autonomy, and deep learning.

Rather than reporting a new empirical study, the paper synthesizes prior literature and illustrative findings on AI-supported learning, including chatbot use, adaptive learning systems, and AI tutoring. It emphasizes the importance of keeping human instruction, reflection, AI-free practice, and source verification in the loop so that AI supports rather than replaces active cognition.

The article’s practical contribution is a conceptual implementation roadmap for blended learning: conduct needs analysis, choose AI tools that promote engagement rather than dependency, balance AI use with teacher-led guidance, and monitor student outcomes over time. It concludes that responsible AI integration should maximize personalization while safeguarding memory retention, independent problem-solving, and learner autonomy.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI tutoring and adaptive learning can improve access, personalization, and performance on standardized tests, but it does not present a new controlled study. It cites an example of a Stanford-related report suggesting a 15% score increase with AI platforms, while also noting evidence that ChatGPT practice can worsen conceptual understanding (17% lower concept-understanding test scores in a cited study).
finding.measure: Standardized test scores and concept-understanding test performance (cited studies)

finding.finding_summary: The article synthesizes evidence and theory indicating that AI can support competence through customized learning, but overdependence may reduce autonomy and motivation. It does not report a new experiment; instead, it argues that excessive AI reliance can lower intrinsic motivation and engagement, and recommends teacher mediation, gamified challenges, and self-directed tasks to preserve these outcomes.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, autonomy, and relatedness (theoretical discussion plus cited literature)

finding.finding_summary: A central claim of the paper is that AI can support lower-order tasks but may erode durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and independent reasoning if students over-rely on it. The article cites prior studies on memory retention, critical thinking concerns, and divergent thinking, but provides no original sample or effect estimate itself.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, recall, and creative/divergent thinking (cited evidence and conceptual synthesis)

finding.finding_summary: The paper emphasizes implementation, governance, transparency, and fairness in AI adoption, arguing that institutions should use AI only with monitoring, feedback, explainability, and bias mitigation. Its findings are conceptual rather than empirical, but it substantively addresses how schools and policymakers should structure AI integration to avoid dependency and inequity.
finding.measure: Implementation roadmap, transparency, fairness, and monitoring practices

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT: Bullshit spewer or the end of traditional assessments in higher education?
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article examines ChatGPT and its implications for higher education assessment, teaching, and learning. The authors ask whether ChatGPT represents a major disruption to conventional student assessment, especially essay-based assignments, and whether it should be treated as part of the broader field of Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIEd).

The paper is primarily a desktop analysis and literature review, supplemented by informal experimentation with ChatGPT. The authors describe ChatGPT’s functionality, strengths, and limitations, then situate it within established AIEd categories: student-facing, teacher-facing, and system-facing applications. They discuss AI-powered writing tools, automated essay scoring, feedback systems, and the possibility that ChatGPT could be used for student learning support as well as for academic misconduct.

The article is not an empirical evaluation of an intervention in a student sample; instead, it offers a conceptual and practical review focused on higher education. Its main conclusion is that ChatGPT is powerful but limited, especially in factual accuracy and higher-order reasoning, and that educators should adapt assessment practices rather than assume the tool can simply be banned. The authors recommend more innovative assessments, greater teacher use of AI-supported feedback, and institutional policies to manage both the risks and opportunities of generative AI.

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports informal experiments showing that ChatGPT could quickly generate a short essay in response to a prompt, but the output was generic, lacked depth, and did not reliably include accurate citations. The authors conclude that ChatGPT can support conceptual explanations and drafting, but is weak for critical/analytical writing tasks.
finding.measure: Informal output quality of generated essays and writing responses

finding.finding_summary: In the authors' informal testing, ChatGPT performed better on explanation and routine prompting than on higher-order thinking tasks such as critical and analytical writing. The paper argues this indicates some utility for idea generation and support, but not robust support for deep reasoning or originality.
finding.measure: Ability to generate critical/analytical versus descriptive text in response to prompts

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests ChatGPT can increase efficiency by producing responses, explanations, and draft text quickly, often within 60-120 seconds. It is also discussed as a tool that may reduce instructor workload through AI-assisted feedback, assessment, and writing support, although these claims are conceptual rather than experimentally tested.
finding.measure: Speed of response generation; conceptual discussion of teacher workload reduction

finding.finding_summary: The article argues that ChatGPT has significant implications for assessment policy, academic integrity, and institutional responses in higher education. The authors suggest that institutions will need to revise assessment design, plagiarism policies, and guidance for AI use, but they do not present quantitative institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Conceptual analysis of implications for assessment, plagiarism detection, and institutional policy

paper_profiles.title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
paper_profiles.venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper is a conceptual discussion of how artificial intelligence, especially large language models such as ChatGPT, should be integrated into education. Rather than testing an intervention experimentally, it argues that successful AI use in classrooms depends on three complementary capacities: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. The paper is motivated by the rapid emergence of generative AI in higher education and by concerns that students and teachers may use these tools uncritically, misunderstand their limits, or rely on them in ways that undermine learning and academic integrity.

The paper combines informal observations and discussions from a Swiss University of Applied Sciences with a narrative literature review. It describes the institution’s attempt to establish AI guidelines requiring transparency about model use, purpose, and critical evaluation, and it outlines practical recommendations such as workshops, regular updates, dedicated budgets, and paid staff positions to support responsible AI adoption. It also reviews common classroom uses of AI and provides a conceptual framework for AI literacy and prompt engineering methods, including zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, expert prompting, self-consistency, automatic prompt engineering, generated knowledge prompting, and tree-of-thought prompting.

The main conclusion is that simple prohibitions or unrestricted access are both inadequate. Instead, institutions should build a broader culture of AI use that teaches students and educators how to interact with AI responsibly, critically evaluate outputs, and document use transparently. The paper emphasizes higher education, though it suggests the ideas may also be useful more broadly.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that prompt engineering and AI literacy can strengthen critical thinking by requiring students to evaluate AI outputs, compare alternatives, and verify claims. No empirical effect size is reported because this is a conceptual and narrative review paper, not a controlled study.
finding.measure: Critical thinking / prompt-engineering skill development discussed conceptually

finding.finding_summary: The paper proposes and describes institutional AI guidelines at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences, including required transparency about AI use, critical review, and documentation in appendices. The finding is qualitative/conceptual: the paper argues that a middle-ground governance approach is preferable to banning or fully unrestricted use, but it does not report quantitative institutional outcome data.
finding.measure: Institutional AI policy / guidelines implementation

finding.finding_summary: The paper claims AI tools can improve efficiency for teachers by helping with curriculum construction, case study generation, and other classroom preparation tasks. However, it also notes that prompting can be time-consuming and that benefits depend on staff expertise; no empirical productivity measures are reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / curriculum preparation efficiency

paper_profiles.title: Sparks of Artificial General Intelligence: Early experiments with GPT-4
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper presents a set of qualitative demonstrations of an early, text-only version of GPT-4, aiming to explore whether the model exhibits broad, general intelligence across many domains. The authors do not run a controlled experiment; instead, they use curated prompts and human judgment to probe GPT-4’s abilities in language, coding, mathematics, vision-like tasks via text, tool use, and reasoning about humans. The paper emphasizes both strengths and limitations, arguing that GPT-4 represents a significant step toward artificial general intelligence while still making errors and displaying biases.

A substantial portion of the paper focuses on mathematics and interdisciplinary composition. The authors show examples of GPT-4 solving high-school-level math problems, generating proofs in poetic or Shakespearean style, and handling transformed TikZ code, but they also note persistent weaknesses such as arithmetic mistakes, lack of planning, and hallucinations. These are demonstrations rather than educational interventions, and the paper does not study learners, classrooms, or tutoring implementation.

Because the paper is about model capability characterization rather than K-12 instruction, the direct relevance to education is limited. It offers examples that may be informative for future AI-in-education design, including math support and tool use, but it provides no evidence on student learning, retention, dosage, teacher mediation, guardrails, or classroom outcomes.

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 successfully solved several math prompts, including a high-school-level inverse-function problem yielding f(f(f(6))) = 4, and it produced mathematically correct proofs and reasoning in many examples. However, the authors also report that the model still makes basic arithmetic mistakes and struggles with some reasoning and planning tasks, so the overall mathematical performance is strong but inconsistent.
finding.measure: Performance on curated mathematical reasoning prompts and illustrative math tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper directly frames GPT-4 as showing reasoning, planning, abstraction, and flexible transfer across tasks, especially in its ability to adapt proofs and solutions across styles and contexts. At the same time, the authors explicitly note limitations in planning and coherence, particularly in arithmetic and text-generation tasks, so the evidence is positive but qualified.
finding.measure: Qualitative demonstrations of reasoning, planning, abstraction, and task transfer

finding.finding_summary: GPT-4 was shown generating and manipulating interdisciplinary content that combined mathematics, literature, programming, history, and art, such as Shakespearean proofs and a Gandhi-authored letter supporting a subatomic particle candidate. These demonstrations suggest broad cross-domain composition ability, but they are not evaluated with standardized educational measures.
finding.measure: Qualitative cross-domain generation and composition tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that GPT-4 can assist with coding and tool use, including producing code, debugging transformed code, and passing mock coding interviews quickly. The authors argue these capabilities could be important for real-world applications and productivity, though they do not measure teacher or student workload directly.
finding.measure: Qualitative coding tasks, mock technical interviews, and tool-use demonstrations

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (review article; broad education context, not a specific K-12 sample)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This review article surveys the emergence of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. The paper asks how these tools may transform teaching and learning, what educational benefits they may offer, and what ethical and practical challenges arise when integrating them into instructional settings.

Rather than evaluating a single intervention, the authors synthesize prior literature on AI technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, chatbots, adaptive learning systems, automated grading, and learning analytics. They discuss claimed benefits including personalized learning, instant feedback, increased motivation, reduced teacher workload, and support for assessment and administration, while also noting risks such as bias, privacy concerns, over-reliance, and the need for teacher training and oversight.

The context is broad and cross-sectoral, but the discussion repeatedly references K-12 and higher education examples. The article concludes that AI and ChatGPT have promise for improving individualized instruction and educational efficiency, but responsible implementation requires ethical safeguards, teacher preparation, and continued research. Because it is a narrative review, it does not report original empirical findings or effect sizes.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI tools, including chatbots and automated grading systems, can reduce teacher workload by handling repetitive tasks such as scoring, feedback, and answering routine questions. However, this is a synthesis of prior claims rather than a new empirical estimate, and the paper reports no study-specific effect sizes or sample sizes.
finding.measure: Teacher workload / administrative task reduction

finding.finding_summary: The paper summarizes prior literature suggesting that AI-supported learning can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety. These outcomes are discussed at a conceptual and literature-review level, without a single pooled estimate or original sample reported in this article.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, confidence, anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The review describes AI-enabled personalized instruction, feedback, and tutoring as potentially improving learning outcomes across subjects, but it does not present original evidence for any specific academic domain in this paper. No effect sizes, sample sizes, or domain-specific achievement measures are reported here.
finding.measure: General learning outcomes / academic performance

finding.finding_summary: A central theme is that AI adoption in education raises governance, ethics, privacy, bias, and teacher-preparation issues, implying institutional benefits and risks. The paper provides a narrative discussion of policy and implementation concerns rather than empirical institutional outcomes.
finding.measure: Ethical, policy, and implementation considerations

paper_profiles.title: ChatGPT for Good? On Opportunities and Challenges of Large Language Models for Education
paper_profiles.population: All grade levels (K-12, tertiary, and professional development)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This position paper examines the potential opportunities and challenges of large language models (LLMs), especially ChatGPT, for education. Rather than testing a specific intervention, the paper synthesizes early applications and presents a conceptual analysis of how LLMs may support learning, teaching, assessment, and educational innovation while also introducing substantial risks. The authors frame the technology as promising but immature, emphasizing the need for careful pedagogical integration.

The paper discusses examples across learner and teacher contexts, including personalized practice, quiz generation, feedback, lesson planning, assessment support, and conversational tutoring. It highlights use cases for elementary through higher education, but it does not report original data or an empirical evaluation. The discussion is especially strong on risks and guardrails: bias, privacy, copyright, overreliance, difficulty distinguishing AI-generated from student work, and the need for human oversight, fact-checking, and curriculum design that promotes critical thinking.

Overall, the paper concludes that LLMs could improve educational efficiency and expand learning opportunities if used responsibly, but that their integration must be accompanied by teacher mediation, governance, and technical and ethical safeguards. The paper is a broad conceptual review and recommendation document rather than an outcomes study, so it does not provide evidence about durability, retention, or independent performance after AI removal.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that LLMs can reduce teacher workload by semi-automating lesson planning, quiz generation, feedback, grading, and content creation. However, this is presented as a conceptual claim supported by cited examples rather than original empirical evidence; no study-level effect sizes or samples are reported.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading effort, content-generation efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper repeatedly emphasizes that LLMs could support critical thinking, problem-solving, and fact-checking when used as a complementary tool, but that they also risk increasing reliance, laziness, and reduced independent reasoning. These claims are normative and synthesized from prior work; no empirical effect sizes or sample sizes are reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, fact-checking, independent reasoning

finding.finding_summary: The paper suggests that LLMs may increase student engagement, curiosity, and participation, and may reduce anxiety in some language-learning contexts. These are discussed as potential benefits across cited studies, but the position paper itself does not present direct empirical evidence or quantitative estimates.
finding.measure: Engagement, curiosity, participation, learning anxiety

finding.finding_summary: A major focus of the paper is institutional governance: privacy, security, copyright, fairness, transparency, human oversight, sustainability, and policies for responsible adoption. The authors argue these issues are central to whether schools and educational systems can safely integrate LLMs, but no empirical institution-level outcomes are reported.
finding.measure: Policy, governance, privacy/security, fairness, sustainable adoption

paper_profiles.title: How Does ChatGPT Perform on the United States Medical Licensing Examination (USMLE)? The Implications of Large Language Models for Medical Education and Knowledge Assessment
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can answer medical licensing exam questions at a level relevant to medical education and knowledge assessment. The authors test ChatGPT on four multiple-choice question sets spanning USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 content: two AMBOSS subsets (100 questions each) and two NBME Free 120 sets (87 Step 1 questions and 102 Step 2 questions after filtering out image/table items). They compare ChatGPT’s performance with GPT-3 and InstructGPT and also qualitatively assess the model’s responses for logical reasoning and the use of internal and external information.

The study is not an intervention study with learners; rather, it is an in silico evaluation of a generative AI model as an educational tool. ChatGPT achieved 44% on AMBOSS-Step1, 42% on AMBOSS-Step2, 64.4% on NBME-Free-Step1, and 57.8% on NBME-Free-Step2. Performance decreased with higher question difficulty on AMBOSS-Step1, and the inclusion of AMBOSS Attending Tips improved performance percentile ranks. Qualitatively, ChatGPT always provided some logical justification, usually incorporated information from the question stem, and correct answers more often included external information than incorrect answers. The authors conclude that ChatGPT may be useful as an interactive medical education tool, but they also note that its accuracy is uneven and that further research is needed to evaluate educational uses such as small-group learning and reflective practice.

finding.finding_summary: ChatGPT’s performance on medical knowledge multiple-choice questions was mixed across datasets: 44% correct on AMBOSS-Step1 (n=100), 42% on AMBOSS-Step2 (n=100), 64.4% on NBME-Free-Step1 (n=87), and 57.8% on NBME-Free-Step2 (n=102). The model did better on NBME than AMBOSS questions, and performance dropped as difficulty increased on AMBOSS-Step1 (P=.01), reaching 0% accuracy on the hardest questions in that subset.
finding.measure: Accuracy on USMLE-aligned multiple-choice medical knowledge questions

finding.finding_summary: The paper qualitatively assessed whether ChatGPT provided logical reasoning and explanatory context in its answers, a proxy for interpretability and support for reasoning-oriented study. ChatGPT gave a logical explanation in 100% of outputs on the NBME datasets, used internal information in 96.8% of all responses (183/189), and correct answers included external information more often than incorrect answers (92.9% vs 48.4% on NBME-Free-Step1; 89.8% vs 62.8% on NBME-Free-Step2).
finding.measure: Presence of logical reasoning, internal information, and external information in model responses
finding.study_size: n=189 NBME responses; n=87 Step1 and n=102 Step2

paper_profiles.title: The cognitive paradox of AI in education: between enhancement and erosion
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This opinion paper argues that artificial intelligence in education can function as both a cognitive enhancer and a source of cognitive erosion. Using Cognitive Load Theory, Bloom’s Taxonomy, and Self-Determination Theory as interpretive lenses, the authors discuss how AI may support personalized learning, efficiency, and accessibility while also risking overreliance, reduced active recall, weaker retention, diminished critical thinking, and lower motivation.

The paper is not an empirical study of a specific K-12 intervention; instead, it synthesizes prior studies and examples across higher education and general education contexts to propose an implementation roadmap for responsible AI use. The recommended approach emphasizes balanced integration, teacher-mediated use, reflection points, AI-free solving sessions, source verification, and monitoring/feedback so that AI supplements rather than replaces human instruction.

The article’s main conclusion is that AI should be designed and implemented to preserve intellectual autonomy, deep learning, and motivation. It warns that excessive dependence on AI can encourage cognitive offloading and passive learning, and it calls for pedagogically informed guardrails, transparency, and equity-minded design. Although the paper mentions math tutoring in passing, it does not present original K-12 mathematics data or delayed-retention findings.

finding.finding_summary: The paper argues that AI can improve engagement and motivation through personalization and interactive support, but excessive dependence may reduce intrinsic motivation, autonomy, and relatedness. No new empirical effect size is reported; the discussion is based on cited prior studies and theory rather than original data.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, autonomy, relatedness (theoretical and cited evidence)

finding.finding_summary: The paper centrally focuses on durable skills such as critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, and independent reasoning. It argues that AI can support lower-order cognitive tasks but may weaken higher-order thinking if students over-rely on AI-generated answers; no original sample, effect size, or confidence interval is reported.
finding.measure: Critical thinking, problem-solving, metacognition, independent reasoning (theoretical and cited evidence)

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses AI applications in STEM and language learning generally, including a cited example that AI tutoring increased standardized test performance by 15% in one external source but could also reduce conceptual understanding. The article itself does not conduct a mathematics study or report original academic outcome data.
finding.measure: Standardized test performance; concept understanding; STEM learning (cited examples)

paper_profiles.title: Revolutionizing education with AI: Exploring the transformative potential of ChatGPT
paper_profiles.population: Not applicable (review article; discusses education broadly, including K-12 and higher education examples)
paper_profiles.extended_summary:
This article is a narrative review of artificial intelligence in education, with a particular emphasis on chatbots and ChatGPT. The paper asks what AI tools can do for teaching and learning, what risks and ethical concerns they introduce, and how they might be integrated responsibly into educational settings.

Rather than testing an intervention, the authors synthesize prior literature on AI technologies such as intelligent tutoring systems, automated grading, adaptive learning platforms, and conversational agents. They describe potential uses for students, teachers, and administrators, including personalized instruction, instant feedback, engagement, assessment support, and workload reduction. The paper also highlights concerns about bias, privacy, reliability, academic integrity, over-reliance, and the need for teacher training and supervision.

The discussion is broad and cross-sector, drawing examples from K-12, higher education, and other settings. The main conclusion is that ChatGPT and related AI tools may be educationally valuable, but their successful use depends on responsible design, teacher preparation, ethical safeguards, and alignment with pedagogy rather than technology adoption alone.

finding.finding_summary: The review argues that AI tools, including chatbots and automated grading systems, can reduce repetitive administrative work for educators by evaluating assignments, scoring responses, and providing feedback. The paper does not report new empirical data, but it cites prior studies suggesting that these systems can save teachers substantial time and support lesson planning and student assistance.
finding.measure: Teacher workload, grading/scoring efficiency, and feedback automation

finding.finding_summary: The article emphasizes institutional-level implications of AI adoption, including ethics, privacy, bias, academic integrity, and the need for teacher preparation and policy support. It argues that successful integration requires supervision, maintenance, and governance rather than simple deployment of the technology.
finding.measure: Ethical, policy, and institutional considerations for AI adoption in education

finding.finding_summary: The review states that AI-supported learning can increase student motivation, engagement, confidence, and reduce anxiety, citing prior studies rather than presenting original data. It presents these effects as potential benefits of personalized feedback and interactive learning environments.
finding.measure: Motivation, engagement, confidence, and anxiety

finding.finding_summary: The paper discusses general academic benefits of AI across subjects, including improved learning outcomes, personalized instruction, and instant feedback. Because it is a broad review rather than a subject-specific study, the finding is best characterized as general academic performance improvement rather than a direct test of a particular content area.
finding.measure: General academic performance and learning outcomes
